Authors: Xia X.; Yuruk N.; Wang Y.; Zhai X.
Title: Using Learning Progressions to Guide AI Feedback for Science Learning
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers scalable support for formative feedback, yet most AI-generated feedback relies on task-specific rubrics authored by domain experts. While effective, rubric authoring is time-consuming and limits scalability across instructional contexts. Learning progressions (LP) provide a theoretically grounded representation of students’ developing understanding and may offer an alternative solution. This study examines whether an LP–driven rubric generation pipeline can produce AI-generated feedback comparable in quality to feedback guided by expert-authored task rubrics. We analyzed AI-generated feedback for written scientific explanations produced by 207 middle school students in a chemistry task. Two pipelines were compared: (a) feedback guided by a human expert–designed, task-specific rubric, and (b) feedback guided by a task-specific rubric automatically derived from a learning progression prior to grading and feedback generation. Two human coders evaluated feedback quality using a multi-dimensional rubric assessing Clarity, Accuracy, Relevance, Engagement and Motivation, and Reflectiveness (10 sub-dimensions). Inter-rater reliability was high, with percent agreement ranging from 89% to 100% and Cohen’s κ values for estimable dimensions (κ =.66–.88). Paired t-tests revealed no statistically significant differences between the two pipelines for Clarity (t1 = 0.00, p1 = 1.000; t2 = 0.84, p2 =.399), Relevance (t1 = 0.28, p1 =.782; t2 = -0.58, p2 =.565), Engagement and Motivation (t1 = 0.50, p1 =.618; t2 = -0.58, p2 =.565), or Reflectiveness (t = -0.45, p =.656). These findings suggest that the LP–driven rubric pipeline can serve as an alternative solution. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: GenAI for Cognitive Accessibility: Plain Language
Abstract: This STS brings together six contributions addressing two complementary challenges: the generation of cognitively accessible text through Large Language Model (LLM)-based approaches, and the design of GenAI interfaces that are usable by people with intellectual disabilities. This paper provides an overview of the session’s contributions, highlights cross-cutting themes, and situates them within the broader context of cognitive accessibility research and responsible AI human-centred AI. Together, these works reflect an emerging research agenda at the intersection of NLP, HCI, accessibility, and responsible AI design. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Karidi T.; Amir O.; Roll I.
Title: AI in the Wild: A Large Scale Analysis of Authentic Interactions of College Students with Generative AI
Abstract: Generative AI tools (GenAI) are increasingly used by students during coursework, yet empirical understanding of how students engage with these systems in authentic learning contexts remains limited. Existing studies have largely relied on controlled settings, single-domain analyses, or small-scale qualitative data, leaving open how student-AI interaction unfolds across courses and forms of academic work. We present a large-scale analysis of naturally occurring student-AI interactions collected from undergraduate students across multiple university courses and academic domains. The dataset comprises over 15,000 student-AI interaction units drawn from voluntary use of generative AI during real coursework. To characterize these interactions, we analyze each student turn along two complementary dimensions, cognitive intent and interaction context, capturing whether requests are directed toward the task or domain, the student’s own work, or prior AI output. Using instruction-guided annotation applied at scale, we examine how these interaction patterns are distributed overall and how they vary across courses. Our analysis reveals that student-AI interaction is highly structured. Across courses, interactions concentrate in a small number of recurring patterns rather than exhibiting highly idiosyncratic use. At the same time, systematic differences emerge across courses, giving rise to distinct interaction profiles associated with different forms of academic work. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Development of a Serious Video Game for Pattern Detection in Emotional Behavior
Abstract: Early detection of emotional and motivational alterations is crucial to prevent the chronic progression of affective disorders in adolescents and young adults. This work presents the design, implementation, and preliminary validation of a serious mobile videogame aimed at detecting behavioral patterns associated with emotional vulnerability. The game is grounded in Optimal Foraging Theory, specifically Charnov’s Marginal Value Theorem, and models decision-making processes related to effort–reward trade-offs. Players interact with a patch-leaving task in which they must decide when to abandon a resource node under energetic and temporal constraints. Behavioral metrics such as abandonment thresholds, effort sensitivity, exploration patterns, and decision-making under uncertainty are recorded through a client–server architecture based on Unity, Spring Boot, and PostgreSQL. A qualitative validation was conducted through semi-structured interviews with Product Owners, structured according to established user experience frameworks (SUS, AttrakDiff, meCUE). Results indicate strong conceptual alignment with the initial computational framework, intuitive interaction design, and perceived motivational potential. Overall, findings suggest that the proposed system constitutes a promising tool for computational psychiatry, enabling objective, longitudinal assessment of motivational dynamics prior to clinical validation with end users. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: AN AI-Powered Exoskeleton for Upper-Limb Rehabilitation
Abstract: Shoulder tendinitis is a pathological condition that has a profound affects the quality of life of those who suffer from it. Active rehabilitation processes can improve the well-being in patients with this condition. This study developed a rehabilitation support system for such patients, based on a shoulder exoskeleton adaptable to the user’s anatomy. The system comprises three motors enabling flexion, extension, adduction, and abduction of the upper limbs. The structure accommodates different anthropometric measurements through adjustable segments and joints. The system incorporates a shoulder orthosis. This is equipped with myoelectric sensors and electrical stimulators to measure muscle activity. To personalize rehabilitation, an artificial intelligence application was incorporated. A gyroscope and accelerometer capture shoulder kinematic data, which are used to train a Random Forest model that determines exercise parameters, such as session duration and joint angle ranges for arm movements. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Determinants of Chatbot Adoption and Satisfaction: Drivers and Barriers
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed customer service environments, with chatbots emerging as key tools for improving efficiency, responsiveness and personalization. Despite their growing adoption across sectors such as retail, finance, healthcare and education, uncertainty persists regarding how users perceive these systems and which factors shape their satisfaction. Existing research points to clear advantages of chatbots but also highlights limitations related to trust, empathy and the handling of complex interactions.​ This paper examines how AI-based chatbots influence user satisfaction in customer service contexts and identifies the interactional factors that most strongly shape users’ evaluations. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey was conducted using a questionnaire that explored perceived interaction quality, trust in AI systems, social presence, usefulness, responsiveness and limitations experienced during automated service. Statistical analysis was used to identify relationships between chatbot use, user satisfaction and the variables contributing most strongly to positive or negative evaluations.​ The results show that although most respondents had previous experience with chatbots, their assessments varied across performance dimensions. Ease of use received the most favourable ratings, while problem resolution showed the greatest variability, suggesting that chatbots remain more effective for simple requests than for complex issues. Trust and clarity of information were generally positive but displayed substantial dispersion, reflecting heterogeneous user experiences. More than half of users required human assistance after chatbot interaction, and barriers such as lack of need, privacy concerns and perceived inconsistencies were frequently reported. Despite these challenges, overall satisfaction and recommendation levels were positive, indicating that effectiveness in resolving issues is central to user acceptance. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Li Z.; Zhu X.; Li Z.; Li M.; Li C.; Yin X.; Xie Y.; Liu S.
Title: SA2Pat: enhancing binary security patch function localization via security advisory-guided LLMs
Abstract: In modern software supply chains, security patch function localization seeks to establish a precise correlation between a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry and the function in the codebase that contains its patch. Existing approaches predominantly rely on source code information. Thus, when security audits must be conducted directly on binary files, traditional source-code-based localization methods become ineffective. To address this gap, we propose SA2Pat (Security Advisory to Patch), a framework that accurately localizes security patches by learning from patterns in historical vulnerability fixes. SA2Pat first utilizes IDA Pro and BinDiff to identify pairs of modified functions between vulnerable and patched binaries. It then treats the security advisory text as a query to retrieve reference samples from a constructed external knowledge base containing historical vulnerability patches, thereby guiding a large language model (LLM) to locate the patched function. To mitigate the frequent absence of Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) IDs in security advisories, we employ a fine-tuned SecureBERT model to predict the likely CWE ID, ensuring that the input information remains complete. Experimental results on a dataset of 364 real-world CVEs—constructed by augmenting the PatchDiscovery benchmark with recent vulnerability patches—indicate that SA2Pat improves the F1-score by 19.35 percentage points over baseline methods. An ablation study shows that removing the reference samples decreases the F1-score by 16.6 percentage points, while removing CWE information reduces it by 4.8 percentage points, demonstrating that both components contribute critically to performance. When the oracle CWE is replaced by the SecureBERT classifier’s prediction in an end-to-end setting, SA2Pat still attains an F1-score of 70.8%, close to the 72.2% under oracle CWE. Moreover, SA2Pat remains effective across different LLM backbones. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: McConomy G.; Liu J.; Glass D.; Bond R.; Toner H.
Author full names: McConomy, Gareth (60740156400); Liu, Jun (55705952500); Glass, David (35431698000); Bond, Raymond (36019802200); Toner, Holly (60283748200)
Title: Bridging Causal Reasoning and Fuzzy Calibration for Trustworthy AI Risk Assessment
Abstract: When organisations deploy AI systems in high-stakes domains, they need risk assessments they can trust. Large language models offer a promising path to scalable assessment, but two problems undermine their reliability: shallow reasoning that flags risks without tracing causal mechanisms, and untuned aggregate output that sits systematically above cautious expert postures. We address both problems with a two-layer framework. Causal risk patterns structure the reasoning input: each pattern documents a known harm mechanism with its trigger conditions, causal steps, and empirical evidence. Ordered Weighted Averaging (OWA) calibrates the output by weighting multiple LLM assessments according to rank rather than source, systematically aligning aggregate output with a chosen expert calibration target. In experiments with three frontier LLMs assessing 125 case-pattern pairs across five real estate AI deployments, all models produced ratings sitting +0.07 to +0.16 above our expert target on a 0–1 scale. OWA aggregation calibrated to this target reduced mean absolute error by 7.7% at orness = 0.6 versus the best individual model (p = 0.023); we frame orness as a tunable governance-posture parameter that must be calibrated to context, not a universal constant. Our most surprising finding concerns a layer asymmetry: fuzzy aggregation at the output layer improves calibration, but fuzzy scaffolding at the reasoning layer degrades performance (34.8% error increase). This asymmetry, where LLMs reason better holistically than when forced into structured decomposition, has practical implications for anyone designing human-AI workflows. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Author full names: Minetaki, Kazunori (35322792700); Ting, I-Hsien (8717221100); Hsieh, Ming-Chia (55436431200)
Title: AI-Enabled Knowledge Extraction and Transformation: Comparative Case Studies from Taiwanese Firms
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being adopted not only as a tool for automation and prediction but also as a mechanism for extracting, codifying, and transferring organizational knowledge. This study examines how AI contributes to knowledge transformation in Taiwanese business contexts through a qualitative multiple-case-study design. Based on semi-structured interviews conducted in Taiwan in March 2026, the study analyzes three firms operating in different domains: manufacturing automation, industrial AI platforms, and labor/legal advisory services. The findings show that AI-enabled knowledge transformation does not occur in a uniform manner. Instead, firms differ in how they extract knowledge from operational processes, expert judgment, and legal or advisory experience, and in how such knowledge is codified into digital systems and reused through organizational infrastructures. Across the three cases, a common pattern can be identified in the progression from AI-enabled knowledge extraction to codification, infrastructure formation, and knowledge transfer. At the same time, each case highlights a different organizational function of AI: process replication, analytical support, and expert knowledge formalization. The study contributes to the literature by showing that AI in business should be understood not only as a productivity-enhancing technology but also as an organizational mechanism for transforming tacit and experience-based knowledge into reusable forms. It also offers practical implications for firms seeking to preserve expertise, strengthen learning, and build scalable knowledge systems through AI. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Investigating How Collaborative Conversational Agents Influence the Relationship of Affective and Cognitive Engagement in Student Dialogues
Abstract: Collaborative engagement is a dynamic process in which affective and cognitive states interact to shape group learning. Although collaborative conversational agents (CCAs) can support dialogue, prior research has typically examined affective and cognitive engagement separately, limiting insight into their temporal interplay. This study investigated how affective engagement and cognitive engagement co-evolve during collaborative tasks. In a within-subjects design, 18 undergraduate dyads completed two discussions: one without support and one with a CCA providing prompts based on the Academically Productive Talk framework. Results showed that CCA-supported discussions had higher proportions of neutral affect and statement-making, but lower positive affect. Sequence analyses revealed that with the CCA, engagement patterns were more stable and predictable, with frequent transitions between neutral and positive statements. In contrast, unsupported discussions showed greater variability. Learning performance did not differ between conditions, and engagement patterns were not associated with performance. These findings suggest that CCAs shape engagement dynamics despite no immediate performance gains. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A Data-Driven Framework for Cycle Path Quality: Integrating User Perception and Sensing
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for assessing the quality of cycle path design by integrating subjective and objective measures of user experience. The approach combines static infrastructure attributes, dynamic data from multiple sensors, and user-reported perceptions into synthetic indicators that predict service quality. Unlike traditional infrastructure evaluation methods, this research explicitly considers how users perceive and react to real-world cycling conditions, bridging gaps in current methodologies that often isolate technical measurements from behavioral responses. A segmentation-based graph model of the cycling network, enriched with contextual and environmental features, enables fine-grained data fusion and analysis. On-road trials with different user and vehicle profiles collect multi-source data (accelerometers, GPS, eye-tracking, biometric sensors), aligned in time and space to produce synthetic indicators. Predictive models, developed through both econometric and machine learning approaches, evaluate the relationship between objective indicators and subjective quality ratings. Preliminary results show the feasibility of integrating diverse datasets into a scalable framework capable of informing design, planning, and policy. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Assessment of the Current State of Urban Redevelopment Areas and Their Environmental Impacts: An Analysis to Support the Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA)
Abstract: In metropolitan areas that have encountered various transformation processes and have a complex urban history, there are often undeveloped or abandoned areas, a result of the rapid and continuous change in cities. For this reason, in urban redevelopment and planning processes, it is important to consider these spaces as potential areas for development and to start with them, as they represent urban voids that should be viewed as a key element in the creation of redevelopment strategies. In this context, the Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) procedure becomes mandatory in order to evaluate the environmental impact of transformation strategies. This study proposes a working framework to support the SEA in defining strategies and actions for the development of degraded areas. The method applied consists of two distinct phases. In the initial phase, an analysis of the present state of the territory was developed to assess the current situation, ongoing dynamics, and critical issues to be resolved. This analysis integrated SWOT analysis and Geographic Information System (GIS) tools. In the subsequent phase, the environmental impact of the proposed strategies was assessed. This assessment was based on the results of the initial analysis, and it was conducted by developing coaxial environmental impact matrices. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Human Oversight Is Not Neutral: How AI Grades Shape Human Grading Decisions
Abstract: As Large Language Models are increasingly used to support automatic grading of open-ended response questions, human oversight is commonly proposed as a safeguard to ensure fairness during the grading process. However, little empirical work has examined the practicality of such oversight. In this study, we investigate how exposure to AI grades could influence human graders’ effort, decisions, and grading outcomes. We conduct a within-subject study with 6 teaching assistants (TAs) grading open-ended responses under two conditions: grading from scratch and reviewing AI grades. Our results show that reviewing AI grades does not consistently reduce grading time. Exposure to AI output also increases TA-AI agreement, but this influence does not consistently lead to closer alignment with expert grades. A qualitative analysis of submissions indicates that disagreements between TA and AI frequently arises from ambiguous or partially correct student responses. Human graders also occasionally make errors despite being presented with a correct AI grade. Together, these findings suggest that human oversight in AI-based grading can be a demanding process rather than a simple and quick check. We further discuss implications for the design and deployment of AI-based grading workflows that better support effective human oversight. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Lin C.-J.
Title: Cognitive Apprenticeship AI Agent: A Pilot Study of Feedback Timing in Programming Learning
Abstract: Programming learning for novices is a complex cognitive activity involving problem analysis, logical reasoning, and error correction. Cognitive apprenticeship supports learning by externalizing expert thinking through modeling, coaching, and scaffolding; however, providing continuous and individualized support remains challenging in practice. With advances in generative artificial intelligence, AI agents offer new opportunities to deliver real-time and adaptive cognitive support. This pilot study developed a cognitive apprenticeship-based AI agent to examine the effects of feedback timing on programming learning. Using a quasi-experimental design, 26 novice learners were assigned to either formative or summative feedback conditions during a four-hour intervention. Outcomes included self-efficacy, cognitive load, and learning motivation. Results showed that formative feedback significantly reduced cognitive load, while no significant differences were found in self-efficacy or learning motivation. These findings suggest that feedback timing plays a critical role in cognitive processing, whereas affective outcomes may require longer-term interventions. This study highlights the potential of AI agents as process-oriented cognitive support mechanisms and provides preliminary evidence for designing AI-supported programming learning environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Students, AI, and the Future of Higher Education: A Scoping Review of Perceptions and Concerns
Abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education is transforming learning, teaching, and academic work, heightening the importance of understanding students’ perspectives as primary users of these technologies. This systematic scoping review synthesizes evidence from 56 peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and February 2025 on university students’ perceptions of AI applications in higher education. Following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, three key patterns emerged. First, much of the literature lacked strong theoretical grounding, relying predominantly on adoption-oriented models. Second, research has focused heavily on generative AI tools, particularly chatbots such as ChatGPT, with limited attention to other AI applications. Third, students reported both benefits and concerns: they viewed AI as supportive for writing, personalized learning, and collaboration, while also raising issues related to ethics, academic integrity, overdependence, and unequal access. Many students also noted insufficient institutional guidance, reducing their confidence in responsible engagement. Overall, this review consolidates current findings, identifies critical research gaps, and offers recommendations for future research, policy, and practice to support ethical and student-centered AI integration in higher education. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Ali F.; Yang Y.
Title: Curiosity, Prior Achievement, and Interaction Patterns: Heterogeneity of Generative AI Effects Uncovered by Causal Inference
Abstract: Research on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in education is rapidly expanding, yet little is known about how its effects differ across learners with varying levels of curiosity for learning and prior achievement. This gap is consequential, as GenAI tools may unwittingly impact learning inequalities. In addition, the interaction processes through which GenAI use influences achievement remain insufficiently understood. We addressed these gaps in an intervention study with 378 students in Grades 5–8. Students were randomly assigned to either regular instruction or to a classroom chatbot use over a two-week learning unit. Learning outcome was measured using a content-relevant written assessment administered without GenAI support. Using a causal inference framework that combined heterogeneous treatment effect estimation with causal mediation analysis via Monte Carlo-based g-computation, we found heterogeneity in both GenAI impacts and mediating mechanisms. Treatment effects and mediation by interaction patterns varied systematically by different types of curiosity and prior achievement, suggesting that GenAI-supported learning operates heterogeneously across different learner profiles. Our results suggest that GenAI use can worsen pre-existing inequalities with implications for pedagogy and equitable intervention design. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Gao J.; Zhang J.; Chen D.
Title: To Use or Not to Use: Investigating Student Perceptions of Faculty Generative AI Usage in Higher Education
Abstract: While Generative AI (GenAI) rapidly integrated into higher education, existing research has primarily focused on regulating student use. As a result, student perspectives on faculty adoption of GenAI remained unexplored. In this study, we analyzed survey responses from 156 undergraduate and graduate students to examine their attitudes toward both student and faculty use of GenAI. We classified students into four groups based on their attitudes, including GenAI Optimists, Student Support Group, Faculty Support Group, and Non-supporters. Findings show that 37% of participants do not support GenAI use by either students or faculty, while 31% support GenAI use in both contexts. We also conducted thematic analysis to understand participants’ concerns on faculty GenAI usage. Results revealed that (1) a majority of students (79%) questioned the validity and reliability of GenAI-generated responses, and (2) 37% of students feared that faculty overreliance on GenAI created a “futile cycle” that might reduce faculty critical thinking. Our findings showed that students expressed concerns about GenAI use by faculty in teaching and grading contexts, with pedagogical concerns being most prominent. These findings informed the future use of GenAI in teaching and learning in higher education. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment in Educational Video Games
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: Over the past two decades, educational video games have established themselves as an innovative tool for motivated and engaging learning, in which the player learns the didactic content with less effort and solves various learning tasks with increased interest. One way to improve the learner’s attention, engagement, and motivation is to use the dynamic adjustment of the difficulty of the gameplay and/or the learning content in these games, which is based on changes in certain characteristics of the player. The article presents an overview of player-centric dynamic difficulty adjustment methods in video games for educational purposes. It examines the approaches used for tailoring the difficulty of game tasks, in terms of what tasks in educational video games should have dynamically adapted difficulty, and what features of their execution are subject to dynamic changes. For this purpose, specific characteristics of the learning player appropriate for such adaptation are summarized. Also considered are possible implementations of the feedback loop, i.e., how these dynamic changes could happen, applying a positive, negative, or combined feedback based on the specificities of the player. Title: From Literature Evidence to Method Selection: A Two-Layer MCDA Framework for Project Alternative Evaluation in Public Procurement
Abstract: Multi-criteria decision-aiding (MCDA) methods are increasingly used in public procurement to compare project alternatives when evaluation depends on technical, environmental, social, and economic criteria. Yet method selection is often treated as a purely analytical matter, whereas in regulated procurement it is also constrained by requirements of transparency, ex ante definability, auditability, and effective competition. Building on prior review evidence on MCDA applications in public procurement, this paper proposes a two-layer framework for method selection. The first layer assesses normative compatibility, filtering out methods whose inferential structure is difficult to predefine, explain, or verify within award procedures. The second layer assesses methodological adequacy in relation to the decision problem, considering weighting needs, compensatory logic, uncertainty, criteria interdependence, and robustness of the final ranking. The framework is then translated into an operational selection matrix linking recurrent procurement settings to coherent method families and modular configurations. The contribution is both conceptual and practical: it shows that MCDA method choice in public procurement is not method-neutral, but a design decision at the intersection of decision theory, procurement regulation, and evaluation practice. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Tools, Teammates, or Threats? How Pedagogical Reasoning Shapes Novice Instructional Designers’ Judgments About AI in Education
Abstract: As generative AI becomes embedded in instructional design, understanding how novice designers reason about AI’s pedagogical implications is critical. This study examines how principle-based pedagogical reasoning and AI integration reasoning co-develop in 27 instructional design graduate students across four learning science modules. Students completed paired pre/post constructed responses scored on two analytic rubrics and two categorical codes capturing agency framing and locus of control. Both principle-based pedagogical reasoning (d=1.39) and AI integration reasoning (d=1.31) improved substantially, with AI integration gains more uniform across modules than principle-based gains. Principle-based pedagogical reasoning was significantly associated with AI integration reasoning, with positive cross-dimensional correlations across all rubric criteria. This indicates that the association extends beyond surface familiarity to recognition, strategy, and explanatory components. Students’ agency framings shifted significantly toward human-led conceptions, as “Human Leads + AI Supports” nearly doubled (11.5% to 20.6%) while “AI Threatens” decreased (8.7% to 3.7%). However, their perceived locus of control remained comparatively stable. These findings suggest that grounding in learning science principles supports more sophisticated reasoning about AI’s pedagogical role and more collaborative conceptions of human-AI partnership in instructional design. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Attention-Pruned SHAP: Accelerating SHAP-Based Explainability with Attention-Guided Feature Pruning
Abstract: Transformer-based models achieve strong predictive performance across natural language processing tasks but remain difficult to interpret. In sentiment analysis and other user-facing applications, understanding token-level contributions is essential for building trust and supporting model debugging. Perturbation-based methods such as SHAP provide theoretically grounded feature attributions; however, their computational cost grows rapidly with sentence length, making token-level explanations expensive in practice. We propose Attention-Pruned SHAP, a hybrid explanation method in which attention scores serve as a pre-filter, selecting a subset of candidate tokens on which SHAP is actually computed, assigning zero contribution to pruned tokens. We introduce fixed pruning strategies based on global top-k and top-p thresholds, as well as an adaptive, length-aware variant that adjusts pruning strength according to sentence length, preserving the perturbation-based semantics of SHAP while reducing the effective feature dimensionality. We evaluate raw attention, full KernelSHAP, and the proposed pruning variants on Arabic social media sentiment classification using both rank-based and distributional similarity metrics: Spearman rank correlation, cosine similarity, top-5 token overlap, and Jensen–Shannon divergence, alongside runtime measurements. Results show that the adaptive variant in particular achieves strong agreement with full KernelSHAP while meaningfully reducing computational cost, offering a practical path toward scalable token-level explainability in Transformer-based NLP. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: PLEISAR: Playful Experiences with Interactive Social Agents and Robots
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and social robotics are transforming how technology can support human well-being in everyday contexts beyond traditional clinical settings. Social interactive agents, including conversational agents, embodied virtual agents, and social robots, offer new opportunities to promote emotional balance, social connectedness, and inclusive participation across the lifespan. However, their deployment in real-world environments raises critical challenges related to affective sensitivity, transparency, ethical responsibility, and long-term user acceptance, particularly when interacting with vulnerable and intergenerational populations. This paper presents a coordinated research project that integrates three complementary subprojects developed by the University of Zaragoza, the University of the Balearic Islands, and a joint team from the University of Granada and the University of La Laguna. The project advances an interdisciplinary approach that combines affective and intergenerational interaction design, explainable and inclusive affective artificial intelligence, and playful, persuasive interventions validated in everyday contexts. Participatory and co-creation methodologies are employed to ensure alignment with users’ values and social realities. At the same time, explainable techniques are embedded as core design principles to foster trust, fairness, and accountability. Through real-world deployments in domestic, educational, and community settings, the project demonstrates how empathetic, transparent, and playful social interactive agents can enhance emotional well-being, social participation, and digital literacy. By articulating a coherent pipeline from affective perception to social impact, this work contributes methodological frameworks, empirical evidence, and design guidelines that support the responsible and sustainable integration of socially intelligent systems for human wellbeing. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: An Empirical Study of LLM-Generated Local Explanations for Linear Additive Models
Abstract: Post-hoc local explanations are widely used to improve the transparency of AI predictions. However, their reliability varies across methods and data settings. This study investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs), using structured prompting and in-context learning (ICL), can function as local explainers for tabular models and compares their performance with Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME). We introduce a reproducible benchmarking framework to evaluate explanation quality by assessing each method’s ability to recover instance-level ground-truth feature contributions from linear additive models. This serves as a sanity check of local explanation validity. We further examine the influence of key factors, including the number of numerical and categorical features and the number of in-context examples (shots). Faithfulness is evaluated using the Model-Intrinsic Additive Scores (MIAS) metric, while robustness is assessed through standard insertion–deletion metrics across multiple public tabular datasets. Empirical results indicate that LLM-based local explanations do not consistently recover instance-level ground-truth contributions. Title: The Effects of Task Similarity on Catastrophic Forgetting in Deep Residual Networks
Abstract: In the field of machine learning today, a large number of methods to mitigate catastrophic forgetting have emerged, such as replay-based methods and methods that restrict parameter updates, all of which have proven effective across a variety of tasks. However, most current methods in this field focus on algorithmic design and still lack a multidimensional, systematic analysis of the underlying optimization mechanisms of forgetting. This paper conducts a multidimensional analysis of catastrophic forgetting based on task similarity. We treat different classes in classification tasks as interrelated sub-tasks and design a single-class-targeted fine-tuning paradigm to quantify the impact of learning the target class on other classes. Building on this, we characterize inter-class relationships across three levels (representation, decision, and optimization) and construct similarity metrics based on feature representations, logits prediction distributions, and gradient directions, respectively. We conducted systematic experiments on the CIFAR-10 and SVHN datasets using the ResNet-18/50 architecture. The experimental results demonstrate a significant correlation between the multi-dimensional similarities we construct and class forgetting; conflicts in deep parameter weight overwriting caused by semantic coupling between classes are the core driver of differential forgetting. This study provides a foundational theoretical framework and a new analytical perspective for the design of anti-forgetting algorithms. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Adaptive Software Energy Feedback for Long-Term User Engagement
Abstract: Adaptive feedback strategies have shown their effectiveness in domains such as health, education, and residential energy, yet software energy feedback remains largely static and primarily oriented toward experts rather than end users. As a consequence, the long-term behavioral impact of adaptive feedback in software energy contexts is still poorly understood. This paper evaluates whether adaptive feedback strategies can sustain user compliance and energy savings in software usage under realistic behavioral dynamics. Using a simulation-based experimental methodology grounded in empirical effects such as fatigue, novelty decay, and preference drift, we compare adaptive and non-adaptive software energy feedback strategies across multiple scenarios. The results show that adaptive software energy feedback consistently outperforms static approaches, particularly under non-stationary user behavior, and reaches effective performance within a few weeks under cold-start constraints. Authors: Li P.-H.; Kinshuk; Huang Y.-M.
Title: A Generative AI-Based Personalized Prompting System Integrating Inquiry-Based Learning and Reflection Levels: Analyses of Reflective Behaviors and Cognitive Load
Abstract: In inquiry-based learning, reflection is frequently treated as a summative activity at the end of the learning process. This lack of continuous support throughout the inquiry cycle limits its effectiveness in cognitive monitoring, reasoning refinement, and knowledge construction. Furthermore, requiring students to reflect consistently across all inquiry stages may impose an additional cognitive burden due to the abstract nature and high cognitive demands of reflective tasks. To address these challenges, this study developed a phased, personalized reflection system integrated with Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), deeply embedding reflection mechanisms within the POEE (Predict-Observe- Explain- Evaluate) inquiry process. Based on the conversational context of each stage, the system dynamically generates personalized prompts to guide students from low-level to high-level reflection. The results indicate that the experimental group experienced significantly lower extraneous cognitive load and significantly higher germane cognitive load compared to the control group, while no significant difference was observed in intrinsic cognitive load between the two groups. Analysis of reflective behaviors further revealed that the experimental group successfully transitioned from non-reflective to reflective behaviors, reaching higher levels of reflective performance. In contrast, the reflective behaviors of the control group remained largely at the non-reflective level. Overall, the personalized reflection system developed in this study effectively reduces the additional cognitive burden during the inquiry and reflection process while promoting engagement in deeper knowledge construction. These findings demonstrate the potential of GenAI as a supportive tool for phased, scaffolded reflection. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A survey of the integration between machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques in software-defined networking
Abstract: Recently, Software-Defined Networking has become one of the key technologies in modern telecommunication networks. Its programmable and flexible architecture enables centralized control of network resources, automation of management processes, and integration with other technologies such as Network Function Virtualization, Edge/Fog/Cloud Computing, and 5G/6G networks. Moreover, SDN provides a natural environment for implementing advanced Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence techniques, which are increasingly applied to anomaly detection, network traffic analysis, load prediction, and flow optimization.This article presents a comprehensive survey of the integration between SDN and AI across diverse networking domains, including core, cloud, edge, wireless, IoT, and vehicular networks. More than 400 publications from 2015 to 2025 have been analyzed and classified according to network domain, application area, and category of AI techniques employed-particularly supervised, unsupervised, and hybrid learning methods. Based on this systematic analysis, a mapping framework was developed to illustrate the relationships between AI techniques and SDN application domains, revealing dominant research trends and existing gaps in the current literature. Unlike many previous surveys that focus on individual SDN aspects, selected network domains, or isolated AI-based applications, this survey provides an integrated cross-domain perspective on AI-enabled SDN. Its main contribution lies in a taxonomy-driven mapping of machine learning paradigms, SDN application areas, and network domains, which clarifies how current research supports the transition from programmable SDN toward more autonomous and intelligent network management.The results of the conducted review indicate that the integration of SDN and AI constitutes a foundation for the development of intelligent network management mechanisms. The machine learning techniques presented in this paper form the basis of the currently emerging AI-driven solutions for SDN environments, supporting prediction, classification, anomaly detection, and network performance optimization. At the same time, it should be emphasized that the supervised, unsupervised, and hybrid paradigms primarily address prediction, classification, detection, and adaptive optimization functions, whereas full network automation also requires interactive learning mechanisms, continuous decision-making, multi-domain orchestration, and closed-loop control. In the final part of the article, the main directions for future research related to the development of more autonomous, adaptive, and explainable network management architectures are also identified. © 2026 The Authors. Title: AI Adoption Phases in Business Intelligence: From Outsourcing to Human-Centered Systems
Abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into Business Intelligence (BI) is vital as it enables businesses to process vast amounts of information quickly and uncover patterns and trends that might otherwise go unnoticed. In this short paper, we propose a five-phase AI adoption in the context of BI drawing from our experience with numerous SMEs in Singapore and internationally. This progression begins with AI for BI 1.0, where businesses rely on outsourced AI services, offering accessible but limited AI capabilities. As organizations seek greater control, AI for BI 2.0 emerges, emphasizing in-house AI development with a focus on interpretability, making AI models more understandable to users. AI for BI 3.0 advances this by adding explainability, clarifying the decision-making processes of AI systems. The transition to AI for BI 4.0 introduces trust as a crucial factor, ensuring that AI models are not only useful and robust but also faithful to the data they analyze. Finally, AI for BI 5.0, integrates human-centered design, enhancing decision-making through continuous feedback and adaptation. This phased evolution reflects the growing demands for transparency, trust, and collaboration in AI-driven BI, ultimately transforming AI from a tool into a trusted partner in business strategy. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: RILEE: Reasoning-Intensive Legal Element Extraction via Hierarchical Re-answering
Abstract: Traditional Legal Element Extraction (LEE) tasks often treat legal elements as isolated labels, failing to capture the logical reasoning used in judicial decisions. By using a specialized dataset of Chinese civil loan disputes with 89 expert-defined elements, we further introduce a hierarchical re-answering method. This approach allows Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively refine their judgments through legal rationales and structural context. Title: Linking Affective Experience and AI Trust: The Role of a PERMA-Based AI Agent in Higher Education
Abstract: Students’ affective experiences play a critical role in learning. Although generative AI has been increasingly explored in educational settings, limited empirical work has examined how learners’ affective experiences are shaped through interaction processes with AI agents. This study designed a PERMA-based AI agent grounded in positive education to support university students’ affective experience. A total of 146 students interacted with the AI agent over a two-week period. Data sources included pre- and post-intervention measures of positive and negative affect, an AI trust survey, reflective diary entries, and dialogue data. Results indicated that interaction with the PERMA-based AI agent was associated with a shift toward more positive and balanced affective experiences. In addition, students with higher AI trust profiles demonstrated more balanced affective changes and a broader range of affective experiences compared to those with lower trust. Analysis of interaction content identified recurring thematic emphases within each PERMA dimension, providing insight into how students’ affective experiences were articulated and interpreted in diary reflections and dialogues. Title: Based on the Perspective of Motivational Factors: The Impact of Generative AI (GAI) on Information Science Students’ Hands-on Learning in Embedded Systems
Abstract: This study, based on Self-Determination Theory (SDT), explores the impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) on the learning motivation and higher-order thinking abilities of students in embedded hands-on courses. A quasi-experimental pre- and post-test design was employed, involving 60 master's and doctoral students. The results were compared between an experimental group (using GAI) and a control group (not using GAI). The findings show that the introduction of GAI significantly enhances students’ intrinsic motivation, including autonomy, perceived competence, associative thinking, and learning interest and enjoyment, demonstrating a positive impact on motivation. Regarding higher-order thinking, some analytical results show that instructional intervention has a significant effect on improving creativity, problem-solving ability, and critical thinking, but some results are not significant, indicating that its influence may be moderated by other factors. Overall, this study confirms that GAI, as a learning support tool, can promote learners’ motivation and learning engagement by meeting their basic psychological needs, and has the potential to benefit the development of higher-order thinking. Title: Translation as an Accessibility-Oriented Interdisciplinary Process: Integrating AI Tools, Digital Standards, and Localisation
Abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies has significantly transformed translation practices and translator education. While traditional translation pedagogy focuses on linguistic equivalence, contemporary practice requires competencies extending beyond text, including accessibility, multimodality, and the use of AI-assisted tools. This study explores how students of Applied Linguistics perceive selected translation-related tasks in the context of digital accessibility. The research is based on a survey conducted among undergraduate and graduate students (N = 157). The questionnaire examined both the perceived importance and difficulty of various competencies, including subtitling, audio description, plain language, and AI-assisted translation. The results indicate a shift from traditional translation tasks towards accessibility-focused and multimodal practices. Tasks such as subtitling and audio description were perceived as highly relevant but also challenging, suggesting a gap between current educational practices and market expectations. Title: The effect of conversational style on children’s self-reporting: Evidence from a field study with an LLM-powered voice diary
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: Sustaining children’s engagement and response quality in self-reporting diaries is a longstanding challenge, as repetitive tasks often reduce compliance and motivation. While conversational agents powered by large language models (LLMs) offer a promising solution, most designs for children emphasize semantic adaptation (e.g., phrasing, wording) and leave underexplored the sound-pattern form of language (e.g., rhyme/rhythm) that may shape children’s enjoyment. Children selected their preferred style before each session, allowing analysis of behavioral preferences, compliance, response quality, and perceived enjoyment. Results show that younger children strongly preferred the rhyming style, whereas older children exhibited more varied preferences, and rhyming preference attenuated over sessions. Session-level rhyming choice was associated with higher completion, fewer skipped days before returning, and higher response quality. Mediation analyses were consistent with enjoyment as a candidate pathway linking style choice to response quality. We contribute a design account of conversational style as semantic scaffolding plus phonological enrichment, with implications for dosage-controlled and adaptive style management in agents for children. © 2026 The Authors. Title: GenAAC: Generative AI-Based Dynamic AAC Symbol System for Overcoming Limitations of Static Databases
Abstract: This study proposes GenAAC, a dynamic symbol generation system for Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) that leverages Large Language Models and text-to-image synthesis. Traditional AAC systems depend on pre-built, static image databases that constrain vocabulary coverage, lack cultural and personal relevance, and require costly manual maintenance. GenAAC addresses these limitations through just-in-time, context-aware symbol creation, incorporating a semantic tokenization algorithm, iconography-focused prompt engineering guidelines optimized for AAC visual standards, and a user-centered generation loop. To resolve concerns regarding the inherent variability of generative AI—where different images might be produced for the same concept—the system integrates a multi-tier caching mechanism that ensures visual consistency by reusing previously generated images. Furthermore, a user-controlled regeneration feature allows users to request alternative images if the output does not meet their personal preferences. We conducted a mixed-methods evaluation against the Korean standard AAC symbol set (KAAC)—a localized equivalent to systems like PCS or Widgit—using 100 core vocabulary items. Results demonstrate that GenAAC achieves 29.5% lower visual complexity (Edge Density: 0.0117 vs. 0.0166; t(99) = -9.69, p <.001, d = 0.97) and significantly higher expert-rated communicative appropriateness (M = 4.29 vs. M = 4.00; t(99) = 4.17, p <.001, d = 0.42). Furthermore, semantic accuracy was statistically equivalent (CLIP Score: TOST p <.001 within \pm1.0 margin). Title: Computational Thinking Development in AI Agent Creation: A Mixed-Methods Study
Abstract: This mixed-methods study examined computational thinking (CT) development among 93 pre-high school students in a five-day AI agent creation workshop using CocoFlow, a no-code platform. Integrating pre-post assessments, behavioral logs, and interviews, we investigated CT development and how initial CT levels shape learning trajectories. Results revealed significant improvements in abstract thinking (d = 0.71) and algorithmic thinking (d = 0.70). Hierarchical regression identified iterative testing engagement as a predictor of self-efficacy gains (β =.20, p =.050). Notably, students with moderate initial CT levels demonstrated substantially greater gains than both high-CT and low-CT peers, revealing an “Optimal Development Zone” effect (η2 =.55). Qualitative analysis showed moderate-CT students exhibited adaptive expertise, while high-CT students risked over-engineering and low-CT students struggled with task decomposition. These findings challenge linear learning assumptions and provide evidence for differentiated scaffolding in CT education. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Identifying the Characteristics of Brain Regions in Individuals with Different Neurocognitive Characteristics Based on Functional MRI Data
Abstract: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) do not have objective neurobiological markers, and diagnosis is based solely on behavioral scales. Functional resting MRI allows you to study disorders of brain connectivity, but existing approaches face problems of high dimensionality of data, overfitting and low interpretability. The article proposes a methodology for identifying stable, interpretable biomarkers of functional connectivity, reliably distinguishing individuals with ASD and neurotypical controls. To reduce dimensionality and ensure interpretability, two-stage feature selection (t-test with FDR correction, SelectKBest) and logistic regression are used. The model achieved an accuracy of 71.8% (AUC = 80.5%, Sensitivity = 74.4%, Specificity = 69.6%) and identified 22 stable associations. Mapping revealed a predominant localization in the DMN with pronounced hypoconnectivity (17↓ / 4↑), as well as hyperconnectivity of subcortical structures (6↑ / 3↓) and the visual network (2↑). © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: An Integration Framework of InfraHBIM-HGIS for Reconstructing Infrastructure Heritage Evolution: The Taipingling Corridor Along the Chinese Eastern Railway
Abstract: Infrastructure heritage corridors are characterized by large spatial extents, dispersed asset distribution, complex historical transformations, and heterogeneous data sources, which make their documentation and reconstruction particularly challenged. To address these barriers, this study proposes a corridor-oriented InfraHBIM–HGIS framework for the reconstruction and documentation of infrastructure heritage, using the Taipingling Corridor of the Chinese Eastern Railway (CER) as a case study. The framework integrates an archival database, a geospatial database, InfraHBIM-based modelling, and HGIS within a unified workflow. Multi-source datasets, including georeferenced historical maps, raster and vector geospatial data, and point clouds generated through drone-based photogrammetry, are systematically organized and linked through a previously developed 12-digit identification system. A condition-based modelling strategy is adopted to combine forward modelling from archival records with reverse modelling from point-cloud data, enabling the reconstruction of extant, vanished, and transformed heritage assets across multiple historical stages. The integrated results are consolidated in a GIS-centered environment to support cross-scale visualization, semantic linkage, and spatial analysis, and are further disseminated through a WebGIS platform for remote access and interactive exploration. The study demonstrates that the proposed framework provides an operational approach for the multi-scale and multi-temporal integration of documentary, spatial, and model-based information in corridor-scale infrastructure heritage. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Revisiting code readability improvement with LLMs: A critical assessment of fine-tuned models
Abstract: Code comprehension is vital for software development. Still, unreadable code remains a significant issue, costing substantial time and money losses. While tools to identify code exhibiting a low readability exist, take actions to improve such a quality aspect is far from trivial. To support developers in such a task, Vitale et al. introduced at ASE’23 an approach using a transformer model (T5) fine-tuned on code commits in which developers explicitly stated their goal to improve code readability. The authors reported that their model is able to generate readability-improving changes being identical to those implemented by developers (exact matches) in 21% of cases and that, even when they differ, they still improve readability in the vast majority of cases (80%). Given the major advances in AI made in the last few years, we questioned whether a fine-tuning for such a task was still needed in the era of Large Language Models (LLMs), thus revisiting the work by Vitale et al. with state-of-the-art models. In doing so, we found out one major issue with the original study design: The training-test splitting was performed randomly (i.e., readability-improving commits mined from open source projects were randomly split between training and test) rather than by project, significantly inflating the reported performance due to repeating readability-improving commits done within the same project. Indeed, as we will show, even newer and more powerful LLMs fine-tuned for this task can only achieve a 1% of exact matches. Once fixed this issue, we shifted our attention on assessing whether fine-tuning on available developer readability improvements is actually needed given the recent advances in general-purpose LLMs. We compare the performance of fine-tuned state-of-the-art LLMs with what they achieve in zero-shot setting, also including in our study commercial LLMs (GPT-4.1). As we will show, quantitative metrics (e.g., exact matches, CrystalBLEU) tell very little about the readability-improving capabilities of LLMs and, thus, our study is mainly qualitative in nature, with a total of 9,500 inspected LLMs’ change recommendations. While all models do improve code readability, our results clearly show that fine-tuning using mined readability-improving commits does not help and, instead, results in sensibly poorer readability recommendations as compared to LLMs used in a zero-shot setting, with GPT-4.1 being the one achieving the best results. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Beyond the Blank Prompt: Co-Designing Accessible Generative AI Interfaces for People with Intellectual Disabilities
Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) systems offer new opportunities for access to information, content creation, and decision-making, but their dominant interaction paradigm poses important barriers for people with intellectual disabilities (ID). In particular, open-ended prompts, long and poorly structured responses, and limited support for refinement, verification, and personalization can increase cognitive load and hinder effective use. This paper presents an exploratory, expert-informed co-design workshop aimed at rethinking GenAI interfaces from the perspective of cognitive accessibility for people with ID. The workshop involved ten researchers with expertise in accessibility, Human-Computer Interaction, Artificial Intelligence, and inclusive design, and was structured around five key interaction challenges identified in previous empirical work: question generation, response refinement, information verification, context management, and personalization. The workshop generated a set of preliminary design concepts that point toward more guided, structured, and adaptive interaction models, including mechanisms such as step-by-step prompting, explicit refinement controls, support for source interpretation, conversation structuring, and dynamic personalization. Rather than presenting validated interface solutions, this work offers an initial map of design opportunities for cognitively accessible GenAI and provides a foundation for future participatory design, prototyping, and evaluation with people with ID. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Accessible GenAI UI Generation with Post-render Verification
Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to produce user-facing content and interfaces, yet its application to cognitive accessibility remains limited. Accessibility standards are usually applied during evaluation rather than embedded within generation pipelines. This paper presents a standards-aware adaptive interface generation system that operationalizes accessibility requirements as generation-time constraints and combines them with explicit accessibility profiles to shape content structure, multimodal output, and interaction properties. A central contribution is the shift from intended accessibility to measured accessibility through post-render verification that accessibility-related features remain visible and operational in the final interface. Initial results from a clinical visit-summary use case show profile-sensitive interface variation and inspection-ready trace artefacts. Title: A Scoring Strategy to Assess AI Prediction Reliability: Validation and Impact on Medical Decision Making
Abstract: Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (AI) is essential for safe deployment in healthcare, where erroneous predictions may have serious clinical consequences. In this work, we propose a predictive reliability approach based on two continuous and complementary scores: a similarity score, measuring how closely a new sample resembles the training distribution, and a local performance score, estimating the model’s expected accuracy in the neighborhood of that sample. Together, these scores provide an interpretable assessment of prediction reliability. We evaluated their impact on medical decision-making through a two-stage survey with medical residents from a research hospital in Pavia, Italy. Participants first judged AI predictions based on patient data alone; then, after reliability disclosure, they confirmed or revised their decisions. By comparing responses before and after the disclosure of reliability information, we provide a preliminary analysis of how adding a reliability measure influences the perception and acceptance of AI predictions. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Xu M.; Li S.; Sun W.
Title: AI-enabled intelligent computing service and pricing decision-making mechanisms of the edge-cloud collaboration system
Abstract: With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, the demand for high-performance computing services has expanded across a wide range of industries. As a key integration of cloud computing and edge computing technologies, the service quality of cloud-edge collaboration has a direct bearing on industrial upgrading and digital transformation. In this context, how cloud and edge participants choose among alternative service decision-making structures for service provision under complex scenarios has become an important research issue. In the AI-enabled intelligent computing service ecosystem, this paper focuses on cloud service providers and edge operators as the main decision makers. A two-stage Stackelberg game is developed under three decision-making structures—centralized decision-making, decentralized edge-intelligence collaboration, and decentralized cloud-intelligence collaboration—to examine how different allocations of service authority and pricing schemes affect equilibrium decisions and the profits of system participants. The results present several important findings. First, across all three decision-making structures, the optimal service price and service level increase with initial market demand. Second, when the initial market demand is sufficiently high, the centralized decision-making structure outperforms the two decentralized structures by generating higher system profit and consumer surplus. Third, the demand-expansion effect induced by service-level improvement is jointly constrained by service costs and users’ price sensitivity. Fourth, the effectiveness of pricing mechanisms depends critically on the nature of AI tasks. Fifth, scenario-adaptive governance structures are better suited to competitive markets. These findings contribute to the literature on cloud-edge intelligent service systems and provide useful managerial implications for decision-making structure selection and pricing decisions in intelligent computing service systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: A Gaussian Distribution-Based Oversampling Method on SPD Manifolds for Imbalanced Physiological Signal Classification
Abstract: Manifold learning techniques under Riemannian geometry exhibit excellent capability in nonlinear feature representation for signal data. Accordingly, classification frameworks integrated with Riemannian manifold learning have been extensively investigated in the fields of signal processing and pattern recognition. Medical physiological signals such as EEG and ECoG possess inherent characteristics including strong spatiotemporal continuity. By modeling such signals using symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrix manifolds, the classification performance of related models can be effectively enhanced. Nevertheless, medical physiological signal datasets frequently suffer from the class imbalance problem, mainly due to limited data acquisition conditions and strict privacy constraints. This issue tends to induce the majority-class bias in learning models, thereby directly degrading the accuracy of signal recognition tasks. As a typical solution, SMOTE generates synthetic minority samples via linear interpolation to balance the data distribution across different classes. However, conventional imbalance processing methods designed in Euclidean space often destroy the positive definiteness and intrinsic spatial structure of SPD matrices. To address this limitation, this paper presents SPD Gaussian-SMOTE, an imbalance learning method tailored for SPD matrix manifolds. The proposed approach implements probabilistic sample synthesis based on Gaussian distribution in the Riemannian manifold space. Comprehensive experiments are conducted with multiple evaluation metrics, including F1-score, G-mean and AUC, whose average values are adopted for performance validation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm can effectively alleviate the class imbalance problem and achieve competitive performance compared with existing methods. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Toward global interpretability of neural networks via Boolean transformation
Abstract: Interpretability remains a central challenge in the deployment of deep neural networks, particularly in safety-critical and decision-sensitive fields. This work proposes a unified framework for post-hoc global interpretability by transforming general neural network architectures—including the Residual Network and Transformer—into equivalent decision diagrams over real-valued inputs and multi-class outputs. These decision diagrams provide a transparent, structured view of the neural network’s overall behavior, where each path encodes a tractable and interpretable decision rule. We identify a counterintuitive yet effective modification in the node merging process during diagram construction, which leads to faster entropy reduction and smaller equivalent intervals, thereby significantly reducing the diagram size while maintaining equivalence with the original network. The resulting representations not only support the exploration of logical properties, such as decision boundary tracing, equivalence checking, robustness analysis, and model counting, but also serve as globally interpretable surrogates for the original neural networks. Experiments validate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed methods, highlighting their potential for reliable neural network analysis and verification. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Generative AI Guidance Based on Computational Thinking: The Impacts on Problem-Solving Skills and Reflective Thinking
Abstract: This study aims to address the challenges encountered by novice programmers, particularly high cognitive load and a lack of immediate diagnostic feedback. To mitigate the risk of students developing an over-reliance on generative artificial intelligence (GAI) as a means of directly obtaining answers, which may consequently undermine their capacity for self-directed learning, this study developed a learning platform that integrates GAI, computational thinking (CT), and formative assessment. Within the platform, GAI is designed as a “thinking facilitator” that guides students through progressive questioning and immediate feedback, rather than providing definitive answers. This design is intended to scaffold students’ engagement in problem decomposition, logical reasoning, and reflective debugging. A total of 27 undergraduate students participated in this study, with pre- and post-tests along with questionnaire surveys administered to evaluate the effectiveness of the system intervention. The findings indicate that interaction with the platform not only effectively enhances students’ programming learning outcomes, but also fosters the development of reflective thinking and problem-solving skills. Regarding future research directions, it is recommended that subsequent studies expand the sample size and extend the duration of implementation. By improving the guidance mechanism and providing tiered learning resources, future studies may further validate and enhance the long-term learning outcomes and problem-solving skills of learners with varying proficiency levels. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: The Rise of Agentic Analytics: Towards Autonomous Decision Intelligence Systems

Abstract: The traditional data analytics value chain that spans the phases of description, diagnosis, prediction, and prescription, typically concludes before execution, leaving a critical gap between analytical insight and action. This “last-mile” gap is widely noted in the prescriptive analytics literature and contributes to unrealized value [1]. This gap often results in measurable value loss, particularly in data-rich and time-sensitive domains. The latency or cost of inaction manifests as millions of dollars in inefficiencies, suboptimal resource allocation, and diminished responsiveness to market dynamics, therefore establishing a critical need to use end-to-end AI enabled decisioning in supply chain This “last-mile” gap is widely noted in the prescriptive analytics literature and contributes to unrealized value [2]. This paper proposes a three-tier agentic architecture [3] for building an end-to-end, closed-loop Decision Intelligence (DI) system designed to significantly reduce decision latency. The framework integrates three purpose-built components: Diagnostic Engine – Automates and scales KPI driver analysis, performing fine-grained variance attribution and contribution analysis to precisely isolate performance drivers; Cognitive Engine – A Large Language Model (LLM)-based module that transforms structured diagnostics into contextual, natural language insights and analytical narratives [4]; Action Engine – An autonomous, LLM-based agent that distills actionable trends from these narratives and can recommend or execute corrective workflows such as rebalancing business volume, onboarding new partners, raising exceptions, or initiating financial recovery [5].The Action Engine operates under a principled, Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) governance framework [6] that ensures safety, accountability, and continuous human oversight. Title: Design, Integration, and Evaluation of LLM-Enhancement Techniques for LMSs: RAG, LoRA Fine-Tuning, and Structured Generation
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer significant potential for enhancing learning management systems (LMSs), yet challenges such as outdated information, hallucinations, and non-determinism limit their reliability in learning contexts. This paper develops and evaluates an end-to-end system that addresses these issues through three techniques: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning, and structured (guided) generation. The system integrates directly with LMSs via plugins or a middleware-based architecture, extracts course materials into reusable formats such as Markdown, to be used by different output enhancement techniques. The techniques are evaluated on both public and synthetic learning materials to avoid pretraining bias. Results show that RAG provides the most substantial improvements in performance, particularly when paired with context-aware retrieval. LoRA fine-tuning also improves results, especially with high-quality synthetic data, but its benefits are more limited compared to RAG. Structured generation eliminates schema errors and ensures machine-readable generation of interactive or LMS-native content, such as personalized quizzes. Together, these methods demonstrate how LLM-based systems can generate course-aligned content that is accurate and easily usable with existing LMS platforms. The findings recommend RAG as the primary strategy when a curated corpus is available and LoRA as a viable alternative when RAG is impractical. In addition, structured generation is found as essential for reliability when generating format specific content. This work contributes both a technical framework and applied evidence for integrating advanced LLM systems into LMS environments to support scalable and high-quality AI-enhanced digital learning. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Identifying Insular Tourism Hotspots at Fire and/or Flood Risk – Case Study Rhodes Island, Greece
Abstract: In the Climate Change (CC) era, frequency, duration, and intensity of wildfire and flood incidents across Mediterranean areas is predicted to amplify, raising thus policy concerns as to the risks inherent in, among others, tourism hotspot regions, including the insular ones. Experience gained from recent CC-related fire/flood incidents and their devastating impacts on the natural/built environment – particularly in Mediterranean highly-urbanized, tourist-overloaded coastal parts – calls for broadening the scope of planning and policy making in order for resilience of these areas to be strengthened. This highlights the necessity for feeding planning endeavours with spatially-defined fire/flood risk assessments, especially in coastal tourism hotspots, i.e., areas displaying an intense accommodation and tourists’ overload. That said, this study develops a framework for identifying tourism hotspot zones that are prone to fire and/or flood risk, with this perceived as a critical input in proactive planning studies aiming to minimize fire/flood risk or conduct fire/flood management plans. This framework integrates: a literature-based indicators’ set for featuring tourism hotspots; the Random Forest algorithm through the Forest-Based Classification tool for fire risk assessment; and the officially-delineated flood-prone zones. Implementation of this framework is conducted in Rhodes Island, i.e., a major flagship of Greek tourism; a well-known, of global reach, destination; and a prominent example of Mediterranean island region, exposed to both CC and (over)tourism repercussions. Linking fire/flood hazards with tourism patterns offers insular destinations a useful ground for featuring proactive CC adaptation strategies and/or emergency planning. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Three Paths to Adaptation: Temporal Profiles of Self-Regulated Learning with Generative AI Support
Abstract: Self-regulated learning (SRL) unfolds dynamically as learners adjust cognitive and metacognitive strategies in response to changing task demands. Yet, many learners struggle to regulate effectively, creating a need for scaffolding.
