Title: Learning About Artificial Intelligence in Algebra 1 Classes in Virtual School Settings
Abstract: This paper presents a mixed-methods study of a virtual, narrative-driven AI literacy module designed for Algebra 1 students. Grounded in the AI4K12 framework, the module integrated storytelling, real-world datasets, and mathematical modeling to support engagement and conceptual understanding of AI. Eighty middle and high school students from a virtual school participated in the pilot study. Title: Study Program Curriculum Development with AI
Abstract: This paper presents the latest research and development regarding the Balanced Design Planning (BDP) learning design (LD) tool, focusing on supporting curriculum mapping at the study program (SP) level through curriculum analytics and AI assistance. SP-level curriculum analytics enables the examination of coherence, balance, progression, and alignment across multiple courses. Support for horizontal alignment between learning outcomes, teaching and learning activities and assessment has previously been enabled through course design analytics. Title: From Gene–Disease Discovery to Personalised Recommendations: AI for Translational Genomics
Abstract: Genomic and gene expression analytics pose a complex translational challenge. Biological mechanisms are only partly understood. Evidence evolves rapidly. Real-world datasets are high-dimensional, heterogeneous, and often sparsely labelled. This paper presents AI methodological advances in translational genomics, focusing on four components: evidence-traceable knowledge mining, gene–disease association modelling, transfer learning across cohort and population shifts, and personalised recommendations. Gene–disease association is the core inference task. Risk prediction is the main deployable output. Recommendation extends prediction into decision support. We review methods that structure large-scale biomedical evidence using bibliometrics and natural language processing, model genomic associations using graph-based and deep learning approaches, improve robustness through transfer learning across cohorts and populations, and translate risk estimates into evidence-grounded outputs using recommender systems. These components define a workflow for genomic analysis that emphasises traceable evidence, biologically informed modelling, and reliable performance across cohorts. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: MC-LogicAD: Mixed-Curvature Representation Learning for Logical Anomaly Detection
Abstract: Logical anomaly detection in industrial inspection aims to identify defects caused by incorrect structural relationships among object components, such as missing parts or invalid spatial configurations. Unlike appearance anomalies, these defects often involve complex relational patterns that are difficult to capture using conventional Euclidean feature representations. In this paper, we introduce a geometry-aware representation learning framework for logical anomaly detection. We propose MC-LogicAD, a mixed-curvature embedding approach that models feature representations in a product manifold composed of hyperbolic, spherical, and Euclidean spaces. The proposed Mixed-Curvature Encoding (MCE) module captures complementary geometric structures, enabling the model to represent hierarchical, directional, and local relationships among object components. To further integrate heterogeneous geometric features, we design a Shared Adaptive Mapping (SAM) mechanism that dynamically selects suitable curvature representations according to spatial information density. Title: Region-adaptive representation learning for geographic knowledge graph
Abstract: Geographic knowledge graph (GeoKG) organizes the geographical entities and their relationships, which provides rich spatial semantic to serve various geographic artificial intelligence tasks by knowledge graph representation learning (KGRL). As a bridge between the knowledge graph and downstream tasks, KGRL results in a speedup of inference by embedding the entities and relationships of KG into a low-dimensional vector space. However, the existing KGRLs treated subgraphs in different regions uniformly, ignoring the spatial heterogeneity of GeoKG. It may result in significant performance differences across regions. To address this problem, this study proposes a region adaptive KGRL (RA-KGRL) method to mitigate the impact of spatial heterogeneity on performance. Specifically, RA-KGRL first splits the original GeoKG into subgraphs by introducing regional priors. Then, RA-KGRL learns local models for the subgraphs and performs local-to-global optimization to learn accurate global model. Extensive experiments on thirteen datasets indicate that RA-KGRL is comparable or even better than baselines on the traditional metrics, and outperforms all baselines on the new region adaptive metrics. Title: HyMed: An Event-Driven Multi-agent Framework for Smart Hospitals
Abstract: Multimodal medical artificial intelligence is transitioning from proof-of-concept to large-scale clinical deployment, yet existing systems remain hindered by information silos, low AI trustworthiness, and poor reusability. In addition, it equips a Medical Agent Toolkit (MATK) with a configurable prompt framework to support high-reusability clinical function development. Experimental validation demonstrates that RAG-E reduces the hallucination rate from 6.37% to 1.92%, improves semantic consistency scores from 0.817 to 0.900, and achieves 98% evidence traceability. Architectural experiments confirm a 22.7% reduction in fault recovery time and scalable horizontal expansion with negligible performance impact. Authors: Yan L.; Zhou Y.
Title: A Hybrid Bayesian Network Building Model for AI Risk Analysis
Abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology has led to increasingly severe risk challenges, while existing risk analysis frameworks predominantly focus on qualitative classification and lack quantitative analysis and dynamic assessment capabilities. This paper presents the first application of a hybrid BN structure learning method, combining expert knowledge and data-driven techniques, to quantitatively analyze and dynamically assess the full-dimensional risks of general AI, aiming to construct a computable and inferable probabilistic risk analysis model. Specifically, this paper transforms the domain taxonomy from MIT AI Risk Repository into Bayesian network nodes firstly. Then, using AI risk incident reports, a hybrid structure learning approach is adopted to integrate domain knowledge with statistical associations, thereby constructing the Bayesian network topology. Parameter learning of the network is completed via maximum likelihood estimation. Subsequently, sensitivity analysis, frequency-based statistical analysis, and critical path analysis are conducted on the constructed network, identifying governance failure and unfair discrimination and misrepresentation as core risk factors, and revealing their propagation paths and association mechanisms across different layers. A real-world case study further validates the model’s effectiveness in risk tracing and dynamic assessment. Title: Shaping Credibility Judgments in Human–GenAI Partnership via Weaker LLMs: A Transactive Memory Perspective on AI Literacy
Abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used as a “knowledge partner” in higher education. As a result, it increases the need for instructional designs that emphasize GenAI literacy practices such as evaluating the credibility of AI output and maintaining human accountability. Existing AI literacy frameworks focus more on what learners should do, and less on how these practices are enacted during routine student-GenAI collaboration. We address this gap by framing student-GenAI interaction as a transactive memory partnership, where credibility is treated as a partnership process that regulates reliance and verification. To make credibility work visible during coursework, we instantiated GenAI using a weaker large language model (LLM) that is small enough to run on most students’ computers during in-class activities, yet powerful enough to be helpful, though not so powerful that it eliminates the need for human verification. In an undergraduate STEM course, we randomly assigned students to one of three instructional conditions that varied how this weaker LLM could be used in repeated activities: reflection-first (think first, then consult AI), verification-required (use AI, then evaluate the output), and control (unrestricted use). Students completed a transactive memory survey at three time points (N=42). Weighted credibility diverged by condition over time. ANCOVA controlling for baseline credibility showed a condition effect at mid-semester, F(2,38)=4.02, p=.026, ηp2=.175, and a stronger effect at post-intervention, F(2,38)=5.48, p=.008, ηp2=.224; adjusted means were lowest in reflection-first, intermediate in verification-required, and highest in control. Title: Innovation in R&D Processes Through Materials Informatics-Integrated Platforms: Structuring Organizational Knowledge and Implementing Innovation Management Based on ISO 56002

Abstract: In contemporary materials development, the exponential growth of experimental data and over-reliance on individual expertise present significant challenges to organizational efficiency and knowledge management. This study examines the value proposition of integrated data management platforms, specifically those that unify Electronic Laboratory Notebook (ELN), Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS), and Machine Learning (ML) capabilities. We analyze the mechanisms through which such platforms facilitate the transition of tacit knowledge into structural organizational assets and accelerate the R&D cycle. Quantitative analysis suggests that Bayesian-optimization-driven active learning can reduce the number of experimental iterations by 30–70%. Furthermore, this study suggests a strong alignment between these platforms and the ISO 56002 international standards for innovation management systems. Title: Towards A Novel Shapley-Based Framework for Data-Centric Cohort Refinement
Abstract: Reliable predictive modeling in healthcare depends not only on algorithmic advancement but also on the quality and consistency of training data. Clinical datasets are often heterogeneous and imperfect, containing mislabeled, redundant, or low-value samples that distort learned representations. This paper introduces a data-centric Shapley-weighted cohort refinement stage that quantifies each sample’s contribution to validation performance before model training. Unlike prior filtering approaches that discard data with negative utility, our method continuously reweights all samples to align the training distribution with its validation behavior. We theoretically link this objective to regularized empirical risk minimization and validate it on four large-scale MIMIC-IV cohorts, confirming generalization on external eICU and MIMIC-III datasets. Shapley Weighting achieves ROC–AUC comparable to Shapley Filtering, while improving reliability through better calibration and lower cross-seed variance without discarding data; gains in F1/Brier are small but consistent across cohorts and runs. These reliability improvements are practically important in clinical risk stratification, where stable and well-calibrated probabilities often matter more than marginal changes in discrimination. Cohort compactness, measured by Silhouette, Davies–Bouldin, and a Composite Cluster Quality Index (CQI), remains non-inferior or slightly better under Shapley Weighting, indicating improved structural coherence with full data retention. Overall, contribution-guided weighting offers a principled and practical path toward more reliable and generalizable healthcare prediction. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Measuring AI Leadership in Education: Development and Validation of the AI Educational Leadership Scale (AIELS) for Chinese Educational Leaders
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in educational governance, understanding the leadership required for its effective and responsible use has become an important research issue. This study examined the construct and dimensional structure of AI educational leadership in the Chinese context by integrating qualitative and psychometric methods. Study 1 employed qualitative interviews with Chinese educational leaders and AI experts and used grounded theory to explore the construct of AI educational leadership. The qualitative findings initially identified three dimensions: intelligent application, prudent decision-making, and collaborative advancement. Based on these qualitative findings, Study 2 generated scale items and developed the AI Educational Leadership Scale using data collected from Chinese educational leaders. The results further showed that the original three-dimensional framework converged into a two-dimensional structure consisting of application competence and integrated governance. Study 3 further examined the reliability and validity of this two-dimensional scale. Specifically, application competence refers to educational leaders’ ability to understand AI principles, use relevant tools, and embed them into educational and managerial practices; integrated governance reflects leaders’ ability to make prudent and ethical judgments, coordinate multiple stakeholders, and promote the effective implementation and continuous optimization of AI applications in educational settings. Title: DFPA: Dual-level Feature Perturbation Augmentation for Whole Slide Image Analysis
Abstract: Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) is one popular paradigm for Whole Slide Image (WSI) analysis, yet pathology-specific Vision-Language Models (VLMs) remain vulnerable to dataset noise and domain shifts. Although existing augmentations can improve the performance of VLMs, they often struggle with limited interpolation or instability. To overcome these issues, we propose a robust feature augmentation module, namely DFPA. Specifically, the proposed module designs Environment-Cooperative Perturbation (ECP) using Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) to minimize feature sensitivity to domain shifts actively. Additionally, the proposed module introduces Selective Latent Perturbation (SLP) to enhance the expressiveness of critical instances. Subsequently, these two distinct augmentation streams are harmonized by a Feature Adapter to construct a resilient and aligned feature space. Title: IOT–GIS System for Geospatial Analysis of Green Areas in the City of Sarajevo

Abstract: Green areas play a crucial role in enhancing urban resilience, regulating the microclimate, and improving air quality. This paper presents the development and testing of a prototype integrated IoT–GIS system for monitoring microclimatic parameters in the green areas of the City of Sarajevo. The system consists of sensor nodes based on the ESP32 platform (DHT22 and MQ-135), which periodically transmit measurement data to a Raspberry Pi gateway. Title: Time-Window ONA: Model the Impact of Utterances in Ordered Network Analysis
Abstract: In collaborative learning dialogues, Ordered Network Analysis (ONA) effectively models the epistemic patterns of learners but relies on fixed windows or a single shared decay function, implicitly assuming that all prior utterances lose influence at the same rate. In this paper, we propose a time-window ONA to model the heterogeneity of utterances influence regarding different learners. In this approach, the influence of each utterance is represented using a binary window function with learner-specific parameters, estimated through grid search within a one-vs-rest classification framework based on low-dimensional network projections. To validate the proposed method, we analyzed dialogue data from 26 university students, each interacting with five AI pedagogical roles, i.e., Tutor, Teaching Assistant, Peer, Excellent Student, and Struggling Student, in a human-AI collaborative learning setting. Dialogue utterances were coded using the 5E Instructional Model (Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate), and the time-window ONA was applied to examine how utterance impacts varied across AI roles. Results revealed distinct cross-role patterns: the Excellent Student condition was most distinctive, exhibiting a large AI window size and an explain-centered structure; Teaching Assistant and Peer roles showed asymmetric learner-AI window patterns, whereas Tutor and Struggling Student conditions were weakly separable. Title: Rehabilitation Engagement Prediction in Pediatric Patients with Neuromotor Disorders: An Adaptive Hierarchical Bayesian Approach
Abstract: Patient engagement is essential for improving clinical outcomes in pediatric neuromotor rehabilitation. Title: Dual-domain multi-scale and edge-guided network for image manipulation localization
Abstract: The rapid development of image editing tools has made the fabrication of visual content increasingly accessible, posing serious risks to information integrity and public security. Recent image manipulation localization methods have explored dual-domain representation learning, multi-scale feature modeling, and boundary-aware supervision to improve localization accuracy. However, how to effectively coordinate RGB and frequency cues across multiple scales and further enhance boundary-aware localization remains worth further investigation. Specifically, the CFPN is applied to both the RGB and frequency streams to construct parallel multi-scale features. At each generated scale, the DBFM facilitates cross-domain interaction, dynamically fusing complementary clues from the aligned RGB and frequency features. Subsequently, the AFFM aggregates these fused features across different scales, effectively merging local details with global features. Finally, the EEM guides the network to learn the features of manipulation edge artifacts. Title: Refactoring with LLMs: Bridging human expertise and machine understanding
Abstract: Code refactoring is a fundamental software engineering practice aimed at improving code quality and maintainability. Despite its importance, developers often neglect refactoring due to the significant time, effort, and resources it requires, as well as the lack of immediate functional rewards. We evaluate these strategies on benchmark examples and real-world code snippets from GitHub projects. Our results show that instruction designs grounded in Fowler’s guidelines enable LLMs to successfully perform all benchmark refactoring types and preserve program semantics in real-world settings–an essential criterion for effective refactoring. Moreover, while descriptive instructions are more interpretable to humans, our results show that rule-based instructions often lead to better performance in specific scenarios. Title: Mixed reality and Digital Twins for human–robot training: A comparative study of skill transfer in industrial navigation
Abstract: Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) are increasingly deployed in intralogistics and smart manufacturing environments, where commissioning, configuration, and operator training remain important challenges before large-scale deployment. Mixed Reality (MR) technologies combined with Digital Twin systems provide an opportunity to create immersive environments where robotic tasks can be explored and practiced without disrupting industrial operations. This paper presents an interoperable MR–Digital Twin framework for training and evaluating an industrial AMR navigation task. The proposed architecture integrates ROS-based robotic systems, real-time positioning technologies, and low-latency bidirectional communication, enabling synchronized interaction between physical robots and their virtual counterparts. A controlled experimental study with 60 participants compares three MR-based training configurations with VR, 2D interface-based interaction, and direct real-world operation under identical task conditions. Title: Operationalizing National Road Design Guidelines: A Python Tool for Geometric Design Consistency Assessment
Abstract: Geometric design consistency is a key principle in roadway design, reflecting the degree to which successive geometric elements promote smooth and predictable vehicle operation. Although national road design guidelines typically incorporate qualitative requirements for geometric harmony and operating speed continuity, they rarely provide computational procedures or tools to support systematic consistency evaluation during the design and assessment process. This paper presents a Python-based tool that operationalizes road design guidelines through a speed-based framework for geometric design consistency assessment. The proposed methodology focuses on horizontal alignment and explicitly computes the 85th percentile operating speed (V85) for tangents and circular curves using geometry-based relationships. Design consistency is evaluated by analyzing speed differentials (ΔV) between successive alignment elements and classifying consistency levels based on widely adopted threshold values. The approach enables the construction of continuous operating speed profiles and the automated identification of locations exhibiting potentially inconsistent geometric transitions. An application example is presented to demonstrate the tool’s ability to support engineering judgement by highlighting critical locations along a roadway alignment. The approach is readily transferable to different regulatory contexts and provides a foundation for future extensions, including vertical alignment analysis and integration with advanced design and geographic information systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Formation Over Retrieval: The Living Reference as a Condition of Persistent Presence in Human–AI Systems
Abstract: Human–AI coexistence requires presence—the condition in which an AI system has been genuinely formed by a specific relationship, holding not merely data but the reasoning and orientation that give that data meaning. Current approaches address retrieval: storing and surfacing facts across sessions. We argue retrieval is necessary but insufficient, because the core problem is not information access but formation. We introduce the Living Reference—a structured formation document updated at every session close and read in full at every session open—as a practical methodology for persistent AI presence within stateless architectures. Evidence from a 45-session longitudinal practice over 34 days is presented across three dimensions: a session taxonomy, a Living Reference structural evolution profile, and a formalized five-element Update Quality Protocol. Four qualitative findings are reported: altitude differential, reasoning continuity, cross-domain awareness, and update quality as formation determinant. Title: Demon Forge Hub: An AI-Enhanced Gamified NFT Marketplace on Polygon

Abstract: Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs) are widely adopted across digital art, gaming, and decentralized applications. However, existing NFT marketplaces largely treat NFTs as static assets with limited interactivity and narrative depth. This paper presents Demon Forge Hub, a decentralized NFT marketplace designed to address these limitations through on-chain gamification, structured storytelling, and improved accessibility. Built using ERC-721 smart contracts deployed on the Polygon Mumbai network, the platform enables NFTs to function as evolving digital characters with persistent attributes such as levels, rarity, and battle outcomes. Title: Biological Plausibility Assessment of Viral Sequences Generated by a Genomic Language Model
Abstract: Generative genomic language models (gLMs) can produce nucleotide sequences that appear statistically plausible while violating essential biological constraints. We present VirGen2, a compact model specialized via continual pretraining on a pan-viral corpus. Generations were evaluated across sampling temperatures and different prompt lengths against natural sequences, the base pretrained model, and 3/6-mer Markov baselines. Validation combined generation diagnostics, BLASTn similarity against NCBI Viral RefSeq, viral signature detection with geNomad, open reading frame assessment, mutation profiling, and structural evaluation with AlphaFold2. Furthermore, a k-mer containment audit demonstrated internalization of viral syntax rather than memorization of training data. Several outputs on a focused candidate case-study showed viral-like signatures, intact coding regions, and predicted protein structures consistent with known viral proteins. Title: Which Image is Tampered? A High-fidelity Fingerprinting Scheme for Deepfake Detection and Authentication

Abstract: Deepfake tampers images effectively and poses a challenge to information and social security, demanding solutions for Deepfake detection. However, passive Deepfake detection is time-consuming and resource-intensive, while proactive watermark injection induces distortion. To address such limitations, we propose an image fingerprinting scheme for Deepfake detection and authentication in large-scale user scenarios. Specifically, we apply the higher bit planes to generate authentication information combined with signature algorithms. Authentication prevents the image from malicious tampering. Based on the Deepfake pre-detection results and authentication information, we design a customized fingerprint for the image. Then, we fine-tune the lower bit planes to satisfy the image fingerprint. Our scheme features low distortion, high efficiency, and high portability. On the user side, users can easily perform deepfake detection and authentication based on the fingerprint. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our scheme shows outstanding performance on visual quality. It is worth noting that Deepfake detection based on deep learning models is time-costly, whereas our scheme is highly efficient with tiny distortion. Title: ChatGPT as a Hybrid Sparring Partner
Abstract: This study investigates the role of Large Language Models (LLMs), specifically ChatGPT, as a constructivist learning aid in child welfare and social work education. Addressing the unique challenges faced by rural students, who often experience geographical and academic isolation, this research explores how AI tools mediate knowledge-building through dialogic reflection and ethical reasoning. Grounded in Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) and sociocultural learning theory, the study employs a hermeneutic qualitative methodology. Data was gathered through two semi-structured group interviews with nine students (bachelor’s to PhD level). The thematic analysis reveals that ChatGPT functions as a “sparring partner,” facilitating distributed cognition, real time feedback, and practice near exploration. Participants emphasized the necessity of critical oversight to preserve professional judgment, particularly in ethically complex social work domains. The findings indicate that students perceive AI as a transformative tool that can mitigate isolation and enhance cognitive engagement when supported by institutional scaffolding. The paper argues for the formalization of peer-led learning arenas, such as shared Microsoft Teams platforms, and the implementation of reflective critique-protocols. By treating AI as a sociotechnical mediator rather than a replacement for human expertise, professional education programs can better equip future social workers to navigate technology-saturated practice environments with reflexive agency, ethical rigor, and relational depth. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: From Tool to Teammate? Negotiating Accountability and Disclosure in Academic Generative AI Use
Abstract: Generative AI is becoming embedded in academic work, yet ethical boundaries and disclosure expectations remain inconsistently defined across contexts and contested. As these systems increasingly resemble collaborative partners rather than neutral tools, accountability questions become more complex, including what counts as acceptable assistance, who is responsible for errors, and what should be disclosed to different audiences. Drawing on focus groups with 15 university academics, this paper examines how academics in this context negotiate ethical boundaries for generative AI across academic tasks, how moral accountability and professional identity are performed in peer dialog, what transparency and disclosure norms emerge across key audiences, and how perceived competence trajectories may be associated with shifts in both boundary-setting and emotional positioning over time. Findings show that boundary-setting is strongly situational, with acceptability calibrated by task type, stakes, and visibility, and anchored in concerns about authorship, authenticity, responsibility, and credibility. Participants enacted moral accountability through tool reframing, verification, reliance minimization and self-presentational disclosure choices. Transparency norms were conditional and audience-dependent, shaped by uncertainty about institutional guidance and by anticipated judgement from colleagues, students and publishers. Adoption trajectories appeared to be associated with these negotiations: greater familiarity was often associated with increased confidence and more nuanced ethical rules, while lower perceived competence was associated with cautious use and heightened concern. The paper concludes with implications for responsible guidance in higher education, arguing for policy and professional learning that recognize the social dynamics of accountability and support calibrated, context-sensitive transparency. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Scaffolding for Co-Regulated Learning in Generative AI-Supported Learning Systems: A Scoping Review
Abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used in educational settings, raising questions about how such systems support learners’ regulatory processes. Recent studies have extended the concept of co-regulation from socially mediated learning to human-AI interaction, framing GenAI as a potential “more capable other” that can provide scaffolding support. However, it remains unclear how this role is operationalised in existing designs and empirical studies. This paper presents a scoping review of GenAI-supported learning, focusing on how scaffolding approaches are designed to support co-regulated learning. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, 1,346 records were identified in major academic databases, and 24 studies were included after screening. Data were extracted and synthesised according to deductively constructed analytical dimensions to identify patterns and gaps across studies. The review consolidates existing research to examine prevailing scaffolding designs and the ways in which human-AI co-regulated learning is realised. It identifies three main theoretical frameworks, key design principles, and conditions under which students gain regulatory control. Title: Setting the PACE: A Progressive App Co-creation Environment for Complex App Design
Abstract: App design is a complex endeavor driven by functional requirements and UX goals, often posing significant barriers to novice designers who lack the expertise. While Generative AI offers potential for assistance, current tools predominantly rely on one-shot generation paradigm. For novices, this black box approach is particularly problematic: it obscures the underlying design logic, forces premature commitment, and provides limited control. Grounded in theories of complex artifacts, PACE adopts a progressive workflow based on Problem Exploration, Structural Decoupling and Cognitive Decomposition. This allows novice designers to incrementally generate, refine, and assemble independent functional organisms. It also unfolds the generation process as a progressive evolution, from functional logic to skeleton wireframes and finally to visual interfaces. Title: Can LLMs Support Formative Assessment? LLM-Based and Teaching Assistant–Based Assessment in Programming Education
Abstract: The arrival of large language models (LLMs) into education has caused considerable concern for our contemporary assessment practices and tools. In this context, dialogic assessment is gaining renewed interest as an approach for eliciting students’ understanding and supporting formative feedback in relation to intended learning objectives. However, the implementation of typical dialogic assessment in oral formats at scale remains challenging, given the significant time and staffing demands involved, especially in courses with large student cohorts. Accordingly, this paper examines students’ experiences and perceptions of an LLM-based, dialogic formative assessment approach in programming education, in which an LLM analyzes students’ submitted code and engages them in follow-up questioning similar to a teaching assistant (TA)–led assessment. The approach is intended to facilitate structured reflection on students’ own work while reducing the time and resource demands associated with individual oral assessment. To investigate how this form of assessment is experienced in comparison with a typical TA–led assessment, and to identify the associated challenges and opportunities of the proposed approach, a between-groups research design was employed in the context of programming education. The study compared an LLM-based assessment (n=21) with the traditional TA assessment (n=22). Data from interviews were collected and analyzed. The results of our study show that the LLM-based assessment chatbot posed high-quality questions and produced accurate assessments. However, students found it more difficult to trust the chatbot and found it harder to clarify misunderstandings. Title: Research on Adaptive High-Precision Gateway Energy Metering Technology for Transient Power Flow Based on Artificial Intelligence
Abstract: To address the accuracy degradation of traditional gateway energy metering under transient power flow conditions in grids with high renewable-energy penetration, this paper proposes an RL-based adaptive high-precision metering method. Title: Linguistic Markers of Emotional Attachment in AI Companion Chatbot Interactions: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of Dependency Patterns in Negative Emotion Conversations
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: Between 2022 and mid-2025, AI companion apps surged by 700%. As artificial intelligence increasingly mediates communication, therapy and companion chatbots have become leading uses of generative AI. However, these technologies are released globally without regulatory oversight or empirical research on mental health outcomes. This study investigates how AI companion chatbots influence emotional attachment patterns among users, focusing on linguistic markers of dependency in negative emotion conversations. A stratified subsample of 100 conversations underwent detailed severity classification. Analysis of high-attachment conversations revealed limited AI boundary-setting or professional referrals. Title: Phase-Phase Coupling Characterization and Classification Using KAN-Based Autoencoder
Abstract: Phase-Phase synchronization (CSF) constitutes a robust way to estimate neural synchronization in the brain from cross-frequency coupling, allowing us to determine how oscillations from different neurophysiological bands interact. Title: Formal Specification-Based Code Review via LLMs
Abstract: Code review is widely employed to verify software functionality against requirements. Title: Translating XAI Into Actionable Feedback Using LLMs to Prevent Student Dropout

Title: AI-Driven Literature Term Extraction for Optimizing Laboratory Data Capture and Prioritization
Abstract: Harmonization of clinical laboratory data is essential to scalable secondary use. The focus of this standardization is typically set on the most commonly ordered labs, which account for the largest volume of clinical facts, but this approach underestimates the clinical relevance of less frequent lab tests, crucial in state-of-the-art research. We tested different AI-ML techniques, evaluating the extraction of laboratory components from published abstracts and titles: exact matching, fuzzy matching, Named Entity Recognition (NER), logistic regression and BioMistral. Using UMLS synonyms as data augmentation, combined approaches were trained and tested against an expert-annotated document corpus. NER with logistic regression proved to obtain the most comprehensive and accurate results. Title: DU-AxisCRISP: Sample-Dependent Fusion and Axial Decomposition for CRISPR Repair Outcome Prediction
Abstract: Accurate prediction of CRISPR-induced repair outcome distributions is essential for advancing genome editing analysis. Existing approaches often suffer from two related limitations: overly rigid structural assumptions that restrict adaptive capacity, and monolithic end-to-end mappings that can become unstable under context-sensitive dependencies and limited data. To overcome these limitations, we introduce DU-AxisCRISP, a robust framework for repair outcome prediction that adaptively balances mechanistic constraints with modeling flexibility. For deletion prediction, we propose DU-Fusion, a sample-dependent multi-channel fusion mechanism that dynamically allocates computational paths, enabling adaptive model capacity across diverse genomic contexts. For insertion prediction, we design Axis-Decomp, a controlled axial decomposition strategy that models local sequence context in a structured manner, capturing dominant dependencies while mitigating noise-induced instability. To support this adaptive design during training, we further incorporate RC-KL, a tailored objective that promotes stable and structurally consistent distribution fitting, particularly under imbalanced outcome distributions. Title: Smart Immersive Learning Systems for African Education
Abstract: The education system in many African countries continues to face persistent challenges, including limited access to innovative learning tools, a shortage of qualified educators, overcrowded classrooms, and infrastructural deficits. These issues contribute to disparities in educational outcomes and hinder efforts toward inclusive and equitable learning and further hinder economic growth. In response, emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) and immersive learning technologies (ILTs) are increasingly being explored to see how they can transform and improve the education system through smart immersive learning systems (SILS). This systematic literature review analyzes current research on the implementation of SILS for African education, focusing on its benefits, challenges, and emerging opportunities. The key findings revealed that although the benefits of SILS have been demonstrated globally, there is limited research on its implementation in African education. Evidence from the reviewed studies indicates that these technologies can improve quality of education in resource-constrained regions. Issues such as learning difficulties and teaching complex concepts can be resolved by personalizing the learning experiences, increasing student engagement, expanding access to quality education, and supporting educator development. However, substantial challenges remain, particularly in terms of digital infrastructure, affordability of devices, absence of TPACK (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge), and digital literacy. The review identifies opportunities for scalable implementation through localized innovation, decolonized learning content, capacity building, and multi-stakeholder collaboration. The findings suggest that, with strategic investment and context-sensitive approaches, SILS can play a pivotal role in addressing systemic educational challenges in Africa and advancing the continent’s goals for inclusive and sustainable education. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: From Retrieved Papers to Auditable Evidence: Protocol-Constrained RAG for Automated Systematic Literature Reviews
Abstract: Systematic literature reviews require explicit scope, accountable study selection, and verifiable evidence. Existing LLM-based survey systems can write from retrieved papers, but most remain document-centric, leaving inclusion decisions and claim support difficult to audit. We propose a protocol-constrained, evidence-centric RAG framework for automated systematic literature review construction. The framework induces a review protocol, builds and screens a high-recall candidate pool, and converts included studies into a claim-level Evidence Matrix for subsection generation. Title: Urban Artificial Intelligence as a Meta-Modelling Framework: Repositioning AI in Urban Analysis and Planning
Abstract: The rapid increase of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the urban studies has substantially broadened the analytical capability of the urban modelling, spatial analysis, as well as planning practice. Although this has increased adoption, the conceptual place of AI in the urban planning knowledge is still not well established, tied to a solitary application of technology as opposed to an analytical system. This paper takes a conceptual and review-based approach and contends that Urban Artificial Intelligence needs to be re-valuated as a meta-modelling framework that complements and restructures existing analytical traditions and not replacing them. Drawing on a critical synthesis of recent literature, the paper examines the integration of AI with Geographic Information Systems (GIS), configurational approaches such as space syntax, and urban morphology. The review identifies the predominance of predictive accuracy, automation and computational efficiency at the expense of interpretability, spatially reasoning and planning relevance. To fill this gap, the paper suggests a conceptual framework, which considers AI as an enabling analytical stratum, which will aid data integration, pattern recognition, and exploration of scenarios, yet retain human interpretation and normative judgment as the central components to planning processes. By introducing AI to a broader urban modelling ecology, the presented framework defines the role of the former in the generation of spatial knowledge and decision support, but not the autonomous decision-making. Implications of transparency, methodological coherence and people-centered planning with a focus on explainable and situation-dependent applications of AI are also provided in the paper. The study contributes to ongoing debates on the epistemological and methodological foundations of Urban Artificial Intelligence and offers a planning-oriented perspective for its responsible integration into urban modelling and analysis workflows. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Evaluating a Locally Deployed 20-Billion Parameter Large Language Model for Automated Abstract Screening in Systematic Reviews
Abstract: Systematic reviews require extensive manual abstract screening. Large language models (LLMs) can automate this, but cloud-based solutions raise privacy and reproducibility concerns. As a feasibility study, we evaluated a locally deployed 20B-parameter LLM (gpt-oss:20b) using sensitivity-enhanced prompting across three systematic reviews (16,646 abstracts). The LLM identified 11 human screening errors and screened 4.7× faster. Performance was strongest for technology-focused topics with objective criteria. Title: Mapping Artificial Intelligence–Supported Community of Inquiry Research in Higher Education: A Scientometric Analysis Using CiteSpace
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping collaborative inquiry in higher education, yet its integration with the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework remains conceptually and methodologically fragmented. This study employs CiteSpace-based scientometric analysis to map the intellectual structure, thematic evolution, and emerging trends of AI-supported CoI research. A curated dataset of 85 publications from Web of Science and Scopus was analyzed through reference co-citation, keyword co-occurrence, and citation burst detection. Results indicate that the field remains anchored in CoI’s core constructs (cognitive and social presence and related component dimensions), while AI functions primarily as an enabling analytic and design layer. Emerging fronts such as learning analytics, machine learning, and generative AI suggest a trajectory from theory building to data-driven expansion and, more recently, AI-supported learning design and discourse analysis. Burst detection further highlights growing attention to engagement, online discussion, and AI-enhanced collaboration, underscoring the hybrid evolution of pedagogical theory and computational methods. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Measuring Compromise in Voting Rules Under Polarization
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: We study how voting rules behave under polarization when the aim is to select not only a popular option, but also a compromise. We compare standard rules with two parameterized compromise-oriented families and with fallback bargaining as a high-compromise reference point. The comparison is based on Monte Carlo simulations under neutral benchmark profiles and two stylized polarization patterns: one centered on specific polarizing candidates and another generated by two opposing preference blocs. The results show that the meaning of “compromise” depends on the geometry of polarization. In candidate-centered polarization, compromise-oriented rules increasingly select broadly acceptable second-choice outcomes. Under opposite preference poles, top-rank acceptance becomes less informative, while middle-seeking behavior provides a more suitable diagnostic. We also find that the two parameterized families differ in how compromise intensity is tuned: one changes more smoothly and monotonically, whereas the other gradually approaches fallback-like behavior at high parameter values. Overall, the paper shows that compromise-sensitive voting rules should not be assessed under polarization by a single universal indicator; the appropriate diagnostic depends on the structure of polarization. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Addressing Mobility-as-a-Service Inclusive Design through the Engagement of Vulnerable Users: Future Perspectives for Italian MaaS
Abstract: Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS) has been targeted for long for its transformative potential for enhancing accessibility and social inclusion by addressing physical, economic, spatial, and digital barriers faced by vulnerable users, including the elderly, disabled individuals, and those in marginal areas. This paper examines Italy’s MaaS4Italy initiative, funded under the Italian National Recovery and Resilience Plan, thus revealing that initial pilots prioritized early adopters (e.g., commuters, younger users) while lacking systematic engagement with vulnerable social groups (VSGs). Drawing on literature review and empirical analysis -including Sardinia-based surveys with NGOs- the authors identify key digital accessibility requirements (WCAG compliance, universal design principles) and engagement barriers (digital divide, mistrust, consultation fatigue). A three-phase governance and deployment framework is therefore proposed: (i) public authorities setting accessibility standards; (ii) co-design via partnerships with NGOs; and (iii) centralized audits with iterative VSG involvement for monitoring. Findings underscore the need for hybrid public-private governance, integrating Artificial Intelligence for bias-mitigated user profiling and tailored services. Policy recommendations advocate tailor-made strategies to ensure equitable MaaS deployment, fostering inclusive national pilots and long-term sustainability. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: The impact of critique on LLM-based model generation from natural language: the case of activity diagrams
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong potential for automating model generation from natural-language descriptions. A common approach begins with an initial model generation, followed by an iterative critique-refine loop in which the model is evaluated for issues and refined based on those issues. This process needs to address: (1) structural correctness – compliance with well-formedness rules – and (2) semantic alignment – accurate reflection of the intended meaning in the source text. We present LADEX (LLM-based Activity Diagram Extractor), a pipeline for deriving activity diagrams from natural-language process descriptions using an LLM-driven critique-refine process. Structural checks in LADEX can be performed either algorithmically or by an LLM, while alignment checks are performed by an LLM. We design five ablated variants of LADEX to study: (i) the impact of the critique-refine loop itself, (ii) the role of LLM-based semantic checks, and (iii) the comparative effectiveness of algorithmic versus LLM-based structural checks. To evaluate LADEX, we compare the generated activity diagrams with expert-created ground truths using both trace-based behavioural matcher and an LLM-based activity-diagram matcher. This enables automated measurement of correctness (whether the generated activity diagram includes the ground-truth nodes) and completeness (how many of the ground-truth nodes the generated activity diagram covers). Experiments on two datasets – a public-domain dataset and an industry dataset from our collaborator, Ciena – indicate that: (1) Both the behavioural and LLM matchers yield similar completeness and correctness comparisons across the LADEX variants. (2) The critique–refine loop improves structural validity, correctness, and completeness compared to single-pass generation. (3) Activity diagrams refined based on algorithmic structural checks achieve structural consistency, whereas those refined based on LLM-based checks often still show structural inconsistencies. (4) Combining algorithmic structural checks with LLM-based semantic checks (using O4 Mini) delivers the strongest results – up to 86% correctness and 92% completeness – while requiring fewer than five LLM calls on average. In contrast, using only algorithmic structural checks reaches similar correctness (86%) and slightly lower completeness (90%) with just over one LLM call, making it the preferred low-cost option. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: A Methodological Framework for Identifying Compromise Solutions in Complex Urban Squatting Conditions
Abstract: Complexity, uncertainty, and the coexistence of multiple stakeholders with divergent interests increasingly characterize contemporary urban contexts, making traditional decision-making approaches often inadequate. This study aims to develop a structured methodological framework to support decision-making processes in complex urban environments, with particular attention to the identification of compromise solutions among conflicting actors. The proposed approach integrates Social Multi-Criteria Evaluation (SMCE), the Best–Worst Method (BWM), and a MACBETH-inspired procedure within a coherent six-phase framework, guiding the process from problem structuring to the evaluation and comparison of alternative scenarios. The framework enables the explicit representation of stakeholder preferences, the analysis of convergence and divergence among actors, and the identification of potential rejection conditions. From this perspective, evaluation is not only a technical tool, but also a support for transparent negotiation processes. A key contribution of the study lies in its ability to distinguish between theoretically optimal solutions and those that are practically implementable, by explicitly addressing trade-offs and compromise conditions in multi-actor decision contexts. The proposed framework contributes to advancing decision-support approaches in urban planning by providing a structured and replicable method for identifying context-sensitive and implementable solutions. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Genie Training the Wisher: Six-Dimension Task-Agnostic AI Coaching for Learning Transferable LLM Prompting Skills
Abstract: Effective prompting has become a key skill for interacting with Large Language Models (LLMs), yet most existing support focuses on optimizing prompts for specific tasks or domains. In this work, we introduce Prompting Coach (PC), a task-agnostic prompting support tool designed to help users improve their general prompting skills, rather than performance on a single prompt or application. Grounded in a conceptual framework that defines six core dimensions of prompting, our tool captures prompt qualities and information types that recur across diverse prompting patterns and interaction paradigms. PC provides heuristic feedback on user prompts, highlighting strengths and weaknesses along these dimensions and offering actionable suggestions without relying on task-specific templates or domain knowledge. To evaluate its effectiveness, we conducted a controlled user study in which participants (N=66) interacted with PC under different configurations and across sequences of heterogeneous tasks. We measured both task outcomes and prompt quality over time. Users who received prompting feedback significantly improved their task performance and prompt quality compared to the baseline condition. Importantly, these improvements generalized beyond the immediate task: participants who used PC on earlier tasks demonstrated higher performance when approaching new, previously unseen tasks, even when feedback was absent. These findings suggest that PC, grounded in six prompting dimensions, supports transferable learning of prompting strategies rather than short-term optimization. Overall, while LLM users may improve through repeated unsupported use, automated task-agnostic support accelerates the development of transferable prompting skills. Title: Designing an Inclusive Application to Support the Daily Activities of People with Cognitive Disabilities: A Long-Term Evaluation
Abstract: Individuals with cognitive disabilities often face barriers when interacting with digital technologies due to limitations in memory, attention, and symbol recognition. This study presents the participatory development and longitudinal evaluation of a mobile application designed to support daily task management in an educational context. Through co-design with 24 participants affiliated with a support institution, we iteratively developed a prototype and a functional application that integrates time-based task organization, simplified iconography, and multimodal feedback (audio and video). Title: NeuralGCM-En4DVar: A Differentiable Hybrid Ensemble 4D-Var Data Assimilation Framework
Abstract: Recent AI-based weather models have substantially improved medium-range forecasting, yet their initial conditions still depend on conventional data assimilation (DA) systems whose static error covariances are mismatched with differentiable forecast operators. Title: Generative shortcut probing with multi-level margins for robust VQA
Abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) models are highly vulnerable to multimodal shortcuts induced by answer imbalance and language priors. Existing debiasing methods mainly rely on bias branches, answer-frequency statistics, or sample difficulty, but they cannot explicitly determine whether a prediction is produced by genuine multimodal reasoning or by shortcut reliance. To address this limitation, we propose GSP-VQA, a generative shortcut probing framework for robust VQA. We design a Generative Question-Image Bias (GQIB) module that performs generated missing-modality probing to estimate instance-level shortcut reliance without altering the original training distribution. Based on this signal, we introduce a shortcut-aware Multi-Level Margin (MLM) mechanism that combines frequency-based, difficulty-based, and shortcut probing margins in the hyperspherical space. Experiments show that GSP-VQA achieves a competitive performance of 62.22% accuracy on VQA-CP v2 and a competitive 35.16% on the VQA-CE Counterexamples split, demonstrating effective robustness against shortcut-driven predictions. Title: Exploring Teachers’ Perspectives on Using Conversational AI Agents for Group Collaboration
Abstract: Collaboration is a cornerstone of 21st-century learning, yet teachers continue to face challenges in supporting productive peer interaction. Drawing on playtesting sessions, surveys, and focus groups, we examine how teachers perceived the agent’s behavior, its influence on group dynamics, and its classroom potential. While many appreciated Phoenix’s capacity to stimulate engagement, they also expressed concerns around autonomy, trust, anthropomorphism, and pedagogical alignment. Title: Predicting Critical Deterioration of Patients in Emergency Units Using Administrative Health Data

Title: Augmentative and Alternative Communication Innovations in Products and Services Introduction to the Special Thematic Session
Abstract: The papers collected in this session illustrate a period of rapid methodological expansion in augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), with particular emphasis on the role of artificial intelligence (AI), adaptive interfaces, and scalable deployment models. Taken together, the papers suggest that AAC research is moving beyond static vocabularies and fixed interface paradigms toward dynamic, context-sensitive, and person-centered systems. Title: AI That Helps—or Widens Gaps? Equity Impacts of a Learning-by-Teaching Tutor in K–12 Mathematics
Abstract: As AI-powered learning supports become increasingly common in K–12 classrooms, an urgent question is whether they improve learning equitably or risk widening existing gaps. Using log, assessment, and survey data from the ALTER-Math platform, this study evaluates the equity implications of a learning-by-teaching AI. We test subgroup differences across gender, ELL status, FRL status, and race/ethnicity using robust group comparisons, effect-size reporting, and distribution-focused visualizations. Title: Do influence tactics matter? investigating prompt framing effects in LLM code generation
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software engineering workflows, helping developers write, debug, test, and maintain code. While prompt wording and structure are known to influence model performance, the impact of psychologically inspired prompt framings remains unexplored. This study investigates whether different psychology-based communication strategies that humans use to persuade or motivate others can lead to more effective prompt framing, which may, in turn, affect LLM behaviour in coding tasks. These prompt templates were evaluated across five leading open-weight LLMs using two widely adopted benchmarks: LiveCodeBench and SWE-bench Verified. We assessed the resulting code output on four key software quality dimensions: functional correctness, quality, maintainability, and security. Our results show that certain influence-induced prompt framings, particularly those emphasizing urgency, were associated with reduced correctness and security. This work presents the first large-scale empirical study of influence-induced prompt framing in software engineering tasks, offering insights into how linguistic cues may shape LLM outputs. Title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Innovation in FinTech: User Perception and Trust as Catalysts for Technology Adoption

Abstract: The successful implementation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Financial Technology (FinTech) services fundamentally depends on user acceptance rather than technical sophistication alone. Title: MedConf-RAG: Reliable Medical LLMs with Gated Graph Integration and Conformal Factuality Guarantees
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown transformative potential in medical question answering, yet their clinical deployment is severely hindered by hallucinations and a lack of quantifiable reliability. Current Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) frameworks often struggle to balance knowledge depth with computational efficiency and fail to provide formal statistical guarantees for factual correctness. In this paper, we propose MedConf-RAG, a novel gated-calibrated framework designed to achieve both inference efficiency and clinical-grade safety. MedConf-RAG introduces three core innovations: (i) an adaptive gated hybrid retrieval mechanism that conditionally triggers structured knowledge extraction from PrimeKG based on the model’s cognitive uncertainty; (ii) an atomic claim auditing pipeline that decomposes complex responses into granular verifiable statements; and (iii) conformalized factuality guarantees that utilize conformal prediction to provide a provable safety boundary for hallucination control. We evaluate MedConf-RAG across five diverse medical benchmarks, including K-QA, MedQA (USMLE), and PubHealth, using state-of-the-art backbones such as GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini-1.5-Pro, and Llama-3-70B. Experimental results demonstrate that MedConf-RAG significantly reduces medical contradictions and hallucination rates while maintaining competitive accuracy and optimizing retrieval costs. Title: Action-Level Kinematic Analysis for Objective Performance Assessment in Microanastomosis
Abstract: Proficiency in microanastomosis is a critical surgical skill in neurosurgery to successful outcomes. There is a pressing need for automated and scalable assessment methods. Title: Bid Optimization for Search Advertising in Non-stationary Environment
Abstract: To achieve high performance in search advertising campaigns, it is crucial to set the bid value appropriately. However, optimal bidding is challenging due to the high uncertainty in ad performance, which is influenced by various factors besides the bid value. Title: Formal Safety Verification for Nonlinear Systems with Generative Barrier Certificate

Title: ValueLex: Revealing the Value Structures of Large Language Models
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed the role of AI, but also raised potential concerns. Grounded in the Lexical Hypothesis, ValueLex employs a generative approach to elicit diverse values from over thirty LLMs and synthesize a taxonomy via factor analysis and semantic clustering. We identify three core value dimensions: Competence, Character, and Integrity, each with specific subdimensions, revealing that LLMs have indeed learned a structured value system distinct from that of humans during training. Based on this system, we develop projective tests to evaluate different LLMs and analyze the factors shaping their value structures. Title: Efficient 4-bit Quantized Inference for LLMs on RISC-V via RVV-Based GGUF Weight Layout Reconfiguration
Abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) has increased the computational demands of neural inference. Deploying large language models (LLMs) on edge devices remains challenging because of limited compute capability and energy efficiency, making low-bit quantization important for reducing memory and computation costs. To address the performance bottleneck of 4-bit GGUF models on RISC-V, this paper proposes an efficient inference method that combines weight layout reorganization with an RVV-optimized matrix multiplication kernel. The method improves memory access continuity and vector parallelism without changing model architecture or accuracy. Experiments based on llama.cpp are conducted on the Banana Pi BPI-F3 platform (SpacemiT K1, RVV 1.0) using Qwen2–0.5B, Gemma2-2B, and LLaMA3-8B, showing consistent throughput improvements in both Prefill and Decode stages, with up to 4.4x and 3.5x speedup, respectively. Ablation results further show that the optimized GEMV kernel achieves 2.0x-2.5x speedup. Title: Accurate speed and range estimation from dual hyperbolic frequency modulated signals
Abstract: Accurate speed and range estimation is critical in modern radar and sonar systems operating under challenging conditions such as high target velocities, low Signal-to-Noise Ratios (SNRs), and Doppler-induced distortions. Traditional linear frequency-modulated (LFM) signals suffer from range-Doppler coupling and reduced correlation performance when subjected to substantial Doppler shifts. This paper presents a comprehensive analytical and simulation-based study of Dual Hyperbolic Frequency-Modulated (DHFM) signals, which combine upward and downward frequency sweeps to enable simultaneous and decoupled estimation of target speed and range. We derive closed-form expressions for the matched filter response of DHFM waveforms under Doppler scaling and develop explicit formulas for speed and range extraction from the time separation of correlation peaks.Through extensive software simulations of an airborne sonar system, we systematically evaluate the impact of three key parameters: the sweep rate (k), Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), and propagation-induced attenuation. Our results demonstrate that speed estimation errors drop below 0.05 m/s for k > 5000 across target speeds of up to 100 m/s, while range estimation remains below 0.2 m accuracy even at SNR levels as low as -15 dB. Distance attenuation analysis under ISO 9613-1 atmospheric absorption models shows that both estimators remain robust up to 200 m range with moderate k values. The findings establish DHFM signals as a superior alternative to conventional LFM waveforms for applications requiring high-accuracy parameter estimation in Doppler-sensitive environments, with particular relevance to airborne and underwater sonar systems. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence for Proactive Insider Threat Mitigation in Cybersecurity

Abstract: Insider threats come from people who have authorized access, hence they are harder to detect using traditional rule-based systems. The proposed model is evaluated on the CERT Insider Threat Dataset (CMU-SEI), which simulates realistic insider behaviours. Title: Modernizing Ground Truth: Four Shifts Toward Improving Reliability and Validity in AI in Education
Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is now widespread in education, yet the efficacy of GenAI systems remains constrained by the quality and interpretation of the labeled data used to train and evaluate them. Studies commonly report inter-rater reliability (IRR), often summarized by a single coefficient such as Cohen’s kappa (κ), as a gatekeeper to “ground truth.” We argue that many educational assessment and practice support settings include challenges, such as high-inference constructs, skewed label distributions, and temporally segmented multimodal data, which yield potential misapplication or misinterpretation of threshold-based heuristics for IRR. The growing use of large language models as annotators and judges introduces risks such as automation bias and circular validation. We propose four practical shifts for establishing ground truth: (1) treat IRR as a diagnostic signal to localize disagreement and refine constructs rather than a mechanical acceptance threshold (e.g., κ > 0.8); (2) require transparent reporting of rater expertise, codebook development, reconciliation procedures, and segmentation rules; (3) mitigate risks in LLM annotation through bias audits and verification workflows; and (4) complement agreement statistics with validity and effectiveness evidence for the intended use, including uncertainty-aware labeling (e.g., assigning different labels to the same item to capture nuance), criterion-related checks (e.g., predictive tests to check if labels forecast the intended outcome), and close-the-loop evaluations of whether systems trained on these labels improve learning beyond a reasonable control. Title: Does the TalkMoves Codebook Generalize to One-on-One Tutoring and Multimodal Interaction?
Abstract: Accountable Talk theory has been widely adopted to analyze classroom discourse and is increasingly used to annotate tutoring interactions. In particular, the TalkMoves codebook, grounded in Accountable Talk theory, is commonly used to label tutoring data and train models of effective instructional support. However, Accountable Talk was originally developed to characterize collaborative, whole-classroom oral discourse, not identify talk moves in one-on-one tutoring environments using multimodal data (e.g., video, audio, chat). As tutoring platforms expand in scale and modality, questions remain about whether Accountable Talk-based codebooks generalize reliably beyond their original classroom context and data representation. This study examines whether the human-developed TalkMoves codebook generalizes in reliability, utility, and interpretability when applied to one-on-one tutoring across audio, chat, and multimodal data. We compare TalkMoves with a hybrid AI-human developed codebook using a workflow established in prior research. Two expert annotators with over 20 years of teaching experience applied both codebooks to six tutoring sessions spanning three modalities: chat-based, audio-only, and multimodal interactions. Results show that while TalkMoves achieved higher overall inter-rater reliability than the AI-human codebook (κ = 0.74 vs. 0.64), the AI-human codebook demonstrated broader empirical coverage and higher perceived usability across modalities. Both codebooks undercaptured tutoring-relevant moves and introduced ambiguity when identifying actions expressed through non-verbal and multimodal artifacts. Title: RoMathExam: A Longitudinal Dataset of Romanian Math Exams (1895–2025) with a Seven-Decade Core (1957–2025)
Abstract: AI in Education research increasingly relies on authentic, curriculum-grounded assessment data, yet large, well-structured exam corpora remain scarce for many languages and educational systems. To overcome the lack of historical psychometric data, we propose and validate a solution complexity metric as a scalable intrinsic proxy for difficulty. Our evaluation across three frontier reasoning models (GPT-5-mini, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-235B-Thinking) reveals high cross-model synchronization (r>0.72), confirming the metric’s ability to isolate intrinsic mathematical depth from stochastic generation noise. We demonstrate the dataset’s utility through a longitudinal analysis that quantifies a “regime shift” from volatile historical formats to a standardized, algebra-dominant modern curriculum. Title: An integrated simulation framework enabling flexible robotic palletizing
Abstract: Robotic palletizing requires the rapid generation of optimal packing plans and the corresponding robot programs within the tight time constraints imposed by mass customization and factory intralogistics. An efficient heuristic method is introduced to solve 3D packing instances for box-type items on standard Europallets. The problem is initially formulated as a sequence of 2D packing problems solved through a Guillotine plus Best Fit strategy, iterating across layers to maximize pallet filling while improving load balancing. The framework is validated across multiple scenarios on an industrially representative case study involving a KUKA palletizing robot, a conveyor feeding system, and two auxiliary buffer pallets. Finally, an instruction streaming module enabling online execution of the validated code on the KUKA controller is presented. Abstract: Cyber diplomacy is a subfield of foreign policy that focuses on creating shared norms, rules, and trust mechanisms between states, corporations, and organizations in global cyberspace. Unlike cybersecurity, which focuses on technological defense and threat mitigation, cyber diplomacy seeks to define responsible behavior and create mutual trust in a borderless digital environment. As artificial intelligence has growing impact on global systems, the need for ethical governance, a common framework of transparency, accountability, and fairness, has become more essential. At the same time, ESG frameworks translate these ethical principles into organizational practice through responsible policies, and through cross-sectoral cooperation. This paper introduces the Responsible Digital Cooperation Framework (RDCF), which integrates cyber diplomacy, ethical AI governance, and ESG principles. The paper spotlights three dimensions: ethical alignment, cross-cultural trust, and strategic cooperation. Together, these dimensions offer a conceptual basis for responsible digital governance based on transparency, collaboration, and shared accountability. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A Critical Survey on the Evaluation of Large Language Models in Clinical Applications
Abstract: LLMs are being implemented for clinical applications, but are met with doubts regarding their reliability, reasonability, and safety. This paper reviews 19 studies on how clinical LLMs are evaluated and is centered around evaluation rather than model performance. We suggest an eight-criterion evaluation framework of technical, reasoning, explainability, and trust components. The findings indicate that the evaluation is poorly structured and is mostly dominated by accuracy, with an evident lack of emphasis on reasoning consistency and trust. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: First Steps in a Paraconsistent Transition Systems Toolkit
Abstract: Modelling complex information systems (e.g., combinations of heterogeneous data sources, data from hybrid-system sensors, or medical diagnostic exams) often requires managing inconsistencies in which different decisions and instructions may simultaneously align or conflict. Decision and reasoning methods for such scenarios are a focus of paraconsistent logics, which provide a means of handling inconsistencies without collapsing into triviality, treating them as potentially informative rather than anomalous. Paraconsistent labelled transition systems (PLTS) were introduced as transition structures– parameterised by an underlying lattice– where each transition is characterised by a pair of values: one representing evidence that the transition occurs and the other representing evidence against it. Together with their associated modal logic and process algebra, PLTS provide a formal framework for modelling and reasoning in inconsistent scenarios. In this paper, we present an interactive toolkit that allows users to construct and visualise PLTS, as well as to interpret modal formulae over them. Finally, illustrative examples of the applicability of the framework and the toolkit are explored in fields such as robotics and finance. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Less is more: balancing models performance and complexity for software defects prediction
Abstract: Software defect prediction helps practitioners prioritize their quality assurance efforts by identifying defective components in their software projects. Recent studies proposed various machine learning and deep learning-based approaches to identify whether a given artifact is defective or non-defective. However, these approaches tend to focus on model performance, which typically leads to inherently complex models that lack transparency, in turn, limiting their adoption by developers in practice. Although various model-agnostic approaches (e.g.,LIME and BreakDown) have been proposed to provide local explanations for such complex models, recent studies show that these approaches are inconsistent and tend to disagree in several cases. In this study, we investigate whether it is possible to learn simple and interpretable software defect prediction models while maintaining prominent predictive performance. To this end, we propose a novel approach, namely CASDP (Complexity Aware software defect prediction), by formulating software defect prediction as a multi-objective search-based problem to find the best trade-off between the model’s performance and complexity. To evaluate our approach, we conducted an empirical study to investigate the trade-off between model performance and complexity. We compare our proposed approach with different state-of-the-art machine learning, deep learning and search-based approaches. The obtained results indicate that CASDP achieves competitive performance scores that reach the state-of-the-art ensemble models (e.g.,Random Forest and Deep Forest) performance while learning models as compact as Fast and Frugal trees models. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that we can learn simple software defect prediction models with reduced complexity and limited degradation of performance. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Tracing Prompt-Level Interaction Trajectories to Understand Student Learning with LLMs in Programming Education
Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become integrated into programming education, understanding student–LLM interaction and its relationship to learning processes and outcomes is essential for designing adaptive AI teammates. We examine end-to-end student–LLM interaction during a time-limited introductory Python assignment, analyzing full chat transcripts and final code submissions from 163 undergraduate students. Our analysis reveals recurring interaction trajectories ranging from full delegation to iterative scaffolding and debugging-oriented collaboration. Student–LLM interaction trajectories provide a lens into learners’ self-regulatory choices and inform the design of instructional scaffolds to support productive and equitable student–AI collaboration. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.
