Author full names: Wong, Shiau Foong (57210637171); Mahmud, Malissa Maria (57202713786); Ramachandiran, Chandra Reka (54791503300); Wong, Shiau San (57217051274); Thrumalingam, Shobana (60770417200)
Title: Supporting Critical Thinking Through Reflective Assignment: The Use of AI in Mental Health
Abstract: Previous research on artificial intelligence (AI) in education has largely examined students’ attitudes toward AI tools or their learning outcomes. However, less attention has been given to how course-embedded pedagogical activities shape students’ critical thinking about AI use in sensitive domains such as mental health. To address this gap, the present study explores how a reflective assignment in an introductory psychology course supports students’ critical engagement with AI for mental health support. Data was collected from written reflections submitted by undergraduate students (n = 23) in response to two open-ended prompts concerning their experiences with AI for mental health and their evaluations of its benefits and limitations. A qualitative thematic analysis was conducted to investigate the reasoning of the students regarding AI affordances, risks, ethical issues, and the proper use limits. The findings indicate that students demonstrate emerging critical AI literacy by recognising both the potential value of AI for everyday stress management, initial support, and mental health learning, as well as its limitations in crisis situations and complex psychological conditions. Not only did the assignment offer valuable insights into the perceptions of the students about AI, it provided a structured space for articulating critical reasoning in students’ reflections with reference to the ethical consequences, hazards, and limitations of the application of AI in the field of mental health. The findings underscore the importance of critical AI literacy and digital mental health literacy, suggesting that reflecxive assignments represents a pedagogical approach for eliciting students’ ability to navigate and evaluate AI tools in a responsible and informed manner. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: The Methods of User Journey Map Development and Deployment with Cost-Benefit Evaluation
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: The article outlines the methods of creating and developing Customer and User Journey Maps (CJM, UJM) as a tool for forming an effective user experience in digital products. A brand-new hybrid approach to CJM building was introduced, combining graph models and Markov chains to map customers’ behavior on the web. Special attention was paid to UX/UI design principles integration, accessibility, and customer testing tools. The algorithm of prioritizing interface design changes based on a multi-criteria quality function was presented. The multi-criteria quality function addresses rejection factors, levels of user satisfaction, and compliance with WCAG standards indicators. An experimental approbation of the approach based on the web-platform prototype with relevant users’ interaction data was held. The obtained results show a decrease in rejection probability along with upscaling usability and accessibility levels. The suggested method is recommended for implementation in website development, mobile app development, and interactive service development to enhance business process efficiency and user experience quality. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Li T.; Yang R.; Liu Q.
Title: AdTracker: Causal-Chain Detection of Web Ad Traffic Over Encrypted Tunnels
Abstract: Web advertising and tracking services have become deeply embedded in today’s Internet ecosystem, yet existing detection approaches rely heavily on browser-side information and content features that are vulnerable to evasion. We present AdTracker, a novel framework for identifying advertisement traffic at network middleboxes. AdTracker models encrypted web traffic as structured burst sequences and applies causal correlation analysis to extract network-level causal chains that capture the staged and dependency-driven nature of advertisement delivery. A Transformer-based context model further captures long-range dependencies among these chains to classify advertisement flows without payload inspection or browser instrumentation. We also design an automated data collection and dependency-aware labeling pipeline to construct an encrypted traffic dataset for evaluation. Experimental results show that AdTracker achieves the best performance on the self-collected advertisement dataset and shows strong robustness to content-level obfuscation, supporting the feasibility of network-layer advertisement detection in encrypted web traffic. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Authors: Zuo J.; You M.; Lan K.; Fang T.; Zhang J.; Chao L.S.; Wong D.F.
Title: Masked cloze scoring (MCS): Zero-shot automated essay scoring via masked predictions from large language models
Abstract: Traditional Automated Essay Scoring (AES) methods typically require large amounts of labeled data and extensive model training. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled zero-shot AES methods that bypass these requirements. In this paper, we propose Masked Cloze Scoring (MCS), a novel zero-shot method that leverages LLMs’ masked language modeling capacity as its core mechanism for evaluating how well an essay aligns with model predictions. Unlike prior methods that prompt LLMs to assign scores directly, MCS integrates two complementary signals: in-context word prediction for micro-level lexical appropriateness, and relative essay length as a proxy for macro-level writing quality. Experimental results demonstrate that MCS consistently outperforms existing training-free zero-shot baselines on two widely used benchmark datasets, ASAP and TOEFL11. Compared with LCES, the state-of-the-art zero-shot method that requires additional training, MCS underperforms on TOEFL11 but achieves comparable performance on ASAP. Moreover, MCS attains performance competitive with strong supervised cross-prompt methods on ASAP. Beyond holistic scoring, MCS produces word-level diagnostic feedback, offering added pedagogical benefits. Overall, MCS advances the state of training-free zero-shot AES, delivering competitive performance without requiring labeled data or additional training. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Li J.; Du H.
Title: Knowledge-Constrained Causal Discovery for Root Cause Diagnosis in Continuous Steel Casting
Abstract: Root cause diagnosis in continuous steel casting requires distinguishing genuine causal mechanisms from spurious correlations among dozens of interacting process variables. Standard causal discovery algorithms applied to manufacturing data produce dense graphs containing physically impossible edges—for example, post-solidification measurements appearing to cause defects that formed upstream during casting. We propose a three-stage knowledge-constrained causal discovery framework that systematically integrates manufacturing domain knowledge with data-driven structure learning. First, a six-tier variable hierarchy encoding temporal precedence is constructed to generate structural constraints; tier labels are assigned via an LLM-assisted procedure with two-phase validation, and edges violating tier order are prohibited. Second, constrained structure learning is performed using an ensemble of DirectLiNGAM, ICALiNGAM, and GES with 30-round bootstrap aggregation, while a conflict manager enforces tier, temporal, and physical-isolation constraints. Third, diagnostic inference is conducted through path-specific threshold estimation with five-fold cross-validation, transmission probability analysis, backdoor-adjusted confounding control, and counterfactual evaluation. Experiments on industrial data comprising 35 variables across 1,247 heats from a continuous casting line show that the framework removes 83.1% (716/862) of initially proposed edges and identifies 252 physically valid causal paths to defect formation. Ablation analysis indicates that tier constraints contribute most to spurious-edge elimination (59.5%). Among discovered mechanisms, mold-level average exhibits the strongest direct causal effect (weight 0.94), while casting speed emerges as the dominant mediation hub linking 22 upstream factors across 56 causal paths. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Implementing a Statewide AI Curriculum: One Brazilian Experience
Abstract: Since 2024, the Brazilian state of Piauí has incorporated a weekly Artificial Intelligence (AI) subject into the curriculum of public full-time high schools, where it is mandatory, with phased expansion by grade level through 2026. To support this statewide implementation, we developed an AI literacy curriculum aligned with Brazilian education standards. We adapted AI competency references to local constraints and emphasized both learning about AI and learning with AI through plugged and unplugged activitiesrationalized the curriculum through Open teacher-support resources, including a textbook for Basic Education (45 instructional sequences across 24 themes, 300+ pages) and 17 h of video lessons, all released under Creative Commons licensing. In parallel, we delivered an online distance-training program with synchronous sessions (recorded for asynchronous access), tutoring, and sustained teacher support throughout the school year. We present evidence from the first two years of the implementation, combining pre- and post-assessments and module-level evaluations, alongside participation and completion metrics. A total of over 650 unique teachers have been certified through the training across the first two years. The initiative currently reaches approximately 120,000 students across 494 full-time schools offering AI. We discuss design choices for resource-constrained settings and propose practical recommendations for scaling AI education across public-school systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A Conceptual Framework for Human-in-the-Loop Multi-attribute Decision Making Under Uncertainty
Abstract: Decision-making in complex environments is often characterized by multiple decision criteria, uncertainty, and the interaction between humans and intelligent systems. In recent years, human-in-the-loop (HITL) artificial intelligence has emerged as an effective approach to improve the transparency, trustworthiness, and adaptability of decision processes by leveraging the synergy between humans and intelligent agents or machine learning models. At the same time, multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) has become a widely used paradigm for addressing problems involving multiple, often conflicting criteria. Despite growing interest in both fields, their integration in uncertainty-aware environments remains relatively underexplored in the literature. This paper presents a structured survey of recent advancements at the intersection of HITL AI and MCDM under uncertainty. It reviews fundamental concepts in human-centric AI, examines recent studies combining human expertise with intelligent decision-support systems, and highlights application domains such as healthcare, finance, and smart infrastructure. Key challenges—including interpretability, trust, bias mitigation, and human–AI collaboration—are also discussed. A conceptual framework is outlined to illustrate how HITL mechanisms can be integrated into uncertainty-aware MCDM processes. The contribution of this work is primarily conceptual and integrative, aiming to structure existing knowledge and outline future research directions for the development of human-centered intelligent decision-support systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Authors: Luo Z.; Lu M.; Ren Q.; Shi B.; Liu N.; Wu N.
Title: Multi-Step Loss Based Curriculum for Detection of Corrupted Labels
Abstract: Training deep models requires large-scale annotated data, but annotation or collection inevitably introduces label noise, which degrades performance and generalization. Existing methods typically filter clean samples based on the “small loss criterion”, assuming current-step loss suffices to judge label cleanliness. However, due to variations in the learning difficulty of clean samples (e.g., hard samples often have higher losses than easy samples) and the different impacts of various types of noisy labels (such as IDN, CCN, and RCN) on model overfitting, relying solely on single-time-step loss values makes it difficult to set appropriate thresholds and suffers from insufficient information. We argue that compared to single-time-step loss values, loss sequences across multiple time steps can provide richer and more discriminative information for label noise detection. Based on this insight, this paper proposes a curriculum learning-based label noise detection method using multi-step loss sequences (MSL-MentorNet). This method utilizes the loss sequence of each sample over consecutive time steps as a discriminative feature, training an auxiliary neural network to guide base model in selecting clean samples. Experiments show our method achieves significant performance gains on synthetic and complex real-world datasets, outperforming mainstream label noise handling baselines. Title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence: A Survey on Techniques, Ethical Principles, and Emerging Trends

Abstract: Explainability has evolved from a fringe concept to a critical requirement of AI that can be trusted. This work presents a deep synthesis of methods, moral principles and new trends, that in their aggregate shape what is now known as Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). By developing a way of understanding and comparing XAI methods, we aim to systematise model-agnostic and model-specific methodologies, express how transparency, accountability, fairness, privacy, robustness and human oversight emerge in terms of XAI artifacts that are observable from the artifact layers on up, as well as scrutinizing what lines exist to be followed by causality-aware reasoning; explainability relative large language models; evaluation in collaboration with human participants at different levels of expertise/specialization/“stakeholder” interest/focus; documentation whose level is “governance-aligned”. Title: Bridging Innovation and Regulation: Ethical Governance of Medical AI in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
Abstract: Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence (AI) for clinical decision support, triage, and health system optimization, yet governance capacity often lags behind deployment. This creates a high-stakes tension: innovators must move quickly to address workforce shortages and care gaps, while regulators and health systems must ensure safety, privacy, equity, and accountability. We present a practical governance approach, Regulatory-Ethics-by-Design (REBD), that bridges innovation and regulation by operationalizing legal compliance and ethical safeguards across the medical AI lifecycle in LMIC settings. REBD integrates three components: regulatory traceability, context-aware ethical risk assessment, and RegOps (regulatory operations), defined here as lifecycle-integrated processes that embed compliance, monitoring, and documentation into AI development and deployment workflows. Through representative use cases in AI-assisted diagnostics and patient-risk prioritization, we demonstrate how REBD supports transparent oversight and responsible innovation. REBD offers an actionable roadmap for clinicians, researchers, and policymakers to strengthen regulatory readiness while accelerating ethical medical AI adoption in LMIC health systems © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: An Integrated AI Recommendation Support System for Secure Patient-Driven Medical Record Sharing and Search
Abstract: The rapid digitization of healthcare has significantly enhanced the access to patient data, but has also raised significant concerns related to data privacy, ownership, and secure sharing. Typical Electronic Medical Record systems generally store patient’s data on servers managed by a hospital and lacks full transparency and independence for patients. This lack of transparency often leaves patients with no understanding of who has accessed to their record, along with the inability to efficiently search their unstructured medical data. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a Secure Patient-Driven Medical Record Sharing and Search System to restore full control of medical data back to patients. This framework allows the patient to encrypt, manage and share his/her health records with information encoded in Advanced Encryption Standard encryption and hashed metadata to safely search while preserving privacy. Access logs maintain transparency, along with an associated Artificial Intelligence-based doctor recommendation module that processes patient symptoms and suggests specialists without revealing their identity. The experimental results indicate that the system provides enhanced data control, usability, and search efficiency over current Electronic Medical Records systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Xiao X.; He X.; Li Y.; Fang J.; Li Y.
Title: SPARK: A neural-to-symbolic framework for recovering symbolic decision structures in learning performance modeling
Abstract: Learning performance modeling has achieved strong predictive performance, but the decision processes of neural models often remain implicit and difficult to analyze. To address this issue, we propose SPARK, a neural-to-symbolic framework for recovering symbolic decision structures from neural predictors of learning performance. SPARK derives performance-related factors from educational interaction data, learns the decision function with a multilayer perceptron as the teacher model, transfers it to a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN), and then applies structural refinement and symbolic regression to recover compact symbolic expressions. The goal is to convert implicit neural decision behavior into an analyzable symbolic form while preserving its main predictive behavior. Experiments on benchmark educational datasets show that SPARK remains competitive in prediction, preserves most of the teacher model’s decision behavior, and reveals dataset-dependent interaction patterns among student ability, cognition-related factor, and item difficulty. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Gao H.; Hu M.; Gao T.
Title: AI-Generated Image Detection Based on the Most Suspicious Patch
Abstract: In recent years, images generated by advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models have left a deep impression, as they are highly realistic and capable of deceiving human eyes. In this work, we found that only certain regions of a generated image are crucial for detecting it as fake. We hypothesize that advanced generative models are likely capable of capturing visual features and statistical patterns consistent with natural images, such that some regions of the generated images may resemble, or even match, natural image characteristics. This implies that detectors must be highly sensitive to artifacts remaining in local areas of the image. Therefore, we propose the most suspicious patch (MSP) strategy. Specifically, we design a simple yet effective MSP rule that enables a detector to autonomously identify the most suspicious patch, and assess image authenticity based on it. Experiments show that MSP strategy provides satisfactory performance improvements across various detectors. Moreover, we observe that certain detectors achieve new state-of-the-art performance with the support of our MSP strategy. Further investigation reveals that MSP reduces the influence of model-specific signatures and promotes the learning of model-invariant artifacts, which supports better generalization to unseen generators. Title: MFKT: A Parameter-Efficient Modular Knowledge Tracing Framework for Online Judge Systems
Abstract: Existing knowledge tracing models encode student responses as binary signals, discarding richer Online Judge (OJ) submission metadata. Title: SHIELD-SLM: A Dual-Format and Interval-Scored Framework for Small Language Model Evaluation
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: Small Language Models (SLMs, <8B parameters) are critical for resource-constrained deployment, but their evaluation faces two key challenges: simplistic scoring paradigms obscure “model hacking” (exploiting spurious patterns) and oversimplify efficiency metrics, masking performance trade-offs; while complex meta-reasoning benchmarks like MR-GSM8K render SLMs near-zero scoring and require costly LLM-generated chains and expert annotation. For efficiency-sustainability, interval tiered scoring rewards top performers (10% range: +3 points) and near-top models (20% range: +1 point), distinguishing token-per-second (TPS) and token-per-question (TPQ) trade-offs. Experimental validation on math reasoning datasets (GSM8k, AQuA) with 5 SLMs shows SHIELD-SLM effectively discriminates performance: Phi4-mini-instruct (4B) achieves SH-Score=93.89 (outperforming 8B models), while interval scoring identifies it as most efficient (E-score=3) and Qwen3-0.6B as most sustainable (S-score=3). Title: A Review of Human-Centric Evaluation of Cultural Biases in Indic Languages in LLMs: Rethinking Research Directions
Abstract: Indic languages, spoken by more than 1.3 billion people in South Asia, are often underrepresented in AI systems due to their diversity, limited resources, and evaluation challenges. This region, known for its many coexisting developed and endangered cultures, faces significant cultural bias risks as these cultures are not equally represented. These biases can significantly impact the design, development, and deployment of AI in real-life scenarios. Our survey explores cultural bias in Indic languages from a human-centered perspective, combining computational social science and NLP. We interpret different types of bias, critically review different evaluation and mitigation works, and identify research gaps and priorities to focus on to improve AI systems. Based on our review findings, we argue that we need to rethink and reprioritize our research efforts to support other Indic languages except Hindi, and focus on different evaluation approaches for cultural biases. We discuss human-centered perspectives to enhance LLMs, focusing on how they can operate more effectively and equitably within South Asia’s diverse linguistic and rich cultural landscape, thereby creating fairer and more inclusive AI systems for real-world applications. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Rethinking Inner Areas Through AI: Hybrid Approaches for Inclusive Planning
Abstract: This paper critically examines the implications of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for inner area regeneration, serving as a vital testing ground for AI’s contradictions in territorial planning. As non-neutral technologies, AI systems prioritize quantifiable data, often rendering invisible those local resources that resist simple encoding. In these regions, territorial value is deeply rooted in relational, cultural, and ecological dimensions that risk being overlooked by quantitative models. As spatial planning increasingly relies on AI-driven predictive models, there is a danger of standardizing territorial narratives and flattening local specificities. Moreover, predictive models trained on historical data often perpetuate existing inequalities. Inner areas face a “double disadvantage”: scarce, low-quality data produces distorted, self-referential forecasts that reinforce marginalization. To counter these risks, engaging local communities in dataset creation and the rediscovery of cultural specificities is essential. Drawing on the PRIN INSITE project, this paper proposes Hybrid Intelligence (HI) practices where AI systems and local knowledge coexist through participatory processes. Title: From Moderation to Mediation: Can LLMs Serve as Mediators in Online Flame Wars?
Abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has opened new possibilities for AI for good applications. Title: SaltGuard: A Reproducible Data-to-Model System for Enhancing Salinity Intrusion Analysis in the Mekong Delta
Abstract: Salinity intrusion is a critical environmental and socio-economic challenge in the Mekong Delta, yet the deployment of data-driven monitoring and forecasting systems remains hindered by fragmented, heterogeneous, and weakly reproducible climate-hydrological data. In practice, insufficient data readiness, rather than model complexity, often constitutes the primary bottleneck for reliable learning under real-world constraints. We propose SaltGuard, a reproducible and scalable data-to-model pipeline designed to construct AI-ready, multi-resolution climate–hydrological datasets. The framework integrates systematic station standardization, spatial and geometry validation via Google Earth Engine, and temporally aligned monthly covariate extraction for the period 2018–2022, producing complementary point-level and administrative-level (ADM1) representations for sequence-based and spatial analysis. Adopting a strict chronological evaluation protocol (training: 2018–2021; testing: 2022), we validate dataset readiness under deployment-aligned conditions. Results demonstrate that SaltGuard preserves dominant hydro-climatic seasonality, robustly handles data gaps using month-wise climatology, and supports the temporal predictability of a physically informed salinity-risk proxy. By prioritizing data readiness and reproducibility, SaltGuard provides a transferable foundation for robust and scalable AI-based salinity intrusion monitoring, supporting operational water management and early warning systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: When LLMs Give Voting Advice: Bias, Coherence, and Educational Risk
Abstract: When used alongside Voting Advice Applications (VAAs), LLMs serve as informal civic learning systems, pairing stance labels with AI-generated explanations. We audit five commercial LLMs (Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4o, Grok 3, Mistral Large) using four European VAAs (Germany, Netherlands, Luxembourg, Czech Republic), analyzing 7,400 responses. Reasoning contradicts the stated stance in 3.2% of a stratified subsample of 1,000 cases, with a bimodal coherence distribution suggesting two distinct explanation regimes. All models align most strongly with Green and Social Democratic parties, with cross-national differences indicating unequal civic-learning impacts shaped by language-resource and VAA design factors. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Back to the Future: What Can Remixing Teach Us About Coding in the Age of AI

Title: EviGPU: An Evidence Collection Framework for GPU-TEEs
Abstract: GPU-accelerated AI applications are increasingly deployed on cloud platforms. Lightweight GPU-TEEs protect these applications on untrusted clouds with a small TCB. They collect execution evidence offline, such as computation graphs and kernel binaries, and enforce it online to safeguard the computation. However, such evidence is inherently hardware-specific. Collecting it requires access to a GPU identical to the deployment target, which increases cost and reduces usability. This paper presents EviGPU, an evidence collection framework that eliminates this hardware dependency. EviGPU comprises a GPU Generator that emulates the target device without real hardware and an Evidence Collector that collects execution evidence from the emulated environment. We prototype EviGPU for NVIDIA GPUs and evaluate it on representative AI applications. Across all tested configurations and applications, EviGPU produces evidence identical to that collected on real GPUs. Moreover, EviGPU completes evidence collection 2.42 × faster than real execution on average. Title: Visual Attention Transitions and Self-regulated Help Seeking in Programming Comprehension
Abstract: This study uses a process-oriented mixed-method analysis to examine learners solving programming comprehension tasks in an online support system, integrating interaction logs, wearable eye tracking, and reflective interviews. Results indicate that performance differences were more clearly reflected in process coordination patterns than in aggregate exposure measures. Title: A Multi-agent AI System with Collective Intelligence and Adaptive Reasoning for Automotive Fault Diagnosis

Abstract: As AI (artificial intelligence) technology improves quickly, more and more businesses are using AI-powered systems to make their work more efficient and accurate. As the designs of modern cars become more complicated, the need for maintenance support that is quick, accurate, and flexible is growing. This process is not only time-consuming and expensive, but it is also very prone to mistakes made by people. Current onboard diagnostics (OBD) systems give standardized fault reports, but they don’t let you easily understand them and don’t have the important ability to reason about context. Additionally, current systems have trouble understanding natural language inputs or combining unstructured data, like driver complaints, which are important for finding complex problems. Title: Leadership, Cultural Intelligence, and AI-Assisted Governance: A Compliance Perspective on the Pharmaceutical and Medical Device Industries
Abstract: This article examines how transformational leadership and cultural intelligence (CQ) shape regulatory compliance in the pharmaceutical and medical device industries. Compliance, defined here as the sustained organizational capacity to meet regulatory standards through culture and conduct rather than procedural adherence alone, is increasingly challenged by the demands of Compliance 4.0—an era in which human behavioral governance and automated algorithmic oversight must operate in tandem. Despite alignment with international standards, under-reporting persists, limiting organizational learning. Title: When AI Joins the Thread: A Computational Analysis of Gendered Human-AI Interactions on Weibo

Through the integration of computational methods and large language model (LLM)-based annotation, the study demonstrates how these subtle linguistic features vary systematically by user gender. Title: Psychological need experiences inside and outside gaming as predictors of adolescent problematic gaming and well-being: A longitudinal test of the Need Density Hypothesis
Abstract: Video games are a widely valued activity because they are densely packed with elements that can satisfy one's basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness and can, as such, support healthy development. However, drawing on Self-Determination Theory, the Need Density Hypothesis posits that a lack of need satisfaction outside of video gaming in combination with need satisfaction inside of gaming may render adolescents vulnerable to gradually disengage from less satisfying domains, fostering obsessive gaming patterns and poorer mental health. Because empirical support for this hypothesis has been largely cross-sectional, this one-year longitudinal study investigates whether discrepancies in adolescents' psychological need experiences inside versus outside of video gaming predict changes in problematic gaming behavior and associated outcomes over time. We surveyed 661 adolescents (Mean age = 14.36; 55.98% boys) who played video games in two waves conducted one year apart. Results of polynomial regression analyses found partial evidence for the Need Density Hypothesis: Adolescents scoring higher on inside gaming than on outside of gaming need satisfaction showed increases in problematic video gaming, and mental health problems over time, while no interactive effects of need satisfaction inside gaming and need frustration outside of gaming were found. Moreover, low need satisfaction outside of video gaming was identified as a robust standalone predictor of increases in problems. These findings highlight that adolescents' vulnerability to problematic video gaming, as well as to associated mental health problems, is shaped by the interplay between need-satisfying experiences outside and inside the gaming world. Title: From Predictive Models to Actionable Recommendations: A Survey of Counterfactual Approaches in Student Dropout
Abstract: Student dropout remains a critical challenge in global education, representing a significant loss of human capital. Although data-driven approaches like predictive modeling have achieved high accuracy in identifying at-risk students, a “trust gap” persists among educators. Prediction alone is insufficient; stakeholders require interpretable insights to guide effective intervention. This survey explores the paradigm shift from passive “black-box” detection to “actionable prescription” through the lens of Counterfactual Explanations (CFE). Adopting an analytical framework, we systematically interrogate the literature regarding variable risk definitions, data source diversity, prediction horizons, and feature actionability. Our analysis reveals a critical disconnect: while many models prioritize accuracy using immutable features, few focus on the actionable variables necessary for generating feasible pedagogical recommendations. Title: A federated contrastive bifocal distillation approach for heterogeneous IIoT devices
Abstract: Due to the heterogeneity and non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) nature of device data in the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), existing federated learning (FL) algorithms face significant challenges, including global model performance degradation caused by client drift and the potential loss of local dataset performance when clients integrate features from the global model. CBDFL mitigates the negative impact of client drift through a bifocal distillation mechanism that decouples explicit target-class knowledge and implicit non-target-class knowledge. Meanwhile, supervised contrastive distillation is introduced from the server to the clients, enabling client models to integrate global knowledge while preserving their local feature representations. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and the industrial Severstal dataset show that CBDFL consistently outperforms representative FL methods under non-IID and model heterogeneity (MH) settings. In the main benchmark experiments, CBDFL improves accuracy by at least 5.27% in non-IID settings and at least 3.08% in heterogeneous non-IID settings compared with baseline methods. Title: Cascaded Bias Mitigation with Multi-objective Bayesian Optimization for Credit Scoring
Abstract: Machine learning has become a core component of modern credit scoring systems, but it often exacerbates gender disparities due to structural biases in the data. These biases primarily arise from two sources: the underrepresentation of certain groups and confounding correlations between sensitive attributes and predictive features. Existing mitigation techniques typically focus on only one of these sources, resulting in limited fairness improvements or notable accuracy degradation. To address this problem, this paper proposes a cascaded bias mitigation method that targets different types of bias in each stage, because the two sources operate through different mechanisms. Pre-processing stage adopts a data-level rebalancing operator to mitigate data imbalance, and in- and post-processing stages jointly address structural bias induced by sensitive-confounded feature-label correlations. Title: Robust Heterogeneous Federated Learning Against Untargeted Poisoning Attacks via Sign-Space Consistency
Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without sharing sensitive data, but its distributed nature makes the system vulnerable to untargeted poisoning attacks, especially stealthy variants. The challenge is amplified in non-IID settings, where benign update divergence obscure stealthy malicious updates, rendering defenses based on raw-update metrics (e.g., distances or statistics) ineffective. In this paper, we first identify the failure of existing raw-update metric-based defenses and their root cause. Motivated by this, we propose FedSSC, a defense against untargeted attacks which transforms updates into sign-space to mitigate non-IID divergences and extracts robust features via complementary sign-consistency metrics. An adaptive statistical detector is introduced to isolate anomalies. Title: Multimodal fusion for complete motion trajectory reasoning in articulated object manipulation
Abstract: The manipulation of articulated objects for part-level motion is crucial due to their prevalence in real-world applications. Although current manipulation methods have improved interaction quality, they share a common issue: neglecting the completeness of motion trajectories. For example, when we use a front-loading drum washing machine, the expected action is to manipulate the door from fully closed to fully open. However, these methods might only result in it being half-open. To tackle this limitation, we introduce a novel framework for optimizing motion trajectories based on multimodal fusion. Specifically, we explicitly model trajectory completeness and propose a motion trajectory construction paradigm (MTCP). This paradigm is applied to a large-scale dataset containing a wide range of articulated objects, generating high-quality motion trajectories for multimodal fusion. Furthermore, to handle trajectory homogeneity, we propose a trajectory enhancement policy (TEP) that enriches the trajectory set by capturing the multimodal distribution of feasible trajectories. Subsequently, to enhance the learning efficiency and task adaptability of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), we propose a learning strategy for 3D perception inspired by 2D perception (3PI2P), complemented by a progressive reasoning approach. This strategy integrates a dual-branch input design using RGB images and depth maps, combined with six forms of visual question answering tasks, to achieve collaborative reasoning and deep fusion of 2D semantics and 3D geometric information. The robustness and generalizability of the framework are demonstrated through evaluations in both simulation and real-world environments. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: From Exploration to Creation: How Teachers Orchestrate AI-Supported Learning in History Classrooms
Abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into classrooms, how teachers organize AI-supported learning in practice remains underexplored. This study examines teacher orchestration in AI-supported history instruction by analyzing how teachers designed and enacted lessons using HistoriaCraft, an LLM-based platform for authoring and exploring historical simulations, in Grade 6 and Grade 8 classrooms. Following a formative study with 15 teachers, we co-designed three-session lesson sequences with four teachers and observed their implementation with 118 students across six classes. The lessons were structured as a sequence of exploration and creation activities, which we conceptualize as two instructional modes: Exploration Mode, in which students engaged with teacher-authored simulations, and Creation Mode, in which students authored their own. Drawing on classroom observations and teacher interviews, we characterize how teachers organized instruction differently across these modes, adopting distinct roles in structuring sense-making and fostering student ownership and inquiry. We further analyze differences in student engagement across modes using interaction logs, observational data, and surveys, identifying systematic shifts in student discourse, participation structures, and perceived agency. Title: InstructFusionFormer: Instruction-Conditioned Multimodal Fusion for Esophageal Disease Diagnosis and Staging

Title: Cybersecurity Specialists’ Perspectives on the Use of Generative AI in Professional Practice
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: The use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) in cybersecurity is receiving increasing attention, with existing research largely focusing on technical applications such as penetration testing, malware detection, and threat hunting. However, comparatively little is known about how cybersecurity specialists perceive Gen AI, how they currently use it in practice, and what challenges and opportunities they associate with its adoption. To address this gap, we conducted a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with 11 cybersecurity specialists. The interviews explored participants’ current work practices, their experiences and attitudes toward Gen AI, and their views on how Gen AI could support or improve their work. The interviews were transcribed and analysed using a thematic analysis approach. In addition, a user experiment was included to capture insights into commonly used cybersecurity tools and to inform discussions about desired features and requirements for future Gen AI-based solutions. Title: Balancing Privacy and Security: An Ethical Analysis of AI-Driven Surveillance in the UAE, USA, and UK
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: The explosion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in state surveillance presents profound ethical challenges, primarily concerning the loss of individual privacy in the name of national security. This paper conducts a comparative ethical analysis of AI-driven surveillance practices in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the United States (USA), and the United Kingdom (UK). Through a qualitative methodology that examines legal frameworks, key case studies (Falcon Eye, PRISM, Tempora), and theoretical lenses including panopticism and social contract theory, we identify distinct ethical trade-offs shaped by governance models. Our findings indicate that the UAE’s centralized governance enables efficient but high-risk surveillance with minimal transparency or legal recourse, prioritizing state security over individual privacy. The USA’s democratic framework fosters public discourse and judicial oversight, creating a dynamic, although contentious, balance that offers stronger civil liberties protections. The UK employs a hybrid model, combining extensive surveillance powers under the Investigatory Powers Act with formal oversight mechanisms, though it faces criticism for legitimizing bulk data collection. The paper concludes that without robust, transparent legal safeguards and international cooperation, AI-driven surveillance inherently risks violating fundamental human rights. We propose policy recommendations centered on enhanced transparency, independent oversight, ethical AI auditing, and cross-border regulatory alignment to navigate the ethical tightrope between security imperatives and the preservation of privacy. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: AdaGauss: Adaptive, Acoustic, and Pruning for High-Fidelity Audio-Driven Talking Head Generation

Abstract: Existing NeRF-based methods for audio-driven 3D talking head generation incur substantial computational overhead and offer limited control over local facial expressions, such as those in the lips and eyes. It also employs a region-aware progressive pruning-distillation strategy to compress Gaussian primitives by 71% under dense teacher guidance, reducing rendering overhead. Title: Electroencephalogram (EEG) Subband Features During Eye Opening and Closure Enable Classification of Amblyopes and Visually Normal Controls: A Pilot Study
Abstract: Amblyopia is a neurodevelopmental disorder wherein abnormal visual experience during childhood permanently impairs vision in one eye. An EEG biomarker of amblyopia would be useful for screening, diagnosis, and monitoring. We recorded three-channel EEG from amblyopes (n = 7) and visually normal controls (n = 6) instructed to close both eyes, open both eyes, close the right eye, and then close the left eye. A gradient boosting classifier outperformed all others investigated with 78.1% correct accuracy (chance performance 50% correct). Permutation-based analysis revealed the importance of alpha- (8 to 12 Hz) and gamma-band (> 30 Hz) features derived from recordings contralateral to the dominant eye. Title: Pedagogical Values Mediate Teacher Perceptions on Using AI to Support Students’ Learning of Scientific Explanations

Title: HEGait: Optimizing heatmaps with an end-to-end framework for higher-accuracy gait recognition
Abstract: Pose-based gait recognition methods can effectively exclude covariates unrelated to gait (e.g. background, carriers, and clothing), making them a prominent research direction. However, these heatmaps primarily encode static keypoint positions and fail to capture motion patterns, limiting their suitability for gait recognition. Unlike existing methods, HEGait jointly optimizes the pose estimator and gait recognition module under the supervision of gait-specific losses, enabling the generated heatmaps to implicitly encode gait-related motion features. Furthermore, we design a heatmap refinement module (HRM) that integrates keypoint-level and pixel-level attention mechanisms to explore the contributions of different keypoints and heatmap positions. This work provides a novel perspective for gait recognition research: optimizing intermediate representations. Title: When Students Confide in AI: Navigating the ELIZA Effect of Social Presence Through Pedagogical Boundaries in Gen-AI Mediated Education
Abstract: The integration of GenAI chatbots as virtual tutors in online distance learning introduces a persistent tension between social presence and pedagogical focus. Drawing on Design Science Research (DSR), this study reports on two iterative design cycles involving second-year university students in an online distance learning context, this paper examines how the emotional responsiveness of GenAI chatbots, while effective in establishing social presence, risks overshadowing their academic purpose when not designed for it. This is significant as it may lead to emotional dependency and misalignment with educational goals. Tracing how this concern drives spontaneous emotional disclosure, from its earliest manifestation in Weizenbaum’s ELIZA effect through to current GenAI implementations, the paper argues that social presence in GenAI-mediated environments requires ethical calibration rather than maximization. Analyzing chatlog interactions showing students presenting with psychological and situational distress, boundary testing behavior and anthropomorphic projection patterns, the paper argues that optimal facilitation of social presence requires Relational Ethics: a calibrated balance between recognition and restraint that acknowledges student affect without enabling dependency. Three architectural design safeguards are proposed: Adaptive Relational Engagement, the intentional shift from emotional validation to academic strategizing. Ethically Bounded Personalization, which mitigates affective projection through functional identity framing, and Human-in-the-Loop Escalation Protocols for distress recognition and professional referral. These mechanisms embed ethical engagement directly within design logic, negating psychological dependency while preserving the benefits of GenAI-mediated support. Title: Ethical Reasoning About AI in Middle Schools: Students’ Misconceptions and Mental Models in Sociocultural Contexts
Abstract: Transparency and Explainability (TAE) are core ethical principles of artificial intelligence (AI), yet little is known about how young learners reason about relevant ethical issues. Meanwhile, influenced by public misinformation and limited understanding, they often hold naïve and incorrect ideas—misconceptions—about AI. This study examines patterns of ethical reasoning among middle school students regarding TAE, focusing on their misconceptions and the mental models underlying the misconceptions. Using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, we analyzed student responses from a scenario-based multiple-choice test of AI Ethical Competence (N = 1,847) and a stimulus-recall cognitive interview (N = 20) in China. The analysis identified six misconceptions reflected in students’ incorrect test answers. One example was the belief that developers may withhold explanations if users can understand the difficulties involved and if disclosure may threaten commercial interests. Behind the misconceptions, three mental models were specified to show coherent patterns of ethical reasoning: relational or pragmatic explainability, performance-first reasoning, and delegated transparency to authority. Within these models, explainability is frequently treated as relational, situational, or substitutable by interpersonal communication, trust, or expert approval, rather than as a principled requirement linked to accountability and informed consent. Title: Minimizing Data Exposure in Higher Education LLM Applications: Evaluating the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for Preserving Privacy in Academic Advising
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in academic advising and student dashboards. However, traditional full-record integrations send complete student profiles to third-party model providers. This paper checks if the Model Context Protocol (MCP) can lower exposure by making the model retrieve only necessary fields through logged tools. Using fully synthetic U.S. undergraduate records, we compare a traditional full-record tool design that includes seven profile fields in every request with an MCP per-field tool design across two advising tasks. We measure privacy risk with a tiered leakage score and evaluate response quality using an LLM-as-a-judge approach. Across three runs, the traditional approach gives the highest average leakage score of 30, while MCP reduces leakage to about 10 mainly by avoiding access to identifiers. However, this comes with a drop in quality that depends on the task (overall from about 5.0 to 3.1). These findings show that MCP can significantly reduce the exposure of confidential student information while still providing high-quality advising for tasks that require less data. Lastly, the tiered leakage metric and MCP tool-call logs together make privacy exposure transparent and measurable. Title: Integrating Educator-Designed AI Tools in Classrooms: Teachers’ Practices, Perceptions, and Concerns
Abstract: Most prior research has examined teachers’ adoption and perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) in education by positioning teachers primarily as end users of prebuilt, general-purpose AI systems. As a result, existing findings may not generalize to teacher-centered forms of AI integration in which educators have greater agency. AI expertise and education level were associated with perceived difficulty of teaching with AI, whereas AI literacy was associated with perceived helpfulness for both teachers and students. Analysis of teachers’ concerns revealed that student-centered concerns were most prevalent, with system-level concerns more common among K-12 teachers. Title: Influence propagation controlled walks: A representation learning approach for community detection in heterogeneous information networks
Abstract: Community detection in heterogeneous information networks poses significant challenges due to the diverse structural and semantic characteristics inherent in these networks. Subsequently, we employ the skip-gram model on all the IPCwalks of each metapath to learn the low-dimensional latent features for each node. An attention mechanism is then employed to aggregate node features, incorporating a multiplicative factor of the clustering coefficient and influence propagation score. Title: An Integrated Methodological Framework for Urban Well-Being Assessment: An Application to the City of Siracusa (Italy)
Abstract: In recent years, the concept of urban well-being and quality of life has emerged as a central theme for the planning agenda. Orienting urban planning toward enhancing urban well-being, while properly considering its complexity stemming from its multi-dimensional nature, calls for appropriate knowledge bases and assessment tools to support decisions on actions toward urban livability. Based on these premises, the paper proposes an integrated methodological framework for urban well-being assessment, which leads to the definition of an Urban Well-Being (UWB) composite indicator. The proposed framework integrates a “quantitative” and “data-based” approach with a “qualitative” and “perception-based” one, thus overcoming the mere data-based approach to the theme and providing a comprehensive assessment of well-being and its distribution mechanisms within an urban area. The framework’s preliminary application to Syracuse - a mid-sized city in the Sicily Region (Italy) – demonstrates its potential as a decision support tool, together with its limits and future research challenges to effectively orient urban policies towards greater equity, awareness, and quality of life. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Explainable AI Identifies High Retrospective Prodromal Symptom Burden in Parkinson’s Disease
Abstract: Characterizing heterogeneity in Parkinson’s disease (PD) related to prodromal symptom burden may provide insight into early disease mechanisms. Wearable gait analysis offers a scalable approach to capture subtle motor alterations. We developed an interpretable machine learning framework to identify high retrospective prodromal symptom burden (≥3 symptoms) in 275 individuals with PD using single-sensor trunk accelerometry. A three-stage feature selection pipeline identified five key predictors: multiscale entropy (MSE) along three axes, vertical improved harmonic ratio (iHRv), and body weight. A Random Forest classifier achieved ROCAUC = 0.84, PRAUC = 0.86, F1-score = 0.76. Class imbalance was addressed via CTGAN-based augmentation applied within the training set. Explainability analyses consistently identified increased medio-lateral gait complexity (MSEml) and reduced iHRv as dominant contributors. These findings define an interpretable gait phenotype associated with retrospective prodromal burden in PD. While not reflecting true prodromal prediction, this framework provides mechanistic insight into early motor alterations and supports scalable digital phenotyping. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: From Writing Traces to Personalised Support: Guiding LLMs with Stylometric Fingerprints
Abstract: Generative AI holds great potential for personalised learning, yet its outputs often remain generic. A key barrier is the difficulty Large Language Models (LLMs) face in interpreting quantitative learner data. This study introduces StyloPrompt, a three-phase method that converts quantitative writing analytics (stylometric fingerprints) into structured natural language descriptors to enable interpretable conditioning of LLMs. In Phase 1, variance analysis of over 1,000 student essays validated 19 robust features that stably distinguish authors. Phase 2 operationalised these fingerprints in a controlled style transfer task—serving as a proxy for adaptive educational communication—comparing raw numerical prompts against two natural language encodings (NL-Binning and NL-Distribution). Phase 3 evaluated outcomes on held-out data using similarity metrics. Results indicate that the NL-Distribution method most effectively conditioned the LLM, achieving an 89% success rate when transferring between dissimilar writing profiles. Title: Artificial Intelligence in Bosnia and Herzegovina: Scenarios and Strategic Pathways from the Perspective of Public Administration
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in public administration to improve efficiency, services, and decision-making. In post-transition systems such as Bosnia and Herzegovina, the AI adoption raises particular governance, capacity, and coordination challenges. This paper examines the current state and possible future use of AI in state-level public administration in BiH using a foresight-oriented, mixed-method research design. Drawing from a nationwide survey of 516 civil servants and participatory roundtables with representatives from key state institutions, the study combines empirical findings with foresight methods, to explore how institutional capacity, governance gaps, and human capital constraints may shape AI adoption through 2030. The analysis identifies three plausible trajectories: fragmented experimentation, coordinated capacity-building, and externally driven automation, and discusses their implications for public administration. The paper concludes with strategic directions for responsible and context-sensitive AI adoption, contributing to research on AI governance in post-transition public sectors. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A Matter of Perspective: Contrasting User and Subject-Matter Experts’ Sensemaking of LLM Feedback on Instructional Discourse
Abstract: We investigated how lived expertise of users and domain expertise of subject matter experts (SMEs) shapes sensemaking of qualitative LLM feedback aimed at improving instructional practice. We conducted a think-aloud study of the Talk Trees tool that provides LLM-based feedback (strengths and missed opportunities) on the quality of discourse in a high-dosage math tutoring context. Participants included tutors with varying levels of experience, expert annotators of discourse moves (framework SMEs) and an expert in pedagogy grounded in discourse practices. We found that who (type of stakeholder) is doing the evaluating was inextricably linked to what they noticed and how they formed judgements. Tutors prioritized personalized relevance and usefulness over technical accuracy, framework SMEs narrowly evaluated feedback based on definitional correctness, and the pedagogy SME integrated both accuracy and instructional context to provide a more holistic evaluation of the LLM. Notably, technically inaccurate feedback was often perceived as pedagogically useful by tutors, more so than the experts. These findings suggest that evaluating LLM feedback requires multi-perspective, sensemaking approaches that go beyond traditional evaluations of accuracy alone and highlight the importance of situating LLM evaluations in the context of user-facing tools. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: When Teachers Use AI Chatbots and Are Trained for It: Impact on Learning Design Quality and Cognitive Effort
Abstract: AI chatbots are increasingly used by teachers to support learning design, yet evidence is still limited on how AI access and guidance on using AI affect learning design quality and teachers’ cognitive experiences. This study investigated a teacher training aimed at fostering pedagogically-grounded chatbot interactions during learning design. Thirteen higher education teachers completed a within-subjects study across three conditions: designing learning activities without AI, with AI access, and with AI after receiving training on effective AI interaction strategies. Design artifacts were evaluated for attainment of predefined pedagogical goals and complemented with measures of cognitive effort, training evaluation, and adoption intentions. Results show that AI access improved design quality and significantly lowered perceived cognitive effort. Training did not further improve design quality but slightly increased cognitive load, likely due to the deliberate application of newly learned strategies. Title: Less is More: XAI-Driven Feature Selection for Efficient Molecular Property Prediction
Abstract: Molecular descriptors are commonly employed to build predictive models for molecular properties; however, their usage comes with several challenges. The exponential growth of available descriptors and the complexity of the required algorithms often result in opaque, ‘black-box’ models that lack interpretability. Traditional feature selection methods focus on statistical optimization, but they often fail to capture the physicochemical drivers and complex interactions central to the chemical domain. In this work, we propose an explainability-driven feature selection framework that uses Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to identify the minimal necessary subset of descriptors for predicting some molecular properties of the QM9 dataset. This framework serves not only as a dimensionality reduction tool but also as a validation mechanism that ensures the model’s logic is consistent with the laws of chemistry. By iteratively reducing the initial set of 1057 Mordred descriptors, we show that feature selection using SHAP values might outperform traditional methods in several scenarios, such as predicting Rotational Constants C and B, Internal Energy at 0 K, and Electronic Spatial Extent. For other molecular properties, the SHAP-guided feature selection delivers similar performance to baseline feature selection methods, such as LASSO, Random Forest, CFS, as well as Pearson and Spearman correlations. Our findings show that the feature space can be compressed by more than 90% with no loss in predictive capability. For some thermodynamic and electronic properties, the SHAP-guided feature reduction has also improved generalization performance due to the elimination of non-informative features. More importantly, the variables surviving this selection process are not simply mathematical conveniences. They map directly onto recognized physicochemical theory, pinpointing the precise electronic and topological mechanisms responsible for molecular behavior. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Classification of multivariate signals using the Hilbert transform and Riemannian geometry
Abstract: We describe two Hilbert transform-based methods for augmenting covariance matrices from multivariate signals. The two methods are shown to be isometric under the Riemannian affine-invariant metric on the manifold of symmetric/Hermitian positive definite matrices. The augmented representations distinguish cases that standard covariances clearly cannot and, when paired with a Riemannian minimum distance to mean classifier, improve classification of both synthetic data and real electroencephalography (EEG) data without introducing any extra hyperparameters. This novel combination of methods also significantly improves tangent space classifier accuracy on the same dataset, outperforming state-of-the-art classifiers with similarly sized parameter grids. We also examine how the augmented covariances interact with the minimum distance to mean classifier and show how multivariate cross-covariance functions behave under the Hilbert transform. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Graph–language synergy in intelligent information systems: A systems-level review of GNN–LLM integration, GraphRAG, and knowledge-grounded reasoning
Abstract: This review highlights the findings of studies conducted during 2020–2026 on the application of graph neural networks (GNNs), large language models (LLMs), knowledge graphs, and graph-based retrieval approaches (GraphRAGs) to intelligent information systems. These findings have been grouped into a single study framework, namely the framework for intelligent information systems integration, which covers various aspects of integration. The paper provides a unified systems-level approach to linking architectural design decisions with retrieval and reasoning behavior in graph-language systems. Based on a carefully selected set of system-level studies, the authors show that across the reviewed studies, graph-preserving approaches are reported to improve multi-hop reasoning, evidence localization, and interpretability compared with text-only or graph-serialization baselines in several benchmark settings. Good performance is highly dependent on high-quality graph construction, proper retrieval, and the costs of the entire process. The use of graph-language synergy is most effective when the graphs serve as functionally involved parts of retrieval and reasoning, rather than merely as background information. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Evaluating manual and robotic placement of reusable modular formwork for digitally integrated concrete manufacturing
Abstract: The construction industry is under increasing pressure to reduce the environmental impact of concrete while maintaining efficient production. Structural optimisation offers a method for reducing material usage but typically results in non-standard geometries and internal voids that are not economically viable to produce using conventional formwork approaches. In precast concrete production, such features are often not systematically integrated into the manufacturing process, as existing solutions rely on disposable materials or labour-intensive manual procedures. This study investigates a modular, reusable formwork system for the generation of small voids in concrete elements, designed for robotic placement. A robotic pick-and-place process was implemented within a digitally supported production environment, and experimental trials were conducted to compare robotic placement, manual placement, and conventional EPS-based practice. Across all investigated placement scenarios, the mean module displacement amounted to 0.354 mm with a standard deviation of 0.806 mm, while no systematic differences in geometric performance were observed between manual and robotic placement. Subsequent process stages, particularly concrete compaction, contributed the highest to the observed geometric deviations. Manual placement times varied with operator experience and showed higher variability. Simulation results show that removing operator-mediated interruptions and adjusting motion parameters reduced robotic cycle times by 82.5 % under idealised conditions, reaching a level comparable to experienced manual operators in the laboratory experiments. The findings demonstrate the feasibility of robotic and manual placement of reusable modular formwork and provide a quantitative basis for the further development of digitally supported precast concrete manufacturing processes. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Testing Reinforcement Learning Applications with Test Suites Generated from Ontologies
Abstract: Validating and verifying Artificial Intelligence applications is required to assure trust. This is especially important when using automated learning, such as reinforcement learning, to identify behavioral shortcomings before deployment. In this paper, we introduce an ontology-based testing approach for generating test suites for reinforcement learning applications. This approach allows generating scenarios that a system must be capable of handling based on knowledge of its environment. Title: From Tool to Craft: Teaching Ethical Generative AI through Practice-Based Workshops in the Arts
Abstract: As generative technologies continue to evolve, artistic communities and educational institutions face significant ethical challenges. Some integrate generative AI in their pedagogy, as a material, a tool or a mode of critique, while others fundamentally reject it. This paper proposes a reproducible, resource-aware, ethically grounded workshop model for teaching GenAI in arts education. The model is implemented in two pilot workshops conducted by UNATC as part of the EU-funded ELICIA program, which aims to advance AI-driven innovation and entrepreneurial education within Higher Education Institutions. The modules promote AI literacy by adopting the perspective of AI as craft, rather than opaque generative tool. The pedagogical design uses a constructionist and practice-based framework to foster engagement with AI’s unpredictability, limitations, and ethical implications. To ensure transparency, customization and control, locally run models and interfaces (FluxDev, StyleGan, ComfyUI, Ollama etc.) were prioritized over proprietary cloud platforms. For impact assessment, entry and exit questionnaires were provided during each module, with a reflective assignment and a follow-up questionnaire two months after the workshops. Due to the limited number of participants, the results are not statistically generalizable. However, we discern patterns of decreasing AI anxiety from one module to the other, increased usage in the long term and a shift towards more articulated ethical concerns. The paper concludes by reflecting on the workshops’ challenges and subsequent impact, and considering their implications for future phases of the project. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Designing for Accessibility: How Inclusive Practices Enhance Usability and Innovation in Educational Publishing
Abstract: Digital accessibility in educational publishing remains structurally underexplored: existing research addresses generic web platforms or simple interactive environments, leaving complex, multimedia-rich application ecosystems largely unexamined. This paper addresses that gap through a longitudinal case study of laZ Ebook, a cross-platform digital textbook application developed by Zanichelli, in which WCAG 2.2 AA conformance was established as a first-class engineering requirement from project inception. The study operationalises accessibility-by-design within a commercial agile development context and evaluates its outcomes through three independent empirical studies: a moderated assistive-technology evaluation with users with visual impairments conducted at prototype stage; a remote unmoderated mobile usability study (N = 24); and a remote unmoderated desktop usability study (N = 12). Quantitative and qualitative findings converge on three principal results: overall satisfaction rates of 92% (mobile) and 75% (desktop); zero friction points attributable to accessibility-driven design decisions across all evaluation phases; and systematic evidence that semantic structure, contrast standards, and labelling conventions adopted for assistive technology compliance produced measurable usability gains for the general user population. These findings extend the empirical evidence base linking accessibility conformance to universal usability to educational app publishing, and demonstrate that institutional commitment, expressed as a project-level requirement is the operative condition for accessibility-by-design to succeed. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A Framework for LLM Integration in Secondary Education: Insights from Computing Teachers
Abstract: As large language model (LLM)-based tools come to dominate education, computing teachers face a distinctive dual challenge: they must both use AI tools for instruction while also teaching students to work critically with these emerging technologies. Although research has examined teachers’ general use of LLMs and integration of technologies, little is known about the specific processes teachers follow when integrating these tools into their classrooms, particularly in contexts where the technology itself is part of the curriculum. This study addresses this gap through interviews and surveys with 11 secondary computing teachers in the United States currently using LLM tools in their classrooms. We developed and empirically grounded a framework of implementation steps organized into six phases: Prepare, Adapt Curriculum, Lead, Assess, Synthesize, and Share. Our findings reveal that while teachers endorsed the framework overall, significant barriers concentrate in the Preparation phase, including administrative restrictions, resource scarcity, and technical infrastructure limitations. In contrast, classroom implementation steps were rated as both important and manageable, suggesting teachers successfully leverage existing pedagogical practices once preparation barriers are overcome. The institutional context emerged as a primary factor in implementation variation, with successful teachers following two distinct pathways: either strong institutional support with flexible policies or highly developed personal strategies combined with robust professional networks. We conclude with recommendations for targeted interventions, including the development of open-access age-appropriate resources, flexible institutional policies, and professional development focused on preparation-phase challenges. Title: Vision-based human–robot collaboration for wire harness assembly in automotive manufacturing
Abstract: Wire harness assembly exemplifies a non-rigid object assembly task that remains challenging to automate due to object deformability, occlusions, high variability, and workspace constraints. This study introduces a vision-based human–robot collaboration (HRC) framework developed for wire harness assembly in automotive final assembly processes. In this system, the robot performs repetitive, force-intensive tasks, while the human operator handles operations that require dexterity and adaptive decision-making. The proposed approach combines marker-based pose estimation of wire harness components with a hand-triggered control scheme. Detected hand landmarks define a region of interest, enabling intentional, context-aware robot activation. The HRC framework is validated by performing wire harness installation on the vehicle chassis. A two-phase within-subjects experimental study compares manual installation with HRC-assisted installation in both laboratory and industrially relevant environments, corresponding to Technology Readiness Level 4 to 6. The results indicate that robotic assistance significantly reduces localized physical discomfort and physical demand while maintaining a high success rate in wire harness installation. However, overall workload does not differ significantly between HRC and manual conditions. In the HRC condition, both mental demand and average assembly time increase significantly compared to manual assembly. Cycle-time analysis reveals that the robot execution phase accounts for the largest proportion of total time in the collaborative workflow. These findings suggest that vision-based HRC can provide targeted ergonomic benefits for non-rigid object assembly, while also introducing cognitive and temporal trade-offs. Therefore, real-world deployment requires further improvement in interaction fluency and throughput. Title: Evaluating Students’ AI Literacy and Reflective Capacity in an Entrepreneurship Course Using Professor E
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has the potential as a powerful tool to enhance and strengthen student learning experiences. Students depend on GenAI for immediate answer generating rather than cultivating genuine reflection. To fill this gap, the researchers created a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-enabled chatbot, Professor E, which assists students in reflection using Gibbs’s reflective cycle. The researchers used an exploratory methodology to assess students’ AI literacy, reflective capabilities, and their impressions of the system’s educational design. This exploratory study examines students’ AI literacy and reflective capacity, as well as their impressions of the system’s educational design. The researchers gathered data through AI-student conversations to discern the principal themes arising from collaborations between students and AI in an entrepreneurship course in a Hong Kong business school. The focus group interview results highlighted students’ concerns on technical, practical, critical, and ethical factors when utilising Professor E for reflective purposes. The implementation of protected systems, role-playing, and RAG creation helped students in articulating personal thoughts, fostering empathy, and obtaining relevant, customised guidance linked with their project endeavours. Title: Green architectural tactics in ML-enabled systems: an LLM-based repository mining study
Abstract: Context: The increasing adoption of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies raises growing concerns about their environmental sustainability. Developing and deploying ML-enabled systems is computationally intensive, particularly during training and inference. Green AI has emerged to address these issues by promoting efficiency without sacrificing accuracy. While prior research has proposed catalogs of sustainable practices (i.e., green tactics), there remains limited understanding of their adoption in practice and whether additional, undocumented tactics exist. Objective: This study aims to investigate the extent to which existing sustainable practices are implemented in real-world ML-enabled systems and to identify previously undocumented practices that support environmental sustainability. Method: We conduct a mining software repository study on 205 open-source ML projects on GitHub. To support our analysis, we design a novel mechanism based on large language models (LLMs) capable of identifying both known and new sustainable practices from code repositories. Results: Our findings confirm that green tactics reported in the literature are used in practice, although adoption rates vary. Furthermore, our LLM-based approach reveals nine previously undocumented sustainable practices. Each tactic is supported with code examples to aid adoption and integration. Title: Geographic Patterns in Public Response to China’s National Childcare Subsidy: A Large-Scale Social Media Analysis

Abstract: Understanding public reception of major policy interventions is crucial for effective governance, yet traditional methods often lack the scale and timeliness to capture immediate, geographically diverse reactions. This study analyzes 352,448 social media comments posted immediately following China’s announcement of a unified national childcare subsidy system in July 2025. Employing large language model (LLM) classification, we identify six thematic categories that characterize public discourse. Geographic Information Systems (GIS) visualization reveals substantial spatial heterogeneity: while procedural uncertainty dominates nationally (37.11%), its intensity varies from 28.8% in Beijing to 52.8% in Qinghai, with western provinces showing higher concentrations of implementation concerns. Word cloud analysis uncovers distinct vocabularies across themes, from procedural terms to fairness-related expressions and economic considerations. Our findings highlight critical information asymmetries and the geographic digital divide in policy comprehension, suggesting the need for place-based communication strategies. This research demonstrates how computational text analysis, combined with spatial visualization, can illuminate the complex anatomy of public policy reception in the digital age. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.
