Title: Explainable and Accurate Valvular Heart Disease Screening Using Spectrogram-Based 2D-CNNs on PCG Signals
Abstract: Despite the recent advancements in artificial intelligence the cardiovascular diseases remain one of the leading causes of mortality worldwide, emphasizing the need for reliable and accessible diagnostic techniques. For the detection of the cardiac abnormalities, phonocardiography (PCG) which records heart sounds during the cardiac cycle, provides a non-invasive and cost-effective method. Conversely, manual interpretation of PCG signals depends heavily on clinician expertise and is often difficult by co-occurring pathologies, signal noise, and class imbalance in clinical datasets. This research focuses on an end-to-end deep learning pipeline for automated multi-label analysis of valvular heart diseases using PCG recordings. BMD-HS dataset containing 872 recordings sampled at 4000 Hz used for experimentations. The developed system implements a dual-stream learning strategy: handcrafted feature extraction combined with XGBoost for interpretability, and deep learning representations using one-dimensional and two-dimensional convolutional neural networks for improved predictive performance. Experimental results establish that altering raw PCG signals into Mel-Spectrogram representations and then it processes them with a 2D-CNN architecture achieving the best performance, with an AUC of 0.92 and an F1-score of 0.94 for the normal class. Furthermore, Explainable Artificial Intelligence techniques are implemented to confirm that the model focuses on medically significant spectral features. The developed framework provides a robust and low-cost solution for automated cardiac screening in resource-restricted healthcare environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Crowdsourced Data for Urban Planning: Evaluating OpenStreetMap Categorization Reliability in Historical Urban Centres
Abstract: The contemporary shift toward proximity-based urban planning relies heavily on high-resolution spatial data. Although Volunteered Geographic Information (VGI) platforms such as OpenStreetMap (OSM) provide extensive and free datasets, the quality of commercial POIs in dense historic centres has not yet been thoroughly examined through a functional taxonomy. This study assesses the spatial and semantic reliability of crowdsourced commercial data by comparing it with ground-truth surveys in the historic centres of Pisa and Lucca (Tuscany, Italy). Using a 23-tier meso-category classification framework, this research examines the degradation of VGI data through quantitative metrics and an analysis of mapping mismatches. The results reveal significant gaps in data coverage and a marked imbalance in Points of Interest (POIs) in both contexts: whilst tourism-oriented and food-related services are systematically over-represented, traditional retail suffers from severe under-mapping. Expanding spatial matching tolerances yields negligible improvements, confirming that the main constraint is a significant time lag rather than GPS inaccuracy. In both cities, the mapping community must contend with the rapid turnover of urban retail: the accumulation of ‘digital ghosts’ – fuelled by ‘excess’ and ‘replaced/inconsistent’ nodes – highlights a systemic failure to eliminate obsolete data. At the same time, a clear spatial-semantic dichotomy emerges: when a physical entity is actually mapped, its semantic categorisation proves to be remarkably accurate, in direct correlation with the ontological clarity of the object. Ultimately, this article suggests that, within these two densely touristic historic centres, OSM currently functions more as a cumulative historical record than as a real-time synchronised digital twin. This finding cautions against the potential structural risks of integrating unverified VGI into advanced urban computational models without accounting for the friction of urban commercial turnover. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Federated Vision Transformers for Privacy-Preserving Early Lung Cancer Detection
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: Lung cancer is one of the most common and deadly malignancies in the world and, according to the World Health Organization, continues to account for a significant share of cancer-related deaths. Conventional diagnostic methods, such as computed tomography (CT), positron emission tomography (PET), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, chest radiography, and ultimately biopsy, rely heavily on the expert interpretation of oncologists and radiologists. This human reliance can present early diagnosis with challenges such as time-consuming, heterogeneity of expert opinions, and the possibility of diagnostic error. Recently, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in supporting clinical decisions has proven to boost the accuracy, speed, and reproducibility of lung cancer diagnosis. However, sharing medical data between medical centers to train deep models faces serious limitations due to privacy and data security considerations. In this paper, a federated learning (FL)-based early lung cancer detection framework is proposed to train the model without transmitting raw patient data and to maintain confidentiality. To achieve higher diagnostic power, the vision core of the system is designed based on vision Transformers (ViTs) to extract key features from medical images in a robust and generalizable manner. Combining FL for security and privacy with the ViT architecture for robust detection provides a framework that can be used as an effective aid for healthcare professionals in early detection of lung cancer and lays the groundwork for reducing mortality from this disease. Experimental results show that the presented framework provides excellent performance in early detection of lung cancer, achieving an accuracy of 98.18% and an average precision, recall, and F1-score of 0.98 on the test set, which confirms the clinical significance and reliability of the proposed architecture in multicenter screening environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Evaluation of Human and AI-Generated Image Descriptions for STEM Charts by Varying Expertise Groups
Abstract: AI image description tools can facilitate the creation of alt-text for STEM charts; however, evaluating AI-generated results can be challenging. In this investigation, we selected common chart image types of increasing difficulty from educational textbooks. For each image, three descriptions were created, one by an accessibility expert with professional experience in image description for blind readers, and two by AI tools. These descriptions were then evaluated by three groups: a) accessibility experts, individuals with professional experience in image description; b) trained non-experts, individuals who are familiar with digital accessibility concepts; and c) untrained non-experts, individuals with no prior experience or knowledge in digital accessibility but with a background in STEM. The results show that human descriptions are currently preferred over AI-generated descriptions, and that AI-generated image descriptions require correction before they are appropriate for blind users. Accessibility professionals and trained non-experts respond similarly in image description evaluations. Untrained users’ responses differ only in a few instances and are evident when providing qualitative feedback. These findings show that some accessibility principles may be intuitive and that lightweight training in image description guidelines can yield evaluations as good as those of near experts. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: CARVE: Vulnerability Entity Alignment via Semantic Focusing and Staged Selection
Abstract: Cross-source vulnerability intelligence integration is essential for comprehensive threat assessment, offering stakeholders a holistic view for software risk mitigation and threat analysis. Existing work on vulnerability alignment largely follows graph-centered entity alignment pipelines, which often struggle to capture the fine-grained semantic differences needed to distinguish highly similar but non-equivalent vulnerability records across heterogeneous sources. Recent LLM-based entity alignment methods in general domains and emerging LLM-guided studies on vulnerability alignment suggest a promising direction. However, existing approaches either remain tied to graph-based candidate construction or are not tailored to vulnerability records, where identity often hinges on vendor/product scope, affected version ranges, and weakness cues. In this paper, we present CARVE, a supervised-training-free two-stage framework for vulnerability entity alignment inspired by recent purely LLM-based EA workflows. Rather than asking a language model to solve full-pool ranking in one step, CARVE first constructs semantically focused profiling-artifact summaries for full-pool candidate recall and then applies Filter-then-Select reasoning over the recalled Top-K set for contradiction-aware final selection. On CERT-NVD and SF-NVD, CARVE achieves end-to-end H@1 scores of 0.841 and 0.822, surpassing the strongest evaluated baselines by + 0.101 and + 0.187, respectively. On the extended GHSA-NVD supplementary evaluation set built from publicly available records after removing direct linkage cues, CARVE reaches H@1 = 0.952, supporting its robustness beyond the two main benchmarks. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Authors: Kitimoon S.; Mason E.; Mhaskar H.N.
Title: Localized kernel method for separation of linear chirps
Abstract: The task of separating a superposition of signals into its individual components is a common challenge encountered in various signal processing applications, especially in domains such as audio and radar signals. A previous paper by Chui and Mhaskar proposes a method called Signal Separation Operator (SSO) to find the instantaneous frequencies and amplitudes of such superpositions where both of these change continuously and slowly over time. In this paper, we amplify and modify this method in order to separate chirp signals in the presence of crossovers, a very low SNR, and discontinuities. We give a theoretical analysis of the behavior of SSO in the presence of noise to examine the relationship between the minimal separation, minimal amplitude, SNR, and sampling frequency. Our method is illustrated with a few examples, and numerical results are reported on a simulated dataset comprising 7 simulated signals. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier B.V. Authors: Ma Q.; Chai M.; Tan Y.; Choi J.; Kim J.; Harpstead E.; Kauffman G.; Wu T.
Title: “GenAI Defaults to Bias!” Gamify AI Literacy Through Reflections on Prompts
Abstract: As Generative AI (GenAI) becomes widespread, it is increasingly important for the public to understand the model’s behaviors and biases. However, existing AI literacy efforts miss opportunities to engage the general public to reflect on enduring GenAI bias and behaviors (e.g., how GenAI defaults to its internal bias in response to ambiguous or challenging prompts). In this work, we introduce ImaginAItion, a multiplayer game to help adults better reflect on GenAI bias and understand GenAI behaviors. ImaginAItion is grounded in reflective play to surface GenAI limitations by encouraging players to manipulate prompt specificity (e.g., an underspecified prompt “CEO” defaults to a white man). From ten sessions (n=30), we find that the game significantly improved players’ understanding of GenAI behaviors by 35% in accuracy. Qualitative analysis showed how game mechanisms supported player reflections, including on prompting strategies to mitigate GenAI bias. Title: Evaluating Learner Representations for Differentiation Prior to Instructional Outcomes
Abstract: Learner representations play a central role in educational AI systems, yet it is often unclear whether they preserve meaningful differences between students when instructional outcomes are unavailable or highly context-dependent. This work examines how to evaluate learner representations based on whether they retain separation between learners under a shared comparison rule. We introduce distinctiveness, a representation-level measure that evaluates how each learner differs from others in the cohort using pairwise distances, without requiring clustering, labels, or task-specific evaluation. Using student-authored questions collected through a conversational AI agent in an online learning environment, we compare representations based on individual questions with representations that aggregate patterns across a student’s interactions over time. Results show that learner-level representations yield higher separation, stronger clustering structure, and more reliable pairwise discrimination than interaction-level representations. Title: Artificial Intelligence Based Classification of Oral Cancer and Pre-malignant Disorders from Electrical Impedance Spectroscopy
Abstract: Over 180,000 people died of oral cancer worldwide in 2022 with most cases being diagnosed at late stages. Current diagnostic practice requires a scalpel biopsy which is invasive, painful, and time-consuming. In this work we investigated the potential use of electrical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) for fast and non-invasive oral cancer diagnosis. A small, harmless electrical current is applied to an oral lesion to obtain impedance measurements which can be used to infer information about the tissue structure. This work compares three artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms: logistic regression, support vector machines (SVM), and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks in classifying pre-cancerous and cancerous lesions from EIS readings collected from a small cohort of 35 patients. We found that LSTMs performed the best with a balanced accuracy of 82.3%. We incorporate demographic and clinical data into these models and found that performance was improved, with the LSTM achieving a balanced accuracy of 85.1%. This work demonstrates that the combination of EIS and AI can serve as a rapid, non-invasive, and painless diagnostic approach, complementing existing techniques for the detection of pre-malignant lesions and oral cancer. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: AI-based Cyberspace Mapping: Inference of HTTP(S) Message Ownership Information Based on LLM Fine-Tuning
Abstract: In the field of cyberspace mapping, HTTP(S), as the most common application-layer protocol on the Internet, carries rich network asset information in its messages. Extracting named entities such as enterprises and institutions from these messages is crucial for identifying network asset ownership, correlation relationships, and potential risks. Traditional entity recognition methods in cyberspace mapping typically rely on rule-based matching or BERT model extraction; however, both approaches exhibit significant limitations when handling complex message data. To address this issue, this study leverages the powerful reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to propose a reliability-constrained cognitive alignment fine-tuning framework. Through multi-task joint training and chain-of-thought annotation, a high-quality dataset containing 3,000 samples was constructed, and an 8B-parameter LLM was successfully fine-tuned. Test results show that the model can efficiently perform ownership information inference from message data and excels in handling complex scenarios such as implicit entities, multiple entities, and ultra-long messages. Its performance is significantly superior to rule-based matching and BERT models, and it demonstrates good generalization capabilities on conventional natural language text. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: BabeLLM: A unified taxonomy for NLP-based LLM cybersecurity applications
Abstract: As cybersecurity becomes increasingly complex, Large Language Models (LLMs) are emerging as valuable tools for supporting security professionals in routine tasks. However, existing research remains fragmented: no unified, machine-readable reference exists to compare and consolidate LLM use cases across academia and industry, limiting knowledge sharing and encouraging duplicated efforts.This paper presents BabeLLM, a concept-based taxonomy and OWL ontology grounded in established literature and cybersecurity standards (NIST, ISO/IEC, FIRST, JRC, and IETF). BabeLLM integrates NLP tasks, cybersecurity processes, and their intersection as LLM-based cybersecurity applications. Our analysis of 46 taxonomic efforts shows that none covers all three dimensions, leaving 17 LLM application categories absent from existing taxonomies. BabeLLM also introduces an operational architecture organized around three capabilities: exploration of existing work, design of new use cases, and automated ontology maintenance through LLM-assisted metadata enrichment and classification. The ontology is constructed through an umbrella systematic literature review covering more than 1400 publications, combined with a concept-based cross-dimensional analysis of NLP and cybersecurity, and refined through iterative expert review.BabeLLM is validated through complementary evaluations: coverage and agreement analyses across existing taxonomies, a real-world Security Operations Center (SOC) deployment demonstrating practical applicability, and an LLM-assisted classification pipeline benchmarked against human-annotated ground truth. Title: Artificial Intelligence and New Urban planning: Interpretative Paradigms and Impacts on Urban and Territorial Systems
Abstract: Given the current widespread development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), it is now necessary, in all fields of human activity, to study in depth the characteristics, reasoning processes, and actual potential of different Large Language Models (LLM) in order to determine and verify their effective support for humans. Relying uncritically on digital agents can lead to incorrect decisions or outcomes that harm the community. The uncritical “admiration” of the “plausible” answers provided by artificial reasoners may generate new, altered, and potentially dangerous relational dynamics, as observed in the growing use of affective chatbots. In this period of change, scholars from every research field, including experts on urban phenomena, are called to promptly undertake three activities: to understand and formalize the impacts of AI on urban and territorial systems by redefining the systemic interpretive paradigm and evaluating potential transformations of the subsystem components; to prefigure a new governance process for urban and territorial transformations, considering the appropriate and verified adoption of AI in the individual phases and in the prefiguration of planning scenarios for anthropogenic settlements; to promptly analyze the “weights” and the energy-ethical, and socio-environmental implications of the new data-processing megastructures (data centers) indispensable for the development of LLMs. Along these three lines of reflection, comparisons and debates among urban planners should be organized, in light of the transformations already underway in many territories worldwide. The paper offers reflections on these three topics that contribute to defining a new dimension in the management of urban and territorial transformations, in which the human agent appropriately adopts, drives, and validates the support that new digital agents and artificial reasoners can provide to the discipline. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: AI-Human Revoicing in Educational Dialogue: Developing Students’ Academic Voice with an LLM-Based Chatbot
Abstract: As large language model (LLM)-based chatbots become increasingly embedded in educational settings, there is a growing need to understand how learning unfolds interactionally through student–AI dialogue. This study examines revoicing, a discourse strategy theorized by O’Connor and Michaels as a means through which teachers take up and reformulate student contributions to support disciplinary alignment and development of academic voice. While revoicing has been extensively studied in classroom talk, it remains under-theorized in the emerging context of human–AI educational interaction. In this study, we reconceptualize revoicing in student–AI chat as a reciprocal process of linguistic “threading,” whereby ideas are taken up and rearticulated through identifiable lexical and semantic relations across turns. Drawing on a Bakhtinian dialogic lens, we analyzed chatlogs from 22 secondary school students engaging with a customized GPT-4-based chatbot designed for science inquiry. Using adjacency pairs as the unit of analysis, we conducted a two-phase lexical–semantic content analysis of revoicing relations, including lexical repetition and word-family variation, as well as synonymous, specific–general, part-whole and implied relations. Findings indicate both the chatbot and students took up and extended one another’s ideas through multiple ways of revoicing. These interactional patterns extend existing conceptualizations of revoicing and demonstrate how AI systems can function as customizable revoicing agents in educational dialogue. The study calls for further AIED research on how AI-mediated revoicing shapes learners’ participation, agency, and socialization into academic roles, practices and identity. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A Privacy-Preserving, Installation-Free Progressive Web App for Modern Slide Presentations
Abstract: This paper introduces an open-source Progressive Web App that empowers lecturers, researchers, and keynote speakers to deliver more modern and effective presentations, focusing on direct audience engagement and practical usability. With privacy and simplicity at its core, the app requires no installation or setup, making its features instantly accessible and user-friendly. The software is 220KB in size and is based entirely on web technologies that enable the management of PDFs, videos and images. Thanks to the Window Management API, monitors connected to the computer are detected and indexed, and a second window of the same web page can be managed using the Broadcast Channel API, which is available on all modern browsers and provides local message exchange. In this way, from a single codebase that opens the presenter’s window, the programme can control a second browser window to display the presentation to the audience without transferring data over the internet, ensuring that no files from the presented documents are ever transmitted or stored on external servers. Document rendering occurs entirely on the client side using the PDF.js library, released by Mozilla under an open-source license. The built-in features include support for ’split’ and ’bottom’ PDF notes, real-time annotation and highlighting tools, and control of the presenter’s webcam via local WebRTC. If the user wishes, optional features can be enabled, such as remote control of the presentation via smartphone using WebSocket or an anonymous Questions & Answers module for the audience, these are the only features that require data exchange with the server after the initial loading of static files. State-of-the-art analysis confirms there are currently no comparable web-based solutions. The application works on all major browsers and operating systems, making it a viable and accessible alternative to traditional tools. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Bridging the Pathology Communication Gap: Early Experience with Osler, a Patient-Facing AI Chatbot
Abstract: Patients increasingly access pathology reports via electronic portals, yet these clinician-oriented documents are often misunderstood. AI-driven chatbots may support patient understanding, but concerns regarding accuracy, scope, and safety limit clinical use. We developed Osler, a pathology-specific chatbot deployed on MyPathologyReport.com, using curated educational content and embedded guardrails to constrain scope, acknowledge uncertainty, and redirect users to their healthcare team. Title: AI Partners that Support Productive Uncertainty Within “Jigsaw” Activities During Small Group Collaborative Learning in Classrooms
Abstract: We report on the design and formative evaluation of an AI tool, JIA (Jigsaw Interactive Agent), that supports productive uncertainty during a collaborative “jigsaw” activity where students first build individual expertise and then work collaboratively to solve complex problems that require pooled expertise. We developed and contrasted a rule-based, LLM-based, and hybrid (rule + LLM) AI Partner that analyzed students’ open-ended spoken discussions during the jigsaw activity and responded with one of four productive uncertainty intervention types (support, connect, problematize, stabilize). We formatively evaluated JIA in a user study with 16 small groups (n = 64) of middle school students in 11 classrooms. We found that the three approaches differed in the types of interventions provided, and that the LLM and hybrid approaches were deemed to be more appropriate and elicited more affective responses from students. Authors: Tang Z.; Hua Z.
Title: Trust-Based Consensus Reaching with Bridging-Aware Influence Regulation Using ELICIT Information
Abstract: Intelligent decision support systems often involve multiple decision-makers (DMs) whose evaluations are expressed under uncertainty and linguistic ambiguity, making consensus reaching a critical challenge. Existing trust-based consensus-reaching processes primarily focus on opinion adjustment mechanisms, while the role of bridging influence remains insufficiently explored, especially without relying on explicit community structures. Therefore, this paper proposes a trust-based consensus-reaching model with bridging-aware influence regulation using the extended comparative linguistic expressions with symbolic translation (ELICIT). DMs’ evaluations are first modeled using ELICIT, and the consensus measure is constructed by aggregating pairwise opinion discrepancies. When the consensus level is unsatisfactory, a Bridging Index (BI) is introduced to measure each DM’s trust-mediated bridging contribution by capturing both opinion heterogeneity and trust dispersion. Guided by BI, a bridging-aware influence regulation mechanism is developed to adjust evaluations toward trusted peers with higher bridging capability, enabling gradual and interpretable consensus improvement. Upon convergence, the resulting group evaluations provide a reliable basis for collective decision ranking. A case study on offshore floating wind turbine risk assessment demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework for consensus improvement via interpretable and bridging-informed influence regulation. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: An embedding-based approach for measuring science–technology topic linkages using LLMs
Abstract: Traditional citation- and keyword-based methods struggle to capture science–technology (S–T) topic linkages owing to data sparsity, citation bias, and substantial linguistic differences across publication and patent corpora. To address these limitations, we propose a novel embedding-based approach that integrates large language model (LLM) embeddings with the neural embedded topic model (ETM). The approach comprises four steps: (1) encoding a union vocabulary from publication and patent corpora into a unified semantic space via LLM embeddings, (2) extracting science and technology (S&T) topics via ETM within this shared space, (3) quantifying S–T topic linkages via cosine similarity between topic embeddings, and (4) comparing against keyword- and citation-based approaches. When applied to 79,997 3D printing publications and 100,786 patents with a lexical overlap of only 26.43%, the method improves topic coherence via Qwen3 embeddings. The resulting S–T linkages (mean = 0.148) are significantly higher than the keyword-based measures (mean = 0.058), correlating positively with both keyword-based (r = 0.425) and citation-based (r = 0.271) linkages. Expert evaluation confirms that the generated S&T topics are interpretable, complete, informative, and with low bias, while the embedding-based linkages align with real-world knowledge relatedness. These findings demonstrate that the proposed approach transcends the structural sparsity of citations and the lexical limits of keywords, offering a more robust, interpretable, and comprehensive measurement of S–T topic linkages. It also provides evidence-based tools for key stakeholders in innovation systems to monitor translational research impacts and identify innovation opportunities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: CipherMark: An AI-Driven Framework for Encryption Analysis, File Security, and Steganographic Protection
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: This paper presents CipherMark, an AI-powered system that consolidates the analysis of encryption, processing of secure files, and hiding data within images and audio files, all in one service. Unlike prior work which separates these up to four areas, CipherMark consists of four modules: encryption algorithm classification, file encryption algorithm comparison between multiple different algorithms, performance benchmarking of encryption algorithms, and least significant bit (LSB)-based steganography. The classification module employs entropy, byte-frequency, and structural features to classify encryption algorithms such as AES, DES, RSA, RC4, and ChaCha20 using Random Forest with an accuracy of 98.6%. The encryption and comparison modules afford users the ability to benchmark or compare various encryption algorithms based on speed, key size, computational cost, and ciphertext expansion - all in one processing function. The steganography module allows for the embedding of encrypted messages in images and audio files to provide multiple layers of security. The results of the experiment verify the classification model is reliable and can be utilized within the conjunction of all four modules in practice. Overall, CipherMark provides a complete, extensible environment for cybersecurity research, digital forensics, ransomware investigations and or messaging security protocols. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Intelligent Collaborative Edge Caching via Contextual Bandits and Convex Relaxation
Abstract: Edge Data Caching (EDC) enables low-latency delivery and alleviates backhaul congestion by caching data in close proximity to end users. However, current learning-driven methods struggle to capture the multi-dimensional business value of data. Consequently, inefficient resource allocation degrades critical services and compromises the Quality of Service (QoS). Moreover, physical node failures are insufficiently addressed, risking severe backhaul delays. To address these issues, we formulate the Value and Failure-aware Collaborative Edge Data Caching (VF-CEDC) problem as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model jointly optimizing business value and expected latency under physical uncertainties. To solve this, we propose an Online Learning and Convex Relaxation Algorithm (OLCRA). First, OLCRA leverages a Contextual Multi-Armed Bandit (CMAB) to adaptively infer data values. Second, it resolves the discrete caching topology via convex relaxation and probabilistic rounding, yielding near-optimal polynomial-time decisions. Extensive experiments on a real-world dataset show that OLCRA reduces average system cost by 32.3% and expected latency by 38.3% against eight competing methods. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: The Impact of Generative AI Tools on Student Academic Performance: Machine Learning Approach
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) tools like ChatGPT are rapidly transforming higher education, yet empirical evidence on their impact on student academic achievement remains limited. This study investigates how three key AI-related factors, AI comprehension support (Q10), AI task assistance (Q16), and learning satisfaction (Q17), predict student achievement (Q18) in AI-supported learning environments. Using a comparative machine learning approach, survey data from 147 IT university students were analyzed with five algorithms: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, CatBoost, and XGBoost. Random Forest achieved the best performance with 66.67% accuracy, outperforming other algorithms. The model demonstrated excellent recall (94%) for high performances, but struggled with minority classes due to severe class imbalance (60.5% high, 32.7% medium, 6.8% low achievement). Feature importance analysis identified learning satisfaction (Q17) as the most important predictor, followed by AI comprehension support (Q10), while AI task assistance (Q16) showed the weakest influence. These findings indicate that attitudes and perceptions matter more than usage frequency for academic achievement. Title: ADSLT: Aligning and disentangling guided by shared and learnable soft-query tokens for compositional zero-shot learning
Abstract: In recent years, compositional zero-shot learning (CZSL) based on Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) has achieved more progress than traditional CLIP-free CZSL. However, CLIP-based CZSL still faces domain bias and entanglement. Therefore, we use cross-modal attention to design a novel Alignment and Disentanglement Model (ADM) that consists of four alignment modules based on multi-head attention and two disentangling modules. The query tokens of every alignment module are divided into shared tokens, which are obtained by joint training, and exclusive tokens, which are the global tokens of the corresponding encoded vector. Title: Frequency Energy Adaptive Normalization for Non-Stationary Time Series Forecasting
Abstract: Forecasting non-stationary time series remains challenging because both statistical distributions and spectral patterns evolve over time. Existing frequency-domain normalization methods mainly rely on global Fourier analysis to remove dominant frequency components, which overlooks local spectral variations and the cumulative effect of weak but persistent high-frequency signals. To handle these issues, we propose Frequency Energy Adaptive Normalization (FEAN), a plug-and-play time-frequency normalization framework. FEAN partitions the lookback window into patches and computes a high-frequency energy ratio via discrete wavelet transform to measure local non-stationarity. This ratio is then used to adaptively fuse patch-level and instance-level statistics for reversible normalization. In addition, a lightweight predictor estimates future statistics and energy ratios for denormalization. Title: Dual-pathway mask ranking guided selective fine-tuning for backdoor purification
Abstract: A backdoor attack poisons a victim model during training, causing it to predict attacker-specified target label during inference. This has emerged as a critical threat to AI security. To counter this threat, backdoor purification seeks to eliminate or mitigate backdoor effect without compromising clean accuracy. Pruning-based methods alter the model architecture and degrade clean accuracy, while fine-tuning methods rarely explore backdoor-related cues, leaving residual backdoor effects. In this paper, we propose a dual-pathway mask ranking guided selective fine-tuning method for backdoor purification, synthesizing the perspectives of pruning and fine-tuning. Since clean-poisoned separation forms the data prerequisite for backdoor purification, we first develop an erasure-based intervention strategy grounded in our finding that backdoor-related triggers are prioritized for spatial reconstruction. This enables direct trigger erasure, making poisoned data more susceptible to erasure-based intervention than clean data. Building on this, we establish a forget-then-recover mechanism that characterizes the degree of backdoor contamination for each neuron using soft-valued masks. We design a training-free dual-pathway mask ranking module to categorize neurons into distinct types based on the rankings of soft-valued masks. This type information guides the selection of fine-tuning policies (i.e., relearning, unlearning or nolearning) for each neuron. Experimental results across four benchmark datasets (MNIST-M, SVHN, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100) demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms seven baseline competitors under various backdoor attacks. Our method attains the lowest average ASR (Attack Success Rate) ranging from 0.23% to 1.29%, and incurs the smallest average CA (Clean Accuracy) degradation ranging from 0.15% to 1.53%. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of our clean-poisoned separation strategy and selective fine-tuning policy. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: CaribSign - Towards the Preservation of Caribbean Sign Languages Using AI
Abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into the technology sectors within developed countries has yielded significant gains in efficiency and user convenience. These advancements nevertheless have yet to be realized equitably in developing regions such as the Caribbean due to limited financial and infrastructural resources. Consequently, AI innovation in the region continues to lag behind global progress. As Caribbean governments accelerate digital transformation initiatives, vulnerable communities risk further marginalization. Because no regional framework exists to systematically archive or preserve the region’s sign languages, this work focused on the creation of CaribSign, an AI-based prototype application designed for converting CARICOM sign languages into text and speech, thereby supporting their digital preservation. The Google Teachable Machines (GTM) platform was used to train, evaluate, and deploy a Keras-based AI model. The prototype model demonstrated strong performance achieving precision, recall, and overall accuracy scores of 99.78%, 99.8% and 99.8%, respectively, of signs with no changes in their dynamic features. Potential benefits of the system include enhanced education support, improved social inclusion for people that are deaf, and the preservation of an emerging regional cultural identity. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: What do feature branches tell us about feature implementation in open-source projects?
Abstract: Although “feature” is a common term across requirements engineering, product-line engineering, and agile methods, its operationalization in practice–especially through feature branches–has received little empirical attention. Feature branches are widely recommended on platforms like GitHub; yet, empirical evidence on how they are actually used is scarce. This study investigates feature-branch development practices in open-source software (OSS) projects. We conducted a large-scale empirical analysis of 27,103 feature branches from 3,388 popular GitHub repositories. Using branch-naming conventions, we identified feature branches and measured their lifespan, commit history, and commit-share distributions among contributors. In addition, we profiled contributors according to their opened issues, opened pull requests, number of followers, and total stars. Our analysis revealed that feature branches in open-source projects are long-lived, with a median lifespan exceeding two years, diverging from the short, agile iterations typically employed in software development. Commit intensity is low and irregular, averaging fewer than two commits per day. Contribution is highly unequal within feature branches: a small share of contributors accounts for most commits, revealing strong dependence on a small subset of developers. These findings have several practical implications. Our findings suggest that monitoring contribution concentration within feature branches– for instance, by computing the share of commits attributable to the top contributor or a Gini coefficient over the branch’s commit history–can help maintainers identify branches where development knowledge is held by very few individuals. Likewise, rolling commit intensity–computable directly from commit timestamps–may serve as an early signal of branch stagnation in OSS projects. Moreover, these findings establish an empirical baseline for future studies, including analyses of proprietary repositories. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence in Cardiovascular Disease Prevention: A Systematic Review
Abstract: This systematic review evaluates the effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in preventing cardiovascular disease (CVD). We conducted a systematic review using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology, with the protocol registered under CRD42022369548 on PROSPERO. We included studies on all populations who receive or provide care and used AI for risk prediction and prevention of CVD. We searched seven databases from 1999 till October 2022. Two reviewers independently screened the identified records and extracted data from the included studies. We conducted a subgroup analysis on studies that compare AI to standard care. We assessed the risk of bias using a Modified IJMEDI and PROBAST tool, and data are synthesized in narrative form, considering various study aspects. This review adheres to PRISMA guidelines for systematic reviews and meta-analyses. After screening 7,505 identified records, 266 articles were included in the review. Risk prediction and early disease diagnosis were the most common prevention modalities. The subgroup analysis of 16 studies that compared these interventions with standard care included 51,687,627 participants. The Framingham Risk Score was the most used comparator, reported in 8 of the 16 studies (50%). Findings from identified studies suggest that AI, specifically Machine learning models such as Neural Networks, significantly improved the performance of clinical tasks such as risk prediction and diagnosis, suggesting that AI-based models may enhance cardiovascular disease prevention. Further high-quality prospective studies and real-world implementation research are needed before routine clinical adoption. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: An ORID-Structured GenAI Reading Companion Integrating Structured Book Chat and Virtual Labs for Science Reading
Abstract: This study proposes an ORID-structured generative AI reading companion to regulate AI-learner interaction during science reading. The system orchestrates structured AI-supported book chat and, in one condition, integrates a virtual laboratory to connect textual claims with observable phenomena. A nine-week classroom study with 62 sixth-grade students employed an AB/BA counterbalanced design. Students completed pretest, midtest, and posttest measures of science knowledge and reading motivation, and provided open-ended reflections. Linear mixed models with baseline as a covariate and midtest/posttest as repeated measures indicated that science knowledge showed descriptive improvement from baseline to midtest in both sequence groups, but the added effect of the virtual laboratory condition on science knowledge was not statistically reliable after controlling for baseline and within-student dependence. In contrast, over-all reading motivation was significantly higher when the GenAI companion was combined with virtual laboratory support. Qualitative feedback suggested a trade-off: many learners found simulations engaging and helpful for making ideas concrete, while some reported distraction that reduced focus on reading. Overall, the findings provide classroom-based evidence and practical design guidance for orchestrating ORID-structured GenAI book talk with virtual laboratories to support elementary science reading, with motivational benefits emerging more clearly than knowledge gains. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: From Large Language Model Predicates to Logic Tensor Networks: Neurosymbolic Offer Validation in Regulated Procurement
Abstract: We present a neurosymbolic approach to validating offer documents in regulated public institutions. We employ a language model to extract information and then aggregate it with an LTN (Logic Tensor Network) to make an auditable decision. In regulated public institutions, decisions must be made in a manner that is both factually correct and legally verifiable. Our neurosymbolic approach allows existing domain-specific knowledge to be linked to the semantic text understanding of language models. The decisions resulting from our pipeline can be justified by predicate values, rule truth values, and corresponding text passages. Our experiments on a real corpus show that the proposed pipeline achieves performance comparable to existing models, but its key advantage lies in its interpretability, modular predicate extraction, and explicit support for XAI (Explainable AI). © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Assessing the Availability of Crowdsourced Street-Level Imagery for Urban Perception Mapping
Abstract: The integration of urban science with spatial artificial intelligence, referred to as Urban-AI or Geo-AI, is playing an increasingly important role in monitoring cities, supporting urban planning, and addressing urban challenges. In this context, investigating how cities are perceived by individuals and understanding the effects of urban environments on people have emerged as important research topics that can directly influence individuals’ quality of life. In recent years, street-level imagery (SLI) has been widely used to evaluate urban perception through artificial intelligence-based algorithms. In particular, generative artificial intelligence offers growing potential for analyzing urban environments and supporting the development of spatial solutions. However, ethical risks such as algorithmic bias, socio-economic inequalities, and data representativeness issues remain important concerns. Therefore, before enabling generative AI-based systems to support transformations in urban environments, it is critical to investigate their functionality and development from a spatial data perspective. This study presents an empirical framework to evaluate the usability of crowdsourced SLI for urban perception research. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Yang Q.

Title: From Verdicts to Maps: Reimagining AI Assessment for ADHD Through a Strength-Based Lens
Abstract: In the high-stakes educational context of China, characterized by Involution (intense academic competition), ADHD assessment is predominantly rooted in a deficit-oriented medical model, often exacerbating parental anxiety and reinforcing pathological labeling. While AI assessment technologies promise greater objectivity, we argue they present a Precision Paradox: when AI systems provide decontextualized quantification of behavioral deficits with high algorithmic confidence, they risk solidifying pathological stereotypes rather than fostering educational understanding. To challenge this paradigm, we introduce AssetLens, a conceptual design probe representing a strength-based AI assessment system that visualizes cognitive potential by simulating a temporal denoising mechanism. Through a qualitative Wizard-of-Oz study with 16 stakeholders (8 parents, 8 teachers), we investigated how this reframed AI visualization influences the interpretation of neurodiverse behaviors. Our findings reveal three key shifts: (1) Cognitive-Emotional Reframing: For parents, assessment results shifted from anxiety-inducing verdicts to foundational tools for understanding capabilities; (2) Pedagogical Shift: Teachers moved their focus from defensive behavioral management to leveraging unique strengths for learning; and (3) Dialogic Transformation: The system functioned as a neutral boundary object, converting home-school communication from adversarial blame-games to collaborative sensemaking around shared data. This study contributes to the societal dimension of AIED by demonstrating that in special education, AI’s value lies not merely in automated judgment, but in its capacity to mitigate anxiety and mediate collaborative dialogue. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Writing Instructors’ Pedagogical Decisions About Generative AI
Abstract: College-level writing instructors are under growing pressure to determine how, or if at all, to integrate generative AI tools into their curricula. While some theoretical scholarship promotes generative AI integration as a means of fostering AI literacy, empirical research on how writing instructors are approaching these tools remains limited. This study explores how college-level writing instructors are currently addressing generative AI in their classrooms, what pedagogical rationales and concerns shape decisions to integrate or avoid these tools, and how instructors evaluate the effectiveness of their own approaches. This study combines survey data from 79 college-level writing instructors across a range of institution types with follow-up semi-structured interviews using an explanatory sequential mixed methods design. Survey results revealed a pronounced division among instructors, with respondents nearly evenly split between those who integrate generative AI in some form (43%) and those who avoid its use (57%). Interviews showed that instructors across both groups share similar concerns related to student learning, writing processes, and institutional expectations. Decisions about integration or refusal were strongly shaped by local teaching contexts, perceived pedagogical risks, and a lack of institutional guidance or support. This study aims to inform more confident and context-aware pedagogical decision-making about whether and how generative AI might be incorporated into college-level writing instruction. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Conceptualizing the Depth and Breadth of AI Literacy
Abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across life domains has intensified calls for the development of AI literacy (AIL). While a growing body of research and policy proposes frameworks for AIL, the field remains conceptually fragmented. Existing frameworks list skills and competencies without clarifying their epistemological foundations, leading to ambiguity about what it means to be AI literate. This paper proposes a meta-conceptual framework that conceptualizes AIL as a differentiated space of knowledge. Drawing on philosophical and sociological theories of knowledge, we distinguish AIL along two dimensions: breadth (general vs. specialist) and depth (propositional vs. procedural). This yields four types of AIL: general propositional, general procedural, specialist propositional, and specialist procedural. Title: Unified multimodal computational pathology with missing-modality robustness via Riemannian learning
Abstract: Recent advances in multimodal computational pathology (CPath) have enabled the integration of pathological and molecular data. However, existing studies often rely on a single omics modality (e.g., DNA or transcriptomics), overlooking cross-layer biological dependencies and failing to effectively handle the missing-modality challenge prevalent in clinical settings. In this paper, we propose HuMP, a hyperbolic multimodal CPath framework that unifies molecular, pathological, and clinical data within a biologically motivated hierarchy. HuMP uses the coupling between negative-curvature embedding and directional entailment supervision to model cross-scale relations across molecular, histological, and clinical domains. At the molecular level, HuMP integrates genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics through a hyperbolic aggregation module that models biological pathway interactions, while a hyperbolic entailment loss enforces a directional hierarchy from molecular to tissue to patient representations. Furthermore, to address incomplete multimodal inputs, we introduce a hierarchy-guided modality completion strategy that reconstructs missing embeddings along learned entailment paths in hyperbolic space, ensuring geometric and semantic consistency. Extensive experiments on seven public datasets and an in-house multi-center cohort show that HuMP achieves strong average performance in survival prediction and classification, while maintaining robust missing-modality behavior with a 96.6% average modality completion rate. Title: Embedding Pedagogical Principles into LLMs: A Field Study of AI-Generated Feedback in a Programming Serious Game
Abstract: Providing individualized support in introductory programming is challenging for teachers in secondary classrooms. Although LLMs can effectively deliver automated feedback in this context, they may provide excessive assistance that hinders learning and lack access to the full context of exploratory environments such as serious games. This study investigates the impact of integrating a pedagogically driven LLM-based digital assistant, which integrates distinct constructivist constraints, into Pyrates, a Python programming game for high schools. In a field user study (N = 241), we found that the assistant was positively perceived by students, supported in-game progression, and significantly reduced teacher interventions without negatively affecting learning. Interaction trace analyses revealed distinct post-feedback strategies, advocating for a tight control of LLM content generation. Title: A contrastive learning framework for Transformer-based collaborative filtering
Abstract: In various machine learning tasks, Transformer-based models have attracted significant attention and achieved notable success. To apply Transformers to Collaborative Filtering (CF), we designed a contrastive learning framework called Transformer Collaborative Filtering (TransCF), in which the Transformer serves as a backbone to extract user preferences from global collaborative signals. During training, instead of traditional user-item pairs, we utilize the entire set of items interacted with by each user to capture high-order item-to-item relationships. Additionally, we integrate a Siamese contrastive learning objective to ensure consistent and coherent user representations across different latent spaces, which significantly enhances performance in sparse and cold-start scenarios. Extensive experiments across diverse domains (including E-commerce, Movie, and News) demonstrate that TransCF achieves state-of-the-art results with superior prediction quality. Title: Multimodal information fusion for food nutrition estimation: A survey
Abstract: Food nutrition estimation aims to predict calories, portion size, and nutrient composition from dietary observations, supporting health monitoring and personalized nutrition management. Accurate estimation remains difficult because food appearance often provides limited information about physical scale, hidden ingredients, cooking processes, and nutrient density. Multimodal sensing and learning provide new opportunities to reduce these ambiguities by integrating visual, geometric, semantic, and sensor-based information. This paper surveys multimodal information fusion for food nutrition estimation. Different from existing surveys that mainly organize food analysis studies by tasks, input modalities, or model architectures, this survey adopts a modality-aware and problem-oriented taxonomy. It explains how different modalities support key estimation problems, including portion and scale estimation, hidden-composition inference, nutrient aggregation, and physicochemical analysis. Existing methods are classified into four categories: visual-geometric multimodal learning, semantic and knowledge-augmented estimation, compositional multimodal reasoning, and other multimodal sensing. Representative methods, datasets, evaluation metrics, applications, and Nutrition5k results are reviewed and compared. Current limitations and future research directions are then discussed from the perspectives of accuracy, interpretability, robustness, and deployment. This survey provides a structured reference for developing reliable multimodal nutrition estimation systems. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Exploring the capabilities of vision-language models to detect visual bugs in HTML5 canvas applications
Abstract: The HyperText Markup Language 5 (HTML5) canvas is useful for creating visual-centric web applications. However, unlike traditional web applications, HTML5 canvas applications render objects onto the canvas bitmap without representing them in the Document Object Model (DOM). Mismatches between the expected and actual visual output of the canvas bitmap are termed visual bugs. Due to the visual-centric nature of canvas applications, visual bugs are important to detect because such bugs can render a canvas application useless. As we showed in prior work, asset-based graphics can provide the ground truth for a visual test oracle. However, many canvas applications procedurally generate their graphics. In this paper, we investigate how to detect visual bugs in canvas applications that use procedural graphics as well. In particular, we explore the potential of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to automatically detect visual bugs. Instead of defining an exact visual test oracle, information about the application’s expected functionality (the context) can be provided with the screenshot as input to the VLM. To evaluate this approach, we constructed a dataset containing 80 bug-injected screenshots across four visual bug types (Layout, Rendering, Appearance, and State) plus 20 bug-free screenshots from 20 canvas applications. We ran experiments with a state-of-the-art VLM using several combinations of text and image context to describe each application’s expected functionality. Our results show that by providing the application README(s), a description of visual bug types, and a bug-free screenshot as context, VLMs can be leveraged to detect visual bugs with up to 100% per-application accuracy. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Artificial Intelligence in B&H: Scenarios and Strategic Pathways from the Perspective of Science and the Business Sector
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: Although artificial intelligence is widely framed as a driver of productivity, innovation, and strategic decision-making, Bosnia and Herzegovina has not yet translated this potential into systemic implementation. In a post-transition setting marked by fragmented governance, dependence on imported solutions, persistent talent outflows, and weak technology transfer, the main constraint is less technological availability than institutional capacity, organisational readiness, and coordinated change. This paper addresses that gap by examining how two plausible drivers—(i) the routine standardisation of AI in firm processes and products, and (ii) the global concentration of AI expertise in wealthier economies—may shape labour markets, industrial structures, and institutional capabilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Drawing on two structured focus groups with representatives of academia and the business sector, the study applies a modified Futures Wheel to map primary and secondary effects across economic, social, legal, political, technological, and environmental dimensions, and then uses backcasting to construct scenario-based development pathways for 2025–2033. The results highlight path dependence and an implementation gap between declarative support and delivery capacity, pointing to risks of economic bifurcation, skill polarisation, and knowledge externalisation if early coordination fails. The paper proposes strategic interventions centred on institutional alignment, targeted sectoral prioritisation, human-capital development, governance operationalisation, and structured science–industry collaboration. By conceptualising AI adoption as an institutionally mediated and path-dependent process, the study offers empirically grounded guidance for moving from strategic ambition to feasible deployment in Bosnia and Herzegovina. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Mapping AI Literacy in Medical Education: A Review of Concepts and Teaching Practices
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into high-stakes professional workflows, including clinical decision-making, domain-specific AI literacy is becoming a critical requirement for responsible and ethical practice. In medical education, despite the growing number of AI literacy frameworks proposed for medical students, there has been no systematic synthesis that examines how AI literacy competencies for medical students are conceptualized across frameworks and reflected in teaching practice, making it difficult for educators to determine which competencies are commonly emphasized and how they should be prioritized in teaching practice. To address this gap, this paper reports a systematic review of AI literacy frameworks and teaching practices for medical students. The results show that while existing AI literacy frameworks for medical students share the common emphasis on foundational knowledge of AI and responsible AI use in clinical contexts, they differ in technical depth and the roles medical students are expected to play in AI-enabled healthcare. In contrast, current AI education teaching practices for medical students tend to prioritize fundamental concepts and coding-related skills, with limited attention to clinical integration and ethical considerations, reflecting a persistent theory-practice gap. This review contributes to the ongoing discussion on responsible AI in medical education by clarifying how AI literacy competencies for medical students are conceptualized in theory and integrated into teaching practice, offering insights to support the alignment of AI literacy education for medical students with ethical responsibilities and clinical practice in AI-enabled healthcare. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Assessment of the Impact of an Artificial Intelligence Robot on Meditation and Mindfulness Practice
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: The practice of meditation and mindfulness has been shown to have significant benefits for mental well-being. With advances in technology, social robots and artificial intelligence (AI) are emerging as potential tools to assist in these practices. The main objective of this study was to evaluate the impact and user experience of a guided meditation system assisted by an AI-powered social robot. A pre-post study design was implemented in which 21 participants interacted with the system. The Self-Report Mindfulness Scale (SMS) and Conscious Attention Mindfulness Scale-Revised (CAMS-R) were used to measure mindfulness levels in the pre-intervention phase, and the Post-Study System Usability Questionnaire (PSSUQ) together with an ad-hoc questionnaire on the usefulness of the assistant were used in the post-intervention phase. The results showed a marked improvement in mindfulness levels (SMS) after the intervention. While these exploratory findings are promising, the absence of a control group limits the causal attribution of the improvement specifically to the robot versus a general effect of meditation. The usability of the system (PSSUQ) was rated as excellent, with a total average of 4.08 on a scale of 5. In addition, participants reported a high perception of usefulness and connection with the assistant (average 3.68), highlighting items such as the usefulness of the instructions and the feeling of being understood. These findings suggest that social robots have great potential as effective meditation assistants, offering a positive experience and improving users’ state of mindfulness. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Multi-scale, multi-dimensional data mining for agentic AI micro-dramas recommendations
Abstract: Micro-dramas, also known as micro-short dramas, are ultra-short, serialized video series optimized for mobile viewing, with episodes typically lasting 1–20 min. Multi-scale, multi-dimensional data mining (MSMD-DM) involves extracting patterns from complex datasets that vary across spatial, temporal, or hierarchical scales while managing high-dimensional features. Agentic AI recommendation refers to an autonomous, interactive, and goal-oriented AI system that transcends traditional recommendation paradigms. This study proposes an integrated framework that combines multi-scale (nominal and ordinal scale), multi-dimensional (demographics, preferences, intentions, and actual actions) data mining approach, K-means clustering, and association rule mining to support Agentic AI recommendations for micro-dramas. The framework addresses challenges related to data heterogeneity, dynamic user interactions, and context-aware decision-making. Using a sample of 3,016 Taiwanese consumers, we first segmented users into three distinct clusters via K-means analysis. Subsequently, association rules were mined within each cluster to uncover behavioral patterns and preferences related to micro-drama consumption and cross-screen e-commerce activities. The results provide actionable insights for micro-drama producers and e-commerce operators, enabling the design of personalized content and integrated business strategies. Theoretical and empirical analyses indicate that this integration not only provides a structured knowledge foundation for future agentic recommenders but also Agentic AI system architecture optimization, verifying an example of micro-drama recommendation, providing a structured knowledge foundation for future agentic recommenders, but also endows AI agents with recommendation capabilities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Imitation Learning for Clinical Decision Support in Pediatric ECMO
Abstract: Pediatric critical care is a dynamic, high-stakes process involving constant monitoring and adjustments in life-saving treatments. Modeling these interventions is crucial for effective decision support. In pediatric Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO), where data are scarce and clinical dynamics are complex, we frame clinical decision-making as imitation learning from observational data, in which actions are not directly observed. We consider TabPFN, a recent transformer-based approach for tabular data, and traditional baselines including XGBoost and Multi-Layer Perceptrons on real-world pediatric ECMO data to learn the action models. We find that the TabPFN-based approach consistently outperforms these classical baselines, supporting its use as a strong clinician-behavior baseline for pediatric ECMO decision support. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: When Can We Trust LLM Graders? Calibrating Confidence for Automated Assessment
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for automated grading, but their outputs can be unreliable. Rather than improving grading accuracy directly, we address a complementary problem: predicting when an LLM grader is likely to be correct. This enables selective automation where high-confidence predictions are processed automatically while uncertain cases are flagged for human review. We compare three confidence estimation methods (self-reported confidence, self-consistency voting, and token probability) across seven LLMs of varying scale (4B to 120B parameters) on three educational datasets: RiceChem (long-answer chemistry), SciEntsBank, and Beetle (short-answer science). Our experiments reveal that self-reported confidence consistently achieves the best calibration across all conditions (avg ECE 0.166 vs 0.229 for self-consistency). Surprisingly, self-consistency remains 38% worse despite requiring 5× the inference cost. Larger models exhibit substantially better calibration though gains vary by dataset and method (e.g., a 28% ECE reduction for self-reported), with GPT-OSS-120B achieving the best calibration (avg ECE 0.100) and strong discrimination (avg AUC 0.668). We also observe that confidence is strongly top-skewed across methods, creating a “confidence floor” that practitioners must account for when setting thresholds. These findings suggest that simply asking LLMs to report their confidence provides a practical approach for identifying reliable grading predictions. Authors: Li H.; Xing W.; Li C.; Lyu B.
Title: Who Benefits From Which Voice? Group-Differentiated Effects of Teachable Agent Voice Emotion Design on Achievement Emotions and Engagement Patterns in K-12 Mathematics Learning
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence enables teachable agents to shift from instructional tools to collaborative learning teammates in K-12 mathematics education. However, prior research has emphasized cognitive outcomes while paying relatively less attention to emotional processes and systematic examination of voice characteristics that carry essential socio-emotional cues for human-AI collaboration. This study integrates control-value theory with social voice theory to construct an analytical framework linking voice characteristics, achievement emotions, engagement patterns, and learning gains. We conducted a three-week randomized experiment on Math Nation with 310 middle school students, collecting demographic data and standardized pre- and post-test scores, yielding 731 dialogue records. Manipulating voice emotion (sad, calm, happy) and using fine-tuned language models to annotate student achievement emotions and engagement patterns, we applied multilevel modeling to analyze group-differentiated associations. Results indicate significant group differences: happy tone was associated with enhanced positive activating emotions in males, while exploratory analyses suggest potential suppressive effects for low-SES students (though this finding requires cautious interpretation given the small subsample, N = 13). Achievement emotions were strongly associated with engagement patterns, with positive activating emotions linked to task-oriented engagement while negative deactivating emotions were associated with disengagement. At the student level, voice dialogue frequency and moderate negative activating emotions significantly predicted posttest scores after controlling for pretest performance. This study provides preliminary empirical evidence for designing inclusive adaptive learning environments where AI systems function as responsive teammates through socio-emotional voice design. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Bridging the skills gap in recruitment: A RAG-based LLM framework for cybersecurity job advertisement analysis
Abstract: With the increasing frequency and sophistication of cyberattacks, cybersecurity has become a strategic priority, creating an urgent demand for a skilled workforce. Online job ads in cyberspace are a rich source of information related to the changing dynamics of labor markets, sought-after skills, and employer expectations. However, available methods for extracting relevant information from job advertisements, including for cybersecurity careers, have thus far relied on either manual or semi-automated approaches that, in general, are not scalable, are prone to error, and require prior knowledge and expertise in natural language processing (NLP). This study presents a new, fully automated framework for cybersecurity labor-market analysis with potential for application in other knowledge-intensive industries. The fundamental innovation is the use of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), powered by large language models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4.1, and Meta Llama 3) to turn unstructured job postings into a structured and analyzable format. This methodology is applied to real job postings from LinkedIn, Indeed, and Rekrute, with a particular focus on Morocco’s cybersecurity sector. From a balanced dataset of 27,360 job advertisements, this study analyzes 1681 cybersecurity roles. Results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach: GPT-4.1, used as the master evaluator, achieves the highest scores across the six metrics: 96.276% (Correctness), 100% (Completeness), 99.952% (Relevance), 100% (Format Adherence), 99.762% (Language Consistency), and 99.881% (Clarity). Moreover, this study shows that most job postings target mid-level candidates with three or more years of experience and advanced degrees, primarily master’s or engineering degrees. CISSP is the most sought-after certification. By automating and scaling the analysis of labor market data, this research contributes to a broader societal objective of strengthening the cybersecurity workforce and fostering secure digital societies. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Multi-dimensional Summarization Agents with Context-Aware Reasoning over Enterprise Tables
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: We propose a novel framework for summarizing structured enterprise data across multiple dimensions using large language model (LLM)-based agents. Traditional table-to-text models often lack the capacity to reason across hierarchical structures and context-aware deltas, which are essential in business reporting tasks. Our method introduces a multi-agent pipeline that extracts, analyzes, and summarizes multi-dimensional data using agents for slicing, variance detection, context construction, and LLM-based generation. Our results show that the proposed framework outperforms traditional approaches, achieving 83% faithfulness to underlying data, superior coverage of significant changes, and high relevance scores (4.4/5) for decision-critical insights. The improvements are especially pronounced in categories involving subtle trade-offs, such as increased revenue due to price changes amid declining unit volumes, which competing methods either overlook or address with limited specificity. Authors: Liu X.; Wang S.; Ga R.; Ma B.; Zhang J.; Tong Z.
Title: Prediction of Forest-Grassland Fires Based on Graph Attention Mechanism
Abstract: Fire has become one of the important threats affecting forest and grassland vegetation ecosystems. How to effectively predict the occurrence of fires in different regions has become one of the key research issues in global fire studies. To improve the accuracy and reliability of fire prediction, this study constructed a fire occurrence prediction model using a graph attention mechanism (GAM) by selecting 12 indicators closely related to fires. The results showed that the indicators selected in this study were reasonable, including the fire induced factors net primary productivity (NPP), slope, saturated vapor pressure difference (vpd), slope, wind, and land surface temperature (LST) is consistent across different datasets, and distance to cropland (d2c), NPP, TVDI, and slope show high importance in different regions. However, the impact of the variable altitude (ele) varies greatly in different regions. By comparing the graph attention mechanism model and the random forest model (RF), it was found that both models have high predictive performance on large size samples. However, when the sample size is small, the graph attention mechanism model has better predictive performance than the random forest model. The graph attention mechanism model has stronger interpretability for the mechanism of fire occurrence. This study has significant implications for enhancing the accuracy of forest and grassland fire predictions and strengthening fire management. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Authors: Ding H.; Shen Y.; Chen J.; Wang P.
Title: More vs. less cognitive offloading from ai assistants: impacts on novices’ collaborative performance and skill development
Abstract: Artificial intelligence agents are increasingly deployed as professional teammates. However, it remains unclear how they can enhance collaborative performance without hindering human skill development, particularly for novices in high-stakes domains. Cognitive offloading, using external resources (in this case, AI assistants) to reduce one’s own cognitive effort, is central to this tension.We conducted a controlled experiment using a custom platform and the CAIL 2018 dataset. 130 participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: a no-AI control, high-offloading AI (which provided direct recommendation), moderate-offloading AI (which provided analytical support), or low-offloading AI (which provided evaluative feedback). The results reveal a fundamental trade-off. The high-offloading condition achieved the highest decision accuracy at 68.8% and the shortest decision time (37.55s). However, it diminished skill development, showing a 7.1% lower accuracy improvement than the control. In contrast, moderate- and low-offloading conditions fostered skill gains of approximately 5.5%. Mediation analysis indicated that this impeded skill development was associated with metacognitive miscalibration (a gap between perceived and actual ability) rather than merely reduced behavioral engagement. These findings extend the “AI Competency Paradox” by revealing a critical offloading threshold below which AI can enhance collaborative performance while supporting skill development, and by identifying metacognitive miscalibration (not reduced effort) as a mechanism underlying skill impairment, suggesting that AI assistants for novices should prioritize adaptive cognitive friction and real-time competence calibration over full automation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.
