Title: Strategies for Efficient Cost Management in Hybrid Cloud It Infrastructure
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: Hybrid cloud infrastructures offer organizations substantial flexibility, elasticity, and operational scalability; however, they also introduce complex financial risks associated with multi-cloud environments, including hidden costs related to re-source consumption, data transfers, licensing models, and ongoing maintenance. Effective cost management in such ecosystems requires an integrated governance framework that combines financial discipline with technical optimization and operational efficiency. This study examines key strategies for achieving financial control in hybrid cloud environments, emphasizing the role of FinOps as a collaborative model that aligns IT, finance, and business units in decision-making. Core mechanisms include policy-as-code for automated enforcement of cost-related rules, accurate capacity planning and right-sizing of resources, as well as workload placement based on performance, compliance, and cost metrics. Additionally, techniques such as data location optimization, caching, compression, and the use of spot/preemptible instances are highlighted as essential approaches for reducing operational expenditures. Advanced capabilities including real-time observability, multi-cloud cost dashboards, and artificial intelligence-driven dynamic resource allocation further enhance financial predictability and operational efficiency. Emerging trends such as cross-cloud management fabrics, distributed data mesh governance, and the convergence of cost optimization with security requirements demonstrate that the long-term success of hybrid cloud strategies de-pends on proactive governance, intelligent workload orchestration, and architectural choices designed for economic sustainability. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Constructing Acceptable Use: Instructor Boundary‑Setting with Generative AI
Abstract: Acknowledging Generative AI’s presence in the higher education classroom, instructors must navigate unclear boundaries around acceptable and unacceptable student use. This quantitative study surveyed 89 instructors across four research‑intensive universities in the United States to examine their perceptions of student Generative AI use and the strategies they adopt to manage it. Findings reveal that instructors construct task-specific acceptability judgments rather than applying university rules, with core writing tasks deemed largely unacceptable while supplementary activities have wider acceptance. A perception-acceptance gap was apparent for writing tasks, showing that instructors suspect widespread AI use for the very activities they find most problematic. Prevention strategies emphasize pedagogical over surveillance approaches, but nonetheless almost 40% of the instructors reported catching students using AI to plagiarize, with most cases resolved informally. Title: Logic-Twin: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Autonomous Driving Safety Auditing and Evolutionary Data Curation
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide new capabilities for semantic planning in autonomous driving, but the stochastic nature of their generation process may lead to hallucinations and safety violations. Conventional industrial validation relies heavily on manual annotation and human auditing, which suffers from limited scalability, high latency, and cognitive fatigue. To address these bottlenecks, this paper proposes the Logic-Twin framework, an offline neuro-symbolic architecture for automated safety auditing and evolutionary data governance. The framework serves as an asynchronous offline safety auditing module based on a dual-alignment mechanism, rather than directly participating in real-time vehicle control. Specifically, it uses a Mivar expert system to evaluate the safety of autonomous driving decisions, while employing large language models to extract potential rules from new boundary scenarios, thereby enabling continuous updates to the knowledge base. Experimental results show that the framework achieves a correction success rate (CSR) of 91.7% in filtering hazardous trajectories. Title: NEM: A Numerical Exact Match Subtype-Aware Metric Family for eXplainable Numerical Accuracy in Specialized Chatbots
Abstract: Field-specific chatbot evaluation traditionally relies on metrics such as Exact Match, BLEU, and ROUGE, which require manual benchmarks and emphasize lexical similarity rather than factual correctness. Human evaluation and LLM-as-a-Judge approaches remain costly or subjective. In domains like finance and medicine, numerical accuracy is critical, yet existing frameworks fail to address this need. We propose Numerical Exact Match (NEM), a family of automated eXplainable metrics for evaluating numerical correctness across four subtypes: temporal information (NEM-TI), discrete information (NEM-DI), continuous information (NEM-CI), and identifier-based information (NEM-FI). Combined with the Vietnamese Question/Answer Benchmark Generator (VQABG), NEM enables fully automated, eXplainable, subtype-aware evaluation tailored to isolating languages such as Vietnamese. Experiments show that traditional metrics favor fluency, while NEM provides a more accurate measure of domain specific reliability, reducing cost and improving explainability in Vietnamese chatbot assessment. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Predictive Modeling of the Activation Energy of Petroleum Sludge Pyrolysis Using Artificial Intelligence Approaches
Abstract: This study is about using a hybrid artificial intelligence approach to predict the activation energy (Ea) of petroleum sludge pyrolysis. Three modeling techniques were compared: Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Radial Basis Functions (RBF), and a new hybrid model that combines Radial Basis Functions with a Genetic Algorithm (RBF-GA). Title: Reducing Disparity in Aleatoric Uncertainty for Age Estimation from Facial Images
Abstract: Age estimation from facial images is a challenging task but has diverse applications in real world. Variations in image quality, facial orientation, occlusion, and lighting introduce aleatoric uncertainty (AU), the inherent randomness in data that affects machine learning performance. While previous studies have explored techniques to quantify and mitigate AU, little attention has been given to the disparity in AU across different identity groups, which can introduce biases and exacerbate social inequities. In this work, we investigate AU discrepancies in age estimation models and propose AUFairGAN, a generative AI model based on the generative adversarial network (GAN), to mitigate these disparities. Compared to conventional GANs, we introduce an additional AU-specific discriminator to enforce unbiased AU levels for different identity groups. We also add a penalty term in the generator’s loss function to explicitly penalize large AU discrepancies at the mini-batch level during the model training. This novel architecture ensures that the model generates faithful facial images that reduce aleatoric uncertainty gap across identity groups. We evaluate AUFairGAN on three publicly available facial image datasets and demonstrate that our model successfully mitigates AU discrepancy, leading to improved model trustworthiness while improving the age estimation performance and maintaining the image quality. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Cross-Cultural Differences in Perceptions of the Environmental Impact of Generative AI
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: This study addresses a critical gap in the literature on sustainable information systems by empirically investigating how national culture shapes perceptions of the environmental impact of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). Based on a survey of 434 university students from France, Portugal, the United States, and China, the research employs statistical analyses to test for significant cross-national differences. For instance, while 70% of French respondents express a desire to know the carbon footprint of their AI queries, only 45% of Chinese respondents share this concern. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) confirms that country of residence is a statistically significant predictor of environmental concern and attitudes toward regulatory measures. These findings challenge universalist “one-size-fits-all” approaches to digital sustainability policy. The study concludes that promoting sustainable AI on a global scale requires context-sensitive strategies aligned with local cultural values, institutional frameworks, and technological ecosystems. Title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Digital Ecosystems in Research and Education
Abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques in e-learning ecosystems is expanding, although the algorithms used and decision steps often represent an enigma to learners and educators. Equity issues, plausible privacy risks, scarcity of transparency and trust are major concerns for the adoption of AI in digital education, about individualized teaching and learning recommendations, feedback, and e-assessment. Authors: Sena I.; Mendes J.; Pereira A.I.
Title: A Comparative NLP Study of Semantic and Thematic Changes in AI Research Pre - and Post-generative AI
Abstract: With the advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly with the emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs), has significantly influenced the scope, accessibility, and dissemination of scientific research. This evolution raises important questions regarding how AI-related scientific discourse has changed over time. This study search lexical, semantic, and thematic changes in a dataset of approximately 50,000 AI-related publications retrieved from the Web of Science (WoS), comparing a pre-GenAI period (2015–2019) with a post-GenAI period (2022–2025). Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques were applied, including TF-IDF for lexical analysis, Logistic Regression for temporal classification, and BERTopic for topic modeling. The results achieved an accuracy of 89%, revealing a clear separability between the two periods based on textual features. The analyses reveal a transition from predominantly technical and methodological terminology, focused on algorithms and infrastructure, toward more application-oriented and generative themes, including GenAI and LLMs. Furthermore, topic modeling shows the growing prominence of interdisciplinary domains such as education, healthcare, and business applications in the post-GenAI period. Overall, the findings suggest a significant lexical and thematic evolution in AI-related scientific discourse, reflecting broader transformations in research priorities and application domains following the emergence of GenAI technologies. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Zhang D.; Fan C.; Li Z.; Qin C.; Dan J.
Title: Scale-spectrum-state collaborative fusion network for real-time extreme small object detection in intelligent sports analytics
Abstract: In the realm of intelligent sports decision-support systems, Extreme Small Object (ESO) detection in high-dynamic scenes remains a critical challenge due to severe scale imbalance and complex environmental interference. These factors significantly degrade micro-scale feature preservation, background discrimination, and contextual reasoning capability in real-world deployments. Existing real-time detectors often struggle to preserve fine-grained spatial evidence, suppress structured background interference, and maintain contextual robustness within a unified perception pipeline. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a real-time Scale-Spectrum-State Collaborative Fusion Network (SSSC-Fusion Net), which integrates micro-scale preservation, frequency-aware feature refinement, and global contextual modeling within a unified architecture. First, a Content-Aware Scalable Space-to-Depth (CAS-SPD) mechanism is introduced to preserve micro-scale spatial evidence through lossless spatial-to-channel reorganization. Second, a Frequency-Domain Decomposition Convolution (FDC) module is designed to suppress repetitive background textures via semantic-guided spectral gating while preserving discriminative structural features. Third, a State-Sharing SS2D-Mamba module is incorporated to enhance global contextual reasoning with linear complexity, improving robustness under occlusion and motion blur. To further stabilize optimization under extreme scale imbalance, a Scale-Inverse Gradient Rectification (S3-SIGR) objective is introduced to enhance gradient sensitivity for micro-scale targets. Extensive experiments on SoccerNet Tracking 2023 show that SSSC-Fusion Net achieves 79.1% AP50 and 45.8% AP50: 95, while improving Ball AP50 to 42.8% and retaining 169.1 FPS on an NVIDIA A100. These results indicate that coordinated scale, spectral, and contextual modeling improves the recovery of micro-scale ball instances, which is critical for downstream game-state reconstruction, automated officiating, and tactical reasoning. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Forecasting Gait Dynamics with Foundation Models
Abstract: Foundation Models (FMs) are emerging as promising tools in healthcare thanks to their ability to anticipate signal trends and provide early indications useful for clinical evaluation and decision support. In this study, FMs were used for short-term forecasting of inertial signals acquired during walking, adopting a multivariate approach on the triaxial accelerometer components. FMs (Moirai, Lag-Llama, Chronos) were used in both zero-shot (ZS) and fine-tuning (FT) modes, comparing their performances with baselines of widely used traditional Machine Learning (ML) models (XGBoost, LSTM, DeepAR). The results show that FMs effectively capture the dynamics of walking inertial signals and, especially after FT, offer competitive performance compared to baselines, with greater stability over longer horizons. The use of FMs for short-term predictions in gait analysis may open the way for their integration into multidisciplinary rehabilitation contexts thanks to the ability to forecast gait anomalies that might be useful to assess patient condition. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Sun H.; Wu D.; Liu W.; Yao M.; Yu G.
Title: Emotionally vulnerable subtype of internet gaming disorder: Measuring and exploring the pathology of problematic generative AI use
Abstract: Concerns over the potential over-pathologization of generative AI (GenAI) use and the lack of conceptual clarity surrounding GenAI addiction call for empirical tools and theoretical refinement. This study developed and validated the PUGenAIS-9 (Problematic Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence Scale-9 items) and examined whether PUGenAIS reflects addiction-like patterns under the Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD) framework. Using samples from China and the United States (N = 1508), we conducted confirmatory factor analysis and identified a robust 31-item structure across nine IGD-based dimensions. We then derived the PUGenAIS-9 by selecting the highest-loading items from each dimension and validated its structure in an independent sample (N = 1426). Measurement invariance tests confirmed its stability across nationality and gender. Person-centered (latent profile analysis) and variable-centered (network analysis) approaches revealed a 5–10% prevalence rate, a symptom network structure similar to IGD, and predictive factors related to psychological distress and functional impairment. These findings indicate that PUGenAI shares features of the emotionally vulnerable subtype of IGD rather than the competence-based type. These results support using PUGenAIS-9 to identify problematic GenAI use and show the need to rethink digital addiction with an IDC (Infrastructure-Device-Content) model. This keeps addiction research responsive to new media while avoiding over-pathologizing. © 2026

Authors: Xiao N.; Lang B.; Chen T.; Long Y.; Lu H.; Chen Y.; Hu N.; Jiao J.; Wei Y.
Title: MDFA: LLM-Based Multi-dimensional Fusion Reasoning for Threat Actor Attribution
Abstract: Threat actor attribution (TAA) for advanced persistent threats (APTs) requires multi-dimensional information fusion and associative reasoning. Existing studies usually rely on single-dimensional clues such as malware, indicators of compromise (IOCs), or attack techniques, while methods using hybrid clues often insufficiently analyze the semantics of different clue types. To address these limitations, we propose MDFA, a TAA framework based on large language models that combines per-dimension attribution with multi-dimensional fusion. MDFA focuses on four main dimensions in APT campaign intelligence: malicious code snippets, IOCs, attack techniques, and social context. Specifically, we design dimension-specific attribution methods based on malicious code functionality and intent, attacker-discriminative technique weighting, and campaign-context association with threat actor profiling. We also design a multi-dimensional fusion method that jointly evaluates evidence strength, distinctiveness, and overall consistency across dimensions. Extensive experimental results show that MDFA significantly outperforms various baseline methods, improving the accuracy and explainability of attribution reasoning. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: DA-ECAN: DualAudio-EnhancedCNN feature learning with asymmetric fusion for multimodal emotion recognition
Abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition plays a crucial role in human-computer interaction and sentiment analysis. However, existing methods for multimodal emotion recognition face challenges in handling Chinese data scarcity, insufficient utilization of acoustic-textual features, and inadequate dynamic cross-modal interaction. To address these limitations, we propose DA-ECAN, a DualAudio-EnhancedCNN Cross-Attention Network, which integrates dual-modality feature enhancement and adaptive fusion. First, we construct CH-SIMS v2.0-DA, an augmented dataset leveraging large language models (LLMs) for text diversification and controllable text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis for multi-style speech generation. For feature extraction, the audio branch employs a dual-stream architecture: wav2vec 2.0 captures phoneme-level semantic dependencies from raw waveforms, while MHSA-BiLSTM analyzes MFCC-based spectral-temporal patterns to model prosodic details (e.g., pitch, rhythm). The text branch adopts LLM-enhanced CNN, where Qwen embeddings provide context-aware representations, and multi-scale convolutional kernels extract phrase-level and syntactic patterns. Crucially, a Transformer-based asymmetric fusion module dynamically aligns audio and text features by using text as queries to guide attention over acoustic keys and values, balancing modality contributions and mitigating text dominance. Experimental results on MC-EIU, CH-SIMS v2.0 and its enhanced dataset CH-SIMS v2.0-DA demonstrate that DA-ECAN outperforms existing baseline models across all metrics, validating its effectiveness in emotion recognition tasks. Title: Financial Literacy in an AI/XAI-Driven World: A Systematic Review and Bibliometric Mapping
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: The rapid digitalization of financial services, combined with the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI), is transforming the range of competencies individuals need to make informed, confident financial decisions. This study provides a systematic review and a bibliometric analysis of the growing intersection between financial literacy, FinTech, AI, and algorithmic explainability (XAI). The review is based on 531 peer-reviewed articles published between 2010 and 2025 and indexed in the Web of Science and Scopus databases. To characterise the field, the study draws on co-word mapping, country-level productivity patterns, and LDA topic modelling. Three conceptual clusters (traditional financial literacy, digital inclusion, and algorithmic transparency) are found to structure much of the literature. At the same time, four latent topics reveal evolving concerns related to financial behaviour, digital transformation, and the adoption of AI-enabled financial technologies. The evidence suggests that financial literacy is increasingly understood as a multidimensional capability that involves digital skills, awareness of algorithmic processes, and the ability to interpret explanations based on XAI. Drawing together the three clusters and four topics, the review reframes financial literacy as an “AI-attuned” competence that links traditional financial knowledge with digital inclusion and algorithmic transparency. The findings have implications for financial education, regulatory design, and human oversight, and help outline a research agenda suited to financial ecosystems that are becoming progressively more automated and data-driven. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Teachers’ Perspectives on Decision-Making in AI-Supported Classrooms: A Cross-Cultural Study of Germany and Japan
Abstract: As AI technologies become increasingly integrated into classrooms, the field of AI in Education (AIED) emphasizes the need to understand stakeholder perspectives to ensure AI is designed and implemented in ways that support both teachers and students. However, previous research has not fully examined how these perspectives may vary across cultural contexts. Given the complexity of classroom dynamics and the role of cultural and social values in shaping learning experiences, it is crucial to explore how contextual factors might influence stakeholder views. This study presents a qualitative investigation involving 15 German and 10 Japanese teachers, using a storyboard-based speed-dating approach to examine their perspectives on student-led versus AI-led decision-making in the classroom. Our findings reveal commonalities between the two groups, such as the shared belief in the importance of teacher involvement in both students’ and AI’s decision-making processes and concern about excessive AI monitoring. However, we also identified notable differences: Japanese teachers expressed a stronger preference for greater access to student data, while German counterparts preferred student autonomy in decision making. We discuss these findings in relation to their cultural contexts, including classroom norms such as the “silence” in Japanese classrooms. This study contributes to the field by demonstrating how stakeholder perspectives on AI in education can vary across cultural contexts and highlighting the need to account for cultural and social factors when designing and integrating AI systems in classrooms. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: An Effective AI-Driven Prompting Approach for Video Summarization System Using Flan-T5 Model
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: With the video content multiplying in the educational and professional delivery systems, the automated transcript summarization is becoming critical when it comes to enhancing accessibility and readability. This is the work that explores the influence of systematic prompt engineering on the quality of video transcript summarization with neural language models. Our proposed seven-stage processing pipeline that integrates the FLAN-T5-based prompt refinement and tests its performance on five educational videos, comparing the results with the commercial LLMs such as GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Perplexity based on ROUGE Score metrics. Our findings indicate that structured prompt refinement has quantifiable gains in content coverage (ROUGE-1: 0.2327, which is a 19% increment compared to the unrefined baseline). Our refined model was, however, ranked highly on ROUGE-1 scores (3/7), and low on ROUGE-2 fluency scores (0.0103, 6/7), which is significantly lower than Perplexity 0.0190, which means that prompt engineering only helps to increase lexical overlap but not to fully mitigate the limitations of small models to capture local coherence and bigram frequencies. These results point to both the possibilities and shortcomings of cost-efficient prompt engineering interventions on learning content summarization, indicating that coverage refinement strategies are the most powerful at content coverage instead of conversational transcripts fluency. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Design and Implementation of a Web-Based AI Coach & Counselor: A Dual-Mode Support System for High School Students
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: We present a lightweight web-based AI Coach & Counselor for high school students with two dialogue modes: (1) a coaching mode for goal setting and action planning and (2) a counseling mode for emotional support. To support school deployment, the system includes operational logging and safety-by-design measures, such as discouraging the entry of personally identifiable information and recommending escalation to human support for high-risk situations. We report a pilot deployment and evaluation using interaction logs and a post-use questionnaire. The system recorded 47 sessions (310 messages), with coaching interactions predominating. Questionnaire results (n = 51; 6-point scale) indicated high perceived clarity and ease of use, while intentions for continued use were comparatively lower. A co-occurrence network analysis of the English-translated logs suggested that consultations mainly clustered around goal/option exploration (e.g., goals, interests, values, and next steps), alongside exam- and curriculum-related topics. Students preferred using the system in collaboration with humans and supported human handoff for high-risk situations. Open-ended feedback highlighted detailed responses and idea generation as strengths, and requested faster responses, more actionable suggestions, tone customization, and clearer cues for reliability. We discuss implications for designing school-ready AI support tools that balance usability, trust, and safe human–AI collaboration. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Epistemic Agency, AI Knowledge and Performance in Generative AI-Supported Data Analytics Tasks
Abstract: As generative AI increasingly supports learners’ problem-solving processes, there remains a limited empirical understanding of how individuals exercise epistemic judgment toward AI-generated content in learning contexts. This study examines the roles of epistemic agency and AI knowledge, along with learners’ behavioral use of generative AI in an online data analytics problem-solving task under time constraints. Eighty-five undergraduate and graduate students participated in an open-ended online data analytics task supported by generative AI. With informed consent, participants’ GenAI usage behaviors during the task were recorded, and survey measures of epistemic agency toward AI-generated content and the AI knowledge test were collected. A GenAI usage ratio was then computed as an indicator of learners’ interaction with generative AI during the task. Multiple regression analyses were conducted to examine the relative contributions of GenAI usage ratio, epistemic agency, and AI knowledge to task performance, controlling for sex and prior ability. Results showed that higher epistemic agency and AI knowledge were positively associated with problem-solving performance. In contrast, a higher generative AI usage ratio across the task process was negatively associated with performance, suggesting that higher usage intensity may signal over-reliance on GenAI. Instead, effective problem-solving involves learners’ knowledge of the technical mechanisms, historical foundations, and practical applications of AI alongside a critical awareness of its ethical, social, and environmental impacts. Further, learners’ epistemic agency to critically evaluate GenAI output, assert intellectual ownership, and construct interpretation over machine-generated knowledge is also related to better performance. These findings underscore the importance of instructional designs that cultivate both epistemic agency and AI knowledge to support reflective and purposeful human-AI collaboration in problem-solving contexts. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Timed Games Under Environmental Interference with Real-Time Objectives
Abstract: Classical Timed Games formulations may be unsuitable, or require substantial modeling effort, to capture complex interaction patterns between a controller and its surrounding environment, in which the non-determinism must be resolved after the controller has chosen which action to perform. This paper introduces Timed CLTLoc Games (TCGs), a novel Timed Game variant designed to facilitate the modeling of such patterns. Unlike classical Timed Games, TCGs partition locations rather than actions, and use Constraint Linear Temporal Logic over clocks formulae to specify the controller’s objectives. We implement algorithms for solving TCGs in our C++20 region-based library Tarzan, leveraging OpenMP for efficient parallelization. Title: UTFDAM: An Unsupervised Time-Frequency Dual-Domain Adaptive Method for Cross-Working Condition Fault Diagnosis of Rolling Bearings
Abstract: High-efficiency fault diagnosis of rolling bearings is essential to ensuring the secure and stable operation of rotating machinery. However, when rolling bearings operate under dynamic working scenarios, the generalization capability of most existing fault classification models deteriorates significantly. To tackle the above problems, this study presents an Unsupervised Time-frequency Dual-domain Adaptive Fault Diagnosis Method for rolling bearings under cross-working conditions (UTFDAM). By constructing a 1D-CNN-Transformer model to extract deep features from the original vibration signals and an inception network incorporating the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) to extract deep frequency domain features. Then, the fused multi-domain features are introduced into a feature classification module, enabling the acquisition of reliable and high-precision rolling bearing fault diagnosis results. Throughout the training process, the Multi-Kernel Conditional Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MK-CMMD) method is leveraged to accomplish precise alignment of feature distributions across source and target domains. The presented method was ultimately compared with multiple methods on two cross-working-condition datasets, fully verifying its effectiveness. Title: Do Instructional Behaviors Generalize Across Disciplines? an Empirical Study with Fine-Tuned Multimodal LLMs
Abstract: Instructional behavior description extracts instructional behavior labels and structured descriptions from multimodal classroom data to support teaching evaluation and student feedback. Although instructional behaviors are often assumed to generalize across domains, examining cross-domain differences is essential for understanding how pedagogical intent and classroom enactment vary in practice. Accordingly, this study adopts cross-disciplinary comparison as a concrete research object to empirically examine domain-context dependence in instructional behavior description. We construct a multimodal classroom dataset composed of nearly 1,000 classroom video segments from authentic secondary school lessons, organized into Humanities and Science contexts to provide empirical data support. To enhance Multimodal Large Language Models’ (MLLMs) instructional behavior recognition and description under educational data and computational constraints, we apply LoRA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, to adapt three representative open-source MLLMs. We conduct intra-disciplinary evaluations, cross-disciplinary train–test swap experiments, and discipline-specificity analyses to systematically examine how instructional behavior recognition and description vary within and across disciplines. Results show that LoRA consistently improves performance in both contexts, while cross-disciplinary transfer leads to substantial performance degradation and clear directional asymmetry. Discipline-specificity analysis further reveals systematic differences in instructional behavior distributions and description keywords between Humanities and Science. These results provide empirical evidence that instructional behavior description is discipline-context dependent rather than one-size-fits-all, highlighting the risk of deploying discipline-agnostic instructional analytics in real classrooms and underscoring the necessity of discipline-aware educational AI systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: AI Roles as Multiple-Source Texts: Designing a Detective-Inquiry Writing Activity for Elementary Students
Abstract: This paper presents the design of a writing activity that supports Grade 6 students’ evidence-based narrative writing through multiple-source integration in a detective-style case reconstruction task. Grounded in multiple-text comprehension, the activity requires students to synthesize partial and perspective-bound testimonies to infer what most likely happened. The proposed “case package” includes a fixed case prompt and evidence note, role-based sources with predefined knowledge boundaries, and student worksheets that scaffold cross-source comparison (e.g., marking corroborated claims, contradictions, and unresolved questions). Two delivery modes were implemented: a role-based reading mode in which students read three testimony texts, and an AI role-play dialogue mode in which students interviewed AI characters representing the same roles. The intervention was conducted across four 40-min sessions with four intact Grade 6 classes (approximately 30 students per class; N = 120). Preliminary findings suggest that students in the AI role-play condition reported higher writing motivation and produced stronger case reconstruction narratives. In rubric-based evaluation, AI-group writing more frequently demonstrated broader cross-source coverage, clearer claim–evidence linkage, more explicit source attribution (who said what and how it was known), improved timeline coherence, and more effective handling of contradictions across role testimonies. Title: Public Participation, Spatially-Informed Artificial Intelligence and Territorial Planning: Integrating GIS, Text Mining and Clustering for the Analysis of Stakeholder Preferences
Abstract: The increasing complexity of territorial planning processes, particularly in the context of large-scale infrastructure projects, calls for the integration of participatory approaches, spatial analysis and advanced computational techniques. This paper proposes a comprehensive methodological framework that combines public participation, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), text mining, clustering algorithms, and AI-based analytical techniques within a structured and transparent workflow for the systematic analysis of stakeholder contributions. A central contribution of this work lies in the explicit incorporation of spatial variables into the analysis of stakeholder preferences, with particular attention to the relationship between geographical proximity and expressed sentiment. Based on developed theoretical paradigms such as spatial behavior theory, distance-decay models, and Not In My Back Yard (NIMBY) dynamics, the study explores how distance from an intervention impact on the strength and direction of stakeholder positions. The proposed approach transforms unstructured textual data obtained by participatory processes into structured indicators of territorial consensus and dissent. Title: Evaluating LLMs in ROS robotic software code generation
Abstract: Code generation has emerged as a valuable technique for accelerating robotic software development. However, unlike general-purpose programming, generating code for Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) requires navigating complex, domain-specific frameworks like the Robot Operating System (ROS). Although Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in general-purpose code generation, their capability to synthesize executable, middleware-compliant ROS code remains poorly understood. This task demands that LLMs not only solve robotic tasks but also generate code that seamlessly integrates within the distributed ROS framework. To address this gap, we construct ROSDevEval, a specialized benchmark comprising 240 real-world ROS programming tasks, and conduct a comprehensive empirical study to evaluate four state-of-the-art LLMs alongside a specialized code assistant (GitHub Copilot). Our results reveal a severe domain capability gap: while state-of-the-art LLMs achieve up to 88.4% Pass@1 on general-purpose C++, their performance suffers a precipitous relative decline ranging from 78.8% to 85.4% in robotic contexts, and even the specialized assistant struggles to exceed a 32.5% success rate. Through a rigorous open-coding analysis, we systematically categorize LLMs’ generation failures into two distinct dimensions. In robotic task resolution, LLMs struggle to apply physical constraints and produce functional logic. In ROS framework integration, they systematically violate strict middleware contracts required for system orchestration. Furthermore, our root cause analysis explicitly decouples these surface-level failures from their underlying etiology, revealing a profound dual cognitive deficit: LLMs lack the long-horizon procedural decomposition capability to translate abstract tasks into executable sequences, and they fail to grasp the rigid architectural topology required for distributed system integration. These findings delineate current limitations and provide actionable, architecture-aware implications for advancing the next generation of robotic foundation models. Title: Catching The Correct Answer Trap: Characterising AI Tutor Blind Spots When Analysing Student Reasoning
Abstract: Intelligent tutoring systems increasingly provide automated feedback on student work, but robust feedback requires assessing reasoning, not only final answers. We study a failure mode we call the correct answer trap (CAT): models under-detect misconceptions when students reach a correct answer via flawed reasoning. Analysing real student responses from the Eedi mathematics platform, we show that 71% of these failures concentrate in just two question types, both sharing a common structure where flawed reasoning happens to produce the correct numerical answer. Comparing a fine-tuned T5 with a frontier large language model, we find that improved capabilities reduce but do not eliminate the problem (84% vs 57% detection accuracy). Even the best-performing model generates roughly four false alarms for every genuine detection, making stand-alone screening impractical at realistic class sizes. Our findings demonstrate that high overall accuracy can mask critical failures in reasoning assessment, and that careful analysis of student reasoning still benefits from human judgment. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Xian Y.; Yu H.; Xie Y.; Wang G.
Title: Tabular continual learning from high-heterogeneity feature spaces via memory and forgetting dual-driven
Abstract: Continual learning is plagued by catastrophic forgetting. While storing representative exemplars is an effective mitigation strategy, such exemplars often lack cross-task representativeness and their knowledge may interfere with new task learning. This issue is particularly prominent in tabular settings under high-heterogeneity feature spaces. Inspired by the neurobiological framework of memory and forgetting, we propose a Tabular Continual Learning method from high-heterogeneity feature spaces via Memory and Forgetting dual-driven (MFTCL). Specifically, MFTCL combines two complementary strategies. First, a memory storage strategy based on evidence theory is designed to select exemplars that preserve both intra-task and cross-task representativeness. Second, an adaptive active forgetting strategy based on task similarity is developed to integrate network parameters, reducing interference from old knowledge during new task learning. Extensive comparisons on three benchmark tabular datasets (Isolet, Helena, and Nslkdd) validate the effectiveness of MFTCL in high-heterogeneity feature spaces. Further, a case study on five tabular datasets for disease diagnosis confirms its practical applicability. On the Helena dataset (heterogeneity rate: [0.61, 1.00]), MFTCL consistently outperforms all baseline methods across all evaluation metrics. Title: Medical Relation Extraction via Retrieval and Dynamic Triggering
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong potential for Relation Extraction (RE), but their application in the medical domain is limited by knowledge hallucination, long-tail terminology, and the high cost of static Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). To the end, we propose Hybrid-DR-RE, a confidence-aware hybrid retrieval model for medical RE that balances factual grounding and retrieval efficiency. The model formulates retrieval as cost-sensitive conditional computation and introduces Dynamic Selective Confidence Estimation (DSCE), which estimates knowledge sufficiency using first-token entropy and triggers retrieval only when uncertainty is high. This enables on-demand knowledge augmentation without architectural changes or additional training objectives. We further develop a dual-path retriever integrating BM25 lexical matching with dense semantic retrieval. Extensive experiments on the CMeIE-V2 benchmark show that Hybrid-DR-RE achieves an F1-score of 59.60%, outperforming static RAG baselines while reducing the retrieval rate to 67.0%. Authors: Yuan N.; Zhao S.
Title: TrustMath: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning with Large Language Models
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in symbolic reasoning but arguably struggle with high-precision numerical computation, often producing “hallucinated” results in complex arithmetic tasks. To address this limitation, this paper proposes TrustMath, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that integrates a trusted computing engine (based on the ISReal algorithm) with a generative language model. Unlike existing prompt-engineering approaches, TrustMath employs a log-driven interpretation mechanism. It first performs error-bounded numerical calculations using Taylor expansion and interval arithmetic to ensure mathematical rigorousness, and then transforms the structured computation logs into natural language explanations via an LLM (e.g., Qwen2.5-Math). This approach guarantees both the numerical precision of the results and the logical consistency of the interpretative text. Experimental evaluations on complex transcendental functions (e.g., sin2100) demonstrate that our system achieves zero-error numerical accuracy while generating step-by-step explanations that significantly outperform purely LLM-based baselines in terms of verifiability and trustworthiness. Title: Implementing Risk-Proportionate AI Governance in Banking: A Longitudinal Case Study of ISO 42001 and RBI FREE-AI Integration for Credit Risk Management
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: The deployment of artificial intelligence in high-risk banking applications mandates robust governance frameworks balancing innovation with accountability. This paper presents a comprehensive longitudinal case study of a major Indian bank’s 24-month journey implementing integrated ISO 42001 and Reserve Bank of India FREE-AI governance frameworks for AI-driven credit risk management. Through mixed-methods research combining participant observation, document analysis, and quantitative performance measurement, we examine how dual framework integration operationalizes responsible AI governance in practice. The bank, serving over 5 million borrowers, achieved Level 5 (Optimizing) ISO 42001 maturity and 4.6/5.0 FREE-AI Sutra compliance, resulting in 15% non-performing asset (NPA) reduction, 98% loan processing time reduction (7 days to 4 h), and 25% increase in thin-file customer approvals while maintaining zero regulatory examination findings. Our longitudinal analysis reveals critical success factors including board-level commitment, comprehensive 7-facet fairness testing (monthly frequency), alternative data integration, and proactive regulatory engagement (6 briefings/year). The research contributes four theoretical insights: (1) risk-maturity alignment principle validated through high-stakes credit decisions, (2) fairness-by-design architecture for diverse demographic contexts, (3) governance-innovation symbiosis model demonstrating mutual reinforcement, and (4) phased maturity evolution pathway applicable across banking institutions. Practical contributions include 24-month implementation roadmap, operational control templates for credit AI, comprehensive fairness testing framework for Indian demographic diversity, and proactive regulatory engagement protocols. Title: Accessibility for the Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Introduction to the Special Thematic Session
Abstract: The Special Thematic Session on Accessibility for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing presents research addressing accessibility from three perspectives: context awareness, artificial intelligence, and interaction. The contributions show that accessibility depends on situational factors, such as environment and communication constraints, as well as on the integration of multiple modalities. Studies on artificial intelligence-supported sign language technologies demonstrate progress but also limitations, especially in representing linguistic features required for real-world use. Studies on interaction design indicate that sign language remains the preferred modality, while other solutions provide only partial solutions. Title: Complementing Human Instruction: Student Interaction Patterns with a Pedagogically Aligned AI Teaching Assistant
Abstract: Generative AI–based teaching assistants are increasingly used in higher education, yet questions remain about how pedagogically constrained AI systems shape student interaction and engagement alongside human instruction. This exploratory study adopts an interaction centered perspective to examine the design and use of ThinkCode, a pedagogically aligned AI teaching assistant deployed in a graduate programming course. Drawing on interaction logs, course performance data, and post-course survey responses, we compare students’ interactions with ThinkCode and a human-moderated discussion forum, focusing on interaction volume, temporal alignment with assessments, learning outcomes, and student perceptions. Results show that students generated approximately ten times more interactions with ThinkCode than with the discussion forum, with activity closely aligned with assignment and quiz deadlines. Descriptive comparisons further indicate that ThinkCode users exhibited higher average assignment and quiz scores and lower score variability than non-users. Title: Federated Rationale Extraction with Information Competition
Abstract: The remarkable success of deep neural networks has sparked growing interest in methods to explain their predictions, with rationale extraction emerging as a key approach. Rationale extraction identifies critical text segments from input data that justify and explain the model’s results, making it especially useful in high-stakes fields. However, strict data privacy regulations in these fields often prevent the sharing of sensitive information. Federated Learning (FL) offers a promising solution by facilitating collaborative model training without requiring data exchange. However, the challenge of heterogeneous data across clients remains a significant barrier to optimal model performance. To this end, in this paper, we introduce Federated Rationale Extraction with Information Competition (FedIC), a novel approach designed for FL settings. Specifically, for each client, FedIC leverages an environment projector to map local data to a global distribution, generating counterfactual samples. Then, from the perspective of information competition, two optimization criteria are designed to ensure that the generated samples remain task-relevant and consistent with the global data distribution, addressing the issue of data heterogeneity. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of FedIC. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy
Abstract: Collaboration literacy requires adapting to the evolving demands of group work within complex discussions, making it difficult to develop and assess. Traditional analytics metrics capture behavioral signals while missing the semantic dimensions of how learners approach collaboration and build on each other’s ideas. We present Collaboration Literacy through Artifact Reasoning and Augmentation (CLARA), an agentic analytics system that extracts semantic representations from transcripts as analytics artifacts: concept maps representing emergent ideas and relationships, and collaboration assessment characterizing collaboration quality across seven dimensions. While users explore these artifacts through the dashboard, the same artifacts are indexed into distinct vector database collections for agent retrieval and reasoning. This architecture establishes a human-AI common ground where users and AI can operate over shared representations. Evaluation results show that CLARA produces reliable collaboration quality analysis and, owing to the artifacts serving as knowledge infrastructure, improves both retrieval performance and response quality over transcript-only baselines. Title: Hybrid Multi-logic Reasoning Framework Over Ontologies for Decision Support in Neurodevelopmental Disorders
Abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders pose significant challenges for clinical decision support because their assessment involves heterogeneous data, evolving developmental trajectories, uncertainty, and, at times, conflicting evidence. In this paper, we present the Hybrid Multi-Logic Autism Ontology framework (HML-AutismOnt), a modular, layered architecture developed to extend the Autism Ontology. We designed this extension to address the limitations of traditional decision support systems in Neurodevelopmental Disorders (NDDs) management, particularly the difficulty of representing temporal evolution, conflicting clinical evidence, and normative constraints within care pathways. The framework integrates temporal, fuzzy, modal, deontic, and paraconsistent logics to model evolving states, uncertain observations, guideline-driven obligations, and potentially inconsistent evidence. We describe the system architecture, the hybrid reasoning workflow, and the organizational strategy that combine ontology-based knowledge representation with modular reasoning services. The resulting framework promotes semantic interoperability, enables structured multi-logic inference, and supports consistent reasoning over complex domain knowledge. Authors: Miao Y.; Luo S.; Zhan K.
Title: GeoPaperLLM: A Fine-Tuning Based Two-Stage Framework for Hierarchical Classification of Geoscience Literature
Abstract: The boom in AI4Science has driven the rapid development of geoscience domain-specific large language models (LLMs). Literature subject classification (LSC) is a foundational core task in this process, which screens target domain corpus to support LLM training, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and evaluation. However, this task is plagued by three key challenges: low full-text classification efficiency, inadequate geoscience-specific optimization, and a lack of high-quality hierarchical labeled datasets. To address these challenges, this study designs a two-stage hierarchical classification framework for geoscience subject identification, first judging geoscience affiliation and then identifying 8 secondary sub-disciplines. We construct a dedicated benchmark dataset with 280,000 subject-annotated entries covering papers, dissertations, and books. A lightweight inference LLM is trained via teacher-student paradigm: the teacher model generates CoT reasoning processes for disciplinary affiliation, and the student model is fine-tuned with CoT and subject label data to output JSON-formatted hierarchical results. Comparative experiments demonstrate that our model achieves superior classification accuracy while maintaining a balance between deployment cost and inference efficiency, providing high-quality corpus support for training geoscience LLMs and serving as a valuable reference for discipline classification in other scientific domains. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Authors: Alp A.; Ersöz F.
Title: A Comparative Analysis of Clustering Algorithms for Employee Segmentation in Human Resource Management Information Systems
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: The increasing availability of employee-related data has created new opportunities for human resource management to move beyond intuition-based decision-making toward analytical and evidence-driven practices. However, the multidimensional and unlabeled nature of human resources data makes it difficult to extract meaningful patterns using traditional evaluation methods. In this study, unsupervised machine learning techniques are employed to explore the internal structure of a company’s human resources dataset and to identify potential employee segments based on similarity patterns. The proposed approach integrates data preprocessing, dimensionality reduction, and clustering analysis within a unified analytical framework. K-Means and hierarchical clustering algorithms are applied to the dataset, and their outcomes are evaluated using internal validation measures. Rather than imposing predefined performance categories, the analysis focuses on uncovering natural groupings that emerge from the data itself. The results indicate that while distinct employee segments can be identified, the overall structure of the dataset exhibits a relatively high degree of homogeneity, limiting the sharp separation of clusters. These findings highlight both the potential and the limitations of clustering-based approaches in human resource analytics. From a practical perspective, the study demonstrates how unsupervised learning can support HR decision-making by offering an objective view of workforce structure. From an academic standpoint, it provides an applied example of exploratory analysis in an HR context and emphasizes the importance of cautious interpretation when deploying clustering methods on real-world organisational data. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Selective structural ablation for efficient 3D point cloud signal processing
Abstract: This work introduces a lightweight framework for 3D object classification in point clouds, derived from the Attention-Based Point Cloud Edge Sampling (APES) model. Title: A Credit Risk Digital Twin Framework with Explainability-Guided Feature Engineering and Counterfactual Simulation

Title: Uncertain AI – Better AI? Effects of Uncertainty Indicators in Collaborative Learning with a Human Peer or an Artificial Intelligence
Abstract: In learning, uncertainty is often associated with negative experiences and seen as something to be resolved immediately. However, research shows that uncertainty can increase learners’ motivation, process regulation, and learning intention. In collaborative learning, learners not only confront their own uncertainty but also the uncertainty they perceive in their peers. Nevertheless, little empirical work has examined whether the effects of group uncertainty observed in human collaboration transfer to interactions between learners and AI peers. In this study, we analyzed the effects of group uncertainty in different collaborative settings (with a human peer vs. an AI agent) and investigated mechanisms of uncertainty expression through different uncertainty indicators (uncertainty markers and controversial arguments) as well as the role of perceived social presence. We conducted an online study (N = 343) in which participants learned about a controversial topic with a co-learner. Depending on the experimental condition, the co-learner was a human peer or an AI agent who provided participants with their research results that did or did not include uncertainty indicators. We found that uncertainty indicators increased learners’ perceptions of their peer’s uncertainty (indicating group uncertainty awareness), which affected their individual uncertainty and learning engagement. Individual uncertainty increased learning intention via confusion. The effects were largely independent of whether the partner was human or AI. Perceived social presence strengthened the influence of perceived partner uncertainty on individual uncertainty, though this effect was stronger for the human peer. Title: End-to-End Keyword Spotting on FPGA Using Graph Neural Networks with a Neuromorphic Auditory Sensor
Abstract: With the rapid growth of mobile robotics and embedded intelligence, there is an increasing demand for efficient on-device data processing on edge platforms. A promising research direction is the use of neuromorphic sensors inspired by human sensory systems, which generate sparse, event-based data encoding changes in the environment. In this work, we present the first end-to-end FPGA implementation of a keyword spotting system that integrates a Neuromorphic Auditory Sensor (NAS) and a graph neural network (GNN) on a single FPGA device, enabling real-time processing of raw audio data. The proposed architecture eliminates conventional signal preprocessing and operates directly on event-based audio streams. Leveraging a compute-near-memory network architecture, the system achieves efficient inference with low latency and low power consumption. Experimental results demonstrate an accuracy of 87.43% after quantization on the Google Speech Commands v2 dataset processed through the neuromorphic sensor, with end-to-end latency below 35 μs and average power consumption of 1.12 W. The processed datasets, software models, and hardware modules are available at https://github.com/vision-agh/NAS-GNN-KWS. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Easy Trips: Planning Trips Made Easy through Agentic AI

Abstract: The travel industry has been transformed by the increasing incorporation of Artificial Intelligence (AI).It is changing the way people organize and enjoy their trips. The study mainly explores how AI driven systems is improving scalability, personalization and transparency in tourism while tackling ethical, technical and data privacy issues. It reviews how fast the intelligent agents are growing in tourism sector. This paper also presents EasyTrips, an innovative trip-planning framework which integrates agentic AI principles with real-time data analysis. It provides customized and economical travel options. In contrast to traditional platforms that rely on fixed recommendations, EasyTrips continuously adjusts according to user preferences and financial limitations and situational elements, such as weather conditions or trip cancellations. It is made with multi-agent coordination for modular task completion and also integrates automated cost management. Title: Saving Energy with Compiler Autotuning
Abstract: Improving the energy efficiency of software is increasingly important, not only for reducing operational costs but also for minimizing environmental impact. This work presents nine lightweight compiler autotuning techniques to optimize C programs for reduced energy consumption. These techniques operate at the compiler level and require no developer intervention or code adaptations, making them practical for integration into existing development workflows. We systematically evaluate the effectiveness of each approach across a benchmark suite and demonstrate that our most effective method achieves, on average, a reduction in energy consumption by a factor of 1.51 and a reduction in runtime by a factor of 1.28 compared to the default compiler settings. Title: AI-Based System for Automatic Backlog Generation and Preliminary Estimation from Requirement Documents
Abstract: In the context of digital transformation and Agile software development, requirement analysis and backlog preparation remain largely manual processes that rely heavily on individual experience and interpretation. These activities are time-consuming, error-prone, and often inconsistent, particularly in large-scale software projects. This paper presents an AI-based system for automatic backlog generation and preliminary effort estimation from requirement documents, designed to support Business Analysts (BAs) and Project Management Offices (PMOs) in Agile environments. The proposed system automatically analyzes software requirement documents, such as User Requirement Documents (URD) and Requirement Specification Documents (RSD), and generates structured Agile backlog artefacts, including Epics, User Stories, Acceptance Criteria, and Tasks/Sub-tasks, together with preliminary effort estimations. The system integrates large language models with rule-based estimation logic and provides seamless integration with enterprise project management platforms through REST APIs, enabling automatic synchronization with tools such as Jira and Confluence. The end-to-end workflow includes document ingestion, requirement extraction, contextual analysis, backlog generation, estimation computation, and structured export to project management systems. Experimental evaluation on real-world software requirement documents demonstrates that the proposed system significantly improves backlog preparation efficiency. The results show that the system can reduce backlog preparation time by approximately 75%, simplify the backlog creation workflow, and generate backlog items with a high level of accuracy and consistency compared to traditional manual approaches. These findings highlight the practical potential of AI-assisted systems in automating requirements engineering activities and improving productivity in Agile software development processes. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Authors: Yuanchao X.; Sen Z.; Anqi J.
Title: Visual analysis of convolutional neural networks for ship-radiated noise classification using Guided Backpropagation and Gaussian mixture models
Abstract: To address the lack of interpretability in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for ship-radiated noise classification, this paper proposes a visual analysis framework integrating Guided Backpropagation (GBP) and Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs). Firstly, a convolutional kernel visualization process based on GBP is constructed, combined with a multi-frame feature alignment algorithm to eliminate time-frequency interference from harmonic line components, enabling the precise reconstruction of deep convolutional kernel response features. Secondly, a GMM-based pattern decomposition method is proposed, which models activation locations to decompose a single convolutional kernel into multiple sub-patterns with distinct frequency distributions. Experiments were conducted on a CNN model with CQT spectrogram inputs, validated on the DeepShip dataset. The visualization results reveal that deep convolutional kernels contain two primary patterns: line spectra and background, detecting harmonic line components and continuous spectrum features in LOFAR spectrograms, respectively. After GMM decomposition, the response regions of the sub-patterns become more concentrated, feature expression becomes more consistent, and an association mechanism linking “convolutional kernel - sub-pattern - ship class” is established. This research provides a quantitative basis for understanding CNN decision logic, filling a gap in interpretability studies for ship-radiated noise classification models. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V.

Title: Six Standard Playing Cards Are Sufficient for All Three-Input Boolean Functions
Abstract: This paper deals with secure computation using a standard deck of playing cards. Since the first protocol using playing cards was devised by Niemi and Renvall in 1999, several secure computation protocols have been proposed. In 2022, Haga et al. proposed a generic protocol that securely computes three-input Boolean functions using six playing cards. However, this did not cover all three-input Boolean functions, and determining whether there exist six-card protocols for all such functions remained an open problem. In this paper, we construct protocols using six playing cards for each three-input Boolean function for which a protocol has not yet been built, thereby resolving this open problem. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Towards embodied AI in manufacturing: Review, Evaluation, and Future directions
Abstract: Embodied artificial intelligence (AI), which integrates perception, decision-making, and execution through interaction with the physical world, has recently emerged as a promising paradigm for enabling autonomous and adaptive manufacturing systems. While AI has been extensively explored in various manufacturing tasks, the major body of work remains fragmented across different processes, model paradigms, and task stages, lacking a unified basis for assessing how far current technologies have actually progressed towards system-level manufacturing intelligence. To address this gap, this paper introduces a task-oriented analytical framework grounded in the Perception, Decision–making, Execution (P-D-E) loop, which provides a common structure for systematically organizing, comparing, and evaluating AI contributions across heterogeneous manufacturing domains. Four representative processes including additive manufacturing (AM), machining, welding, and assembly are examined to map how AI technologies participate in each stage of the manufacturing task cycle. A six-dimensional evaluation criterion covering autonomy, adaptability, objective alignment, domain expertise, physical interaction, and industrial readiness is further proposed to assess the embodied AI readiness of each domain. The cross-process analysis yields several findings that go beyond individual process descriptions: the primary bottleneck towards embodied manufacturing intelligence is not the absence of capable models but the fragmentation of existing AI functions into isolated task-specific subloops; perception and reasoning capabilities have matured considerably faster than safe, reliable physical intervention; and different processes require fundamentally different embodiment pathways shaped by their physical coupling characteristics and deployment conditions. Based on these findings, the paper argues that near-term progress should follow a hierarchical and modular embodiment strategy, consider the problem from a task requirement-driven perspective, and establish standardized workflows and shared platforms to enable scalable, interoperable, and reproducible manufacturing AI systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Identifying Quality Indicators in Student Self-Reflections in Software Engineering
Abstract: Context: Reflection is a fundamental skill in software engineering education, particularly in project-based courses where students learn through extended group work and need to develop their ability to reflect iteratively throughout their work. For students to benefit from reflection, their written reflections need to be assessed so that feedback can guide and improve their reflective practice. However, manually assessing written reflections to guide reflections is time-consuming. Furthermore, assessment of reflections often results in broad, non-specific feedback for a student to improve. Objective: This study builds on reflective writing frameworks to produce an eight-indicator scheme for assessing student reflections in software engineering. Furthermore, this study validates an automated classifier for assessing reflections against the framework, enabling scalable and structured feedback whilst reducing instructor workload. Method: We adapted existing reflection frameworks through iterative refinement to create our eight-indicator framework. Three annotators labelled student reflection texts, establishing moderate to reliable inter-rater agreement. We then trained and evaluated multiple encoder-only transformer models and compared them with decoder-only large language models using zero-shot prompting. Results: The fine-tuned RoBERTa model achieved the strongest performance, substantially outperforming decoder-only models in both accuracy and speed. The classifier demonstrated human-level agreement on most indicators whilst enabling near-instantaneous classification. We provide two model variants optimised for different assessment priorities. Conclusions: Our fine-tuned encoder-only models enable efficient automated assessment of reflective writing. The framework and automated classifier offer a means to provide timely, structured feedback on student reflections in software engineering. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Digital and AI Tools in Education: Insights from Educators and Learners
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: Digitalization and the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools are increasingly influencing modern education and highlighting the need for its adaptation. Learners and educators in Bosnia and Herzegovina (B&H) are already using these tools, but due to insufficient digitalization of education and the lack of clear guidelines for pedagogically informed use of AI technologies, their application is often inadequate. To better understand the perceptions and needs of educators and learners, we conducted group discussions as part of a workshop with participants from B&H, Montenegro, Albania, and Kosovo. Participants highlighted the risks of maintaining existing practices, including reduced development of learners’ cognitive skills, irresponsible use of digital tools, and lowered social interaction, empathy, and practical skills. Educators also emphasized challenges in integrating technology, including the digital skills gap, insufficient support and training, and financial constraints. In this paper, we present the results of our discussion in detail and examine the potential consequences of maintaining current practices for education and broader societal development in B&H. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Not All Descriptions Help: Efficient Tool Selection via Concise Representations and Dynamic Experience
Abstract: Recent LLM-based agents can leverage external tools to handle complex tasks, mostly relying on natural language tool documentation for comprehension and selection. Nevertheless, practical tool descriptions are usually verbose, inconsistent and noisy, obscuring core functions and impairing decision efficiency as well as execution accuracy. Current mainstream paradigms hold that detailed tool descriptions yield better performance, while this unvalidated assumption may backfire. Most existing methods also regard tools as static modules, ignoring real-world dynamic traits such as fluctuating success rates, latency and usage costs. Driven by these issues, we present ToolDoc, a structured framework for efficient tool representation and selection. It comprises a concise static layer for semantic abstraction with reduced redundancy, and a dynamic experience layer modeling historical signals including success rate, cost, latency and error patterns. This design supports reliability-aware decision-making beyond simple semantic matching. Evaluations on API-Bank, ToolBench and FuncQA validate that ToolDoc steadily boosts tool selection accuracy, execution success rate and retrieval performance, with prominent improvements in noisy and large-scale scenarios. Ablation experiments verify the complementary merits of concise representation and dynamic experience modeling. Different from previous representation-enriching methods, our work minimizes redundancy while preserving core semantics. The results reveal that excessive description details do not optimize tool utilization, and verify the superiority of concise, dynamic-aware representations for tool-augmented LLM agents. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: CLUE-AI: A Collaborative Game-Based Learning Approach to Promote Critical Literacy for Uncovering Errors in AI
Abstract: As generative AI tools become embedded in educational practice, students must develop the skills to critically evaluate AI outputs. However, little empirical work has examined whether they can recognize and avoid incorporating problematic AI responses into their own work. We report results from a pilot study (N=30) investigating a collaborative digital game designed to develop critical AI literacy by teaching students to distinguish facts from AI misrepresentations and hallucinations. After gameplay, participants’ distinguishing ability improved significantly across repeated gameplay cycles (55.9% to 70.6%), and participants’ conceptual definitions of both hallucination and misrepresentation improved significantly from pre to post. Low-performing students benefited most from collaboration, showing significant learning gains following paired discussions. Title: Community Futures: Hybrid and Situated Critical AI Literacy
Abstract: “Community Futures” presents a hybrid digital-physical workshop framework for Critical AI Literacy (CAIL) through making, performance, and design futuring. Title: Operationalizing Adaptive Scaffolding: A State-Driven Design Framework for Hybrid Learning with Digital Teachers
Abstract: The emergence of virtual humans powered by Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) is reshaping educational practice. This paper introduces TeAIcher, an actionable framework supported by eight design guidelines (G1–G8) for creating and deploying digital teachers in online learning environments. We then instantiate the framework in two scenarios: (1) adaptive Socratic scaffolding for conceptual mastery and (2) step-by-step procedural guidance for technical tasks. We evaluate TeAIcher through a two-phase iterative study. Phase 1 comprises individual workshops with ten professional designers to assess the framework’s utility in design processes and to surface new pedagogical opportunities. Phase 2 is a user study with twelve learners examining pedagogical effectiveness and usability. Results indicate that TeAIcher delivers actionable, context-aware guidance that balances proactive support with learner agency. Title: Principled efficient triple-weighting for AUC-oriented imbalanced covariate shift
Abstract: Unlike traditional machine learning tasks under the independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumption, Covariate Shift (CS) tackles the learning problem where training and test (instance) marginal distributions differ while conditional distributions are the same. Further, datasets (or distributions) are often class-imbalanced in practice, where AUC is a widely adopted imbalance-aware evaluation metric. However, few works have investigated the problem of AUC-targeted imbalanced CS learning. In this work, we first provide a theoretical analysis of the ultimate learning goal, revealing key influencing factors. Inspired by the theoretical insights, we propose a new efficient triple-weighting method with univariate surrogate losses. Specifically, the proposed objective jointly incorporates three complementary weighting factors: the instance-level density ratio for correcting covariate shift, the class-wise average density ratios for aligning positive and negative sample contributions under the test distribution, and the imbalance-aware degree for alleviating class-prior bias. This design enables the model to optimize an AUC-oriented objective under the target distribution while avoiding the high computational cost of pairwise AUC losses. The proposed framework can be naturally instantiated with density-ratio-based covariate shift methods, such as static importance weighting and dynamic importance weighting. Theoretically, we provide favorable consistency and generalization guarantees. Finally, experimental results illustrate its effectiveness and robustness compared with related baselines. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced Medical Large Language Models: Challenges, Methods, and Future Directions
Abstract: The rapid emergence of large language models (LLMs) has significantly advanced biomedical text understanding and clinical information analysis. However, medicine is a highly knowledge-intensive domain in which knowledge is inherently relational, involving complex associations and hierarchical structures among diseases, symptoms, drugs, genes, and biological processes. Such knowledge is typically organized in large-scale biomedical knowledge graphs (KGs). Consequently, integrating structured biomedical knowledge with generative language models has become an important direction for developing reliable and interpretable medical AI systems. In this survey, we present a comprehensive review of knowledge graph–enhanced large language models for medical intelligence. We organize the existing literature through a pipeline-oriented framework consisting of three key components: knowledge graph construction, knowledge retrieval, and KG-LLM integration. Beyond providing a taxonomy of existing approaches, we further analyze the distinctive challenges of incorporating knowledge graphs into LLMs in the medical domain compared with general-domain settings, and summarize the corresponding strategies and techniques for improving factual grounding and credibility in medical LLM systems. Our survey aims to provide a systematic understanding of the current research landscape, offer actionable insights, and guide the future development of trustworthy knowledge-enhanced medical AI systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.
