Title: Toward Fair and Scalable Assessment of Socially Shared Regulation of Learning with Large Language Models
Abstract: Effective collaborative learning depends on learners’ ability to collectively regulate their learning processes through socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL). Despite its central role in collaboration quality and learning outcomes, SSRL remains challenging to assess due to its multidimensional, dynamic, and interactional nature. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer promising opportunities to automate discourse-based assessment, yet questions remain regarding their validity, robustness, and fairness across student populations. This study investigates the feasibility of using LLMs, specifically GPT-4o and GPT-5, to automatically code SSRL behaviors in collaborative discourse from a scenario-based science task, comprising 5830 student chat turns. Using a theory-driven coding framework, we compare LLM-based coding across prompt designs and model types, evaluate the consistency of LLM performance across underserved and non-underserved school contexts, and examine how SSRL behaviors differ between these student populations. Results show that LLM-based coding achieves strong agreement with human annotation, approaching human–human reliability, with context-enriched prompting yielding improved performance than general prompting. Importantly, LLM performance is stable across school contexts. Analyses further reveal meaningful differences in SSRL behaviors, with teams from an underserved school context demonstrating more cognitive information sharing behaviors, while teams from a non-underserved context engage more frequently in metacognitive planning and affective regulation. These findings highlight the potential of LLMs for scalable and equitable assessment of collaborative regulation and inform the design of responsible, adaptive AI systems that support collaborative learning for diverse learners. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Young AI Scientists in the New AI Age: Increasingly Early and Growing Dominance of Career Novelty in their Research Trajectories

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a core capability for achieving breakthrough innovation. However, it remains unclear how the degree of cross-domain exploration embedded in a scientist’s research output—termed Career Novelty—shapes long-term scientific success. To address this question, we employ a hypergraph computational framework integrating multidimensional indicators with predictive modeling to systematically examine how scholars’ interdisciplinary characteristics evolve across career stages and the evolutionary phases of AI, and how these dynamics relate to academic achievement. Using a RuleFit model, we identify interpretable rules that reveal structural shifts in the determinants of scientific success as technological paradigms evolve. Our results show that as AI has developed, the key rules for success have shifted from multifactor combinations located in the late career stage toward a concentrated focus on Career Novelty in the early career stage, marking a transition from multidimensional concurrency to early-stage concentration. Young scholars entering the field must enhance their cross-domain exploration early in their careers to thrive within an increasingly competitive and accelerated research environment. Title: Supporting Socially Shared Regulation Through Human-AI Collaboration in Pre-service Teacher Education
Abstract: Collaborative project-based learning (PBL) plays an important role in pre-service teacher education, yet it imposes substantial regulatory demands on novice teachers, who must coordinate tasks, negotiate roles, and align assessment criteria during group work. When curriculum artefacts such as lesson plans, project briefs, and assessment rubrics fail to make regulatory processes explicit, collaborative activity suffers from breakdowns in coordination, participation, and alignment. This exploratory study, grounded in socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) and distributed cognition, reports the initial analytic phase of a design-based research study examining how regulatory processes are represented in preservice teachers’ lesson plans. A qualitative document analysis of eight lesson plans identified three recurring gaps: underspecified task representations, the absence of monitoring checkpoints, and implicit role coordination. These findings suggest that collaborative breakdowns could be rooted in artefact design (lesson plans) rather than in learner interaction. The study refines a conjecture map linking these gaps to AI-mediated curriculum design. Generative AI serves as a design resource that externalizes regulatory structures through provisional artefacts. When AI-mediated artefacts are treated as provisional drafts open to collaborative critique, they can support clearer shared task representations, more consistent joint planning, and productive negotiation of roles. Secondary findings point to tensions around agency, authorship, and trust, which signal the importance of maintaining human control and transparency when integrating generative AI into pre-service teacher education. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Zhang S.; Xie Y.; Sun L.; Wu H.; Zhang L.
Title: Edge-Assisted KV-Cache Collaborative Loading for Split LLM Inference
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a new force and are now widely used in text generation, question answering, and code-related tasks. In long-context LLM inference, the KV cache generated during the prefill stage becomes very large and causes noticeable loading overhead. We have found a lack of research on the optimization of KV cache loading in the split LLM inference, so we design an edge-assisted KV-cache loading mechanism. This mechanism allows part of the KV-cache to be loaded by edge nodes and reduces cloud-side storage I/O overhead. During the inference, the loading tasks are distributed between edge and cloud nodes, and a lightweight scheduling strategy is used to balance workload. Experimental evidence shows that the collaborative loading mechanism reduces KV-cache loading latency under different cache sizes. Compared with the traditional cloud-only loading, this method achieves up to 44% improvement in overall inference performance. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: A mixed-method in-depth study of test-specific refactorings
Abstract: Unlike traditional refactorings, research on test-specific refactoring is limited. This paper presents a comprehensive catalogue of 57 test-specific refactoring types, out of which only 33 were previously documented in the literature. We have identified and classified those refactorings using a mixed-method approach grounded on three sources of data: a) Existing datasets of test-modifying commits, b) Monitoring of latest contributions to popular GitHub repositories, and c) Stack Overflow discussions. Our findings reveal that tools have limited support for test-specific refactorings. And, unlike the existing literature that mainly associates refactoring activity in tests with test smell resolution, test refactoring is driven by various motivations, such as improving test understandability, accommodating changes in production code, and test framework migration. Finally, we provide actionable implications for researchers and tool builders. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Park C.; Kim C.
Author full names: Park, Chanwoo (60012510900); Kim, Chanwoo (56141474800)
Title: LMMSE: A clinically inspired framework for cognitive evaluation of large language models
Abstract: AI is moving fast, but we still lack a broadly accepted, systematic way to evaluate the “cognitive” abilities of large language models (LLMs). We introduce the Language Model Mini-Mental State Examination (LMMSE), an early attempt to adapt the logic of clinical cognitive screening—originally built for assessing dementia and cognitive impairment—to the way LLMs actually behave. LMMSE profiles language, thinking, spatial perception, and reported humor appreciation rather than reducing them to a single score; the humor component measures reported appreciation only and does not by itself license claims about social cognition or Theory of Mind. We run standardized experiments across several state-of-the-art models (including GPT-5.2 and Gemini 3), fitting mixed-effects models to the individual ratings so that reliable differences are separated from run-to-run noise. These “cognitive” skills prove unevenly distributed: models excel in some areas while consistently struggling in others, most notably spatial perception. We propose LMMSE as a developer-facing diagnostic framework for profiling the cognitive-like strengths and weaknesses of LLMs, identifying limitations early and guiding future model improvements. To our knowledge, this is the first study to adapt clinical cognitive-impairment screening—anchored by the MMSE, a dementia-screening instrument—to LLMs, in contrast to prior work based on general-intelligence or knowledge benchmarks. The data and source code are publicly available at GitHub https://github.com/somno123/LMMSE. © 2026

Authors: Wang T.; Chen W.; Xue F.; Li J.; Liu H.; Ba X.; Xiao Y.; Sha Y.
Title: DFM-NC: Disentangling fine-grained multiplex non-literal cues for multimodal sentiment analysis
Abstract: Multimodal Sentiment Analysis aims to automatically infer the affective states conveyed by target individuals using heterogeneous data from multiple modalities, such as text, image, and speech. While existing works have achieved certain performance through advances in modal fusion and feature modeling, they still face two critical challenges: (1) Overlooking implicit non-literal cues. These cues are crucial for accurately capturing emotions, as emotional expression often relies on implicit signals that convey feelings beyond literal meaning. (2) Multimodal sentiment expressions often exhibit uncertainty and ambiguity. Most methods employ static or deterministic fusion strategies, which fail to handle such ambiguity adaptively. To address these challenges, we propose a Disentangling Fine-grained Multiplex Non-literal Cues Network (DFM-NC). First, we propose a Triple Non-literal Cue Module that interprets non-literal affective signals by extracting implicit indicators through language guidance, saliency attention, and probabilistic uncertainty modeling. Second, we propose an Uncertainty-Aware Non-literal Cue Fusion Module to mitigate the risk of overconfident misinterpretations. This architecture enables the system to simultaneously extract implicit affective features and dynamically estimate modality-specific latent uncertainty. Finally, we propose a multiplex feature fusion module to capture and synchronize diverse signals across all three modalities, ultimately yielding highly resilient sentiment representations. Extensive experiments on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI show that DFM-NC achieves competitive or improved performance across multiple evaluation metrics compared with recent strong baselines. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Rho J.; Karumbaiah S.
Author full names: Rho, Jihyun (57201718193); Karumbaiah, Shamya (57194788279)
Title: How Students Interpret Representational Cues in AI-Generated Educational Illustrations
Abstract: As generative AI systems are increasingly used to produce visual materials for educational contexts, students are more frequently encountering AI-generated illustrations that carry social and cultural meaning. While prior work has documented biases in AI-generated illustrations, less is known about how students interpret and reason about these representations when they appear in educational materials. This study examines how students make sense of social and racial cues embedded in AI-generated illustrations and how these interpretations relate to representational patterns in the images themselves. Using AI-generated illustrations derived from a children’s book excerpt, we conducted focus group interviews with 21 Latine undergraduate students to explore how students interpreted identity and social hierarchy in the images. Drawing on a perception-based analytic lens, we show that students actively identified visual contrasts, negotiated stereotypes against lived experiences, and reasoned about implicit social hierarchies rather than passively accepting the images as neutral. To contextualize these interpretations, we conducted a computational analysis of the AI-generated illustrations to characterize salient representational cues that students repeatedly referenced. This analysis revealed patterned visual differences in skin tone across characters occupying different narrative roles, which aligned with students’ interpretations of privilege and marginalization. Together, these findings highlight students’ interpretive agency when critically engaging with AI-generated illustrations and demonstrate how algorithmic representations can become objects of critical sense-making. We discuss implications for the design of educational experiences that support students in critically engaging with AI-generated educational materials. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Analyzing Middle School Students’ Dialogue and Behaviors During Collaborative AI Chatbot Development Using Ordered Network Analysis
Abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) education has become a key component of K–12 curricula, activities such as designing and developing conversational agents are increasingly used as instructional practice. Prior work has primarily examined these activities by focusing on students’ learning outcomes or the quality of final AI artifacts, offering limited insight into the collaborative processes through which learning unfolds during AI system development. Although the AIED community has a long history of studying collaborative learning in STEM and Computing education, the emergence of AI learning environments in which students build AI systems presents new opportunities to understand how collaboration unfolds in AI education contexts. Grounded in these foundational works, the current study examines collaborative interaction among middle school students engaged in the design and development of an AI chatbot. Using Ordered Network Analysis of students’ dialogue and development actions, we characterize how collaboration is organized over time and how interaction patterns relate to chatbot quality and AI knowledge outcomes. Results reveal that higher-quality chatbots are associated with more integrated sequences linking explanation, testing, and refinement. Interaction patterns involving articulated reasoning and repeated testing and revision in response to chatbot output were also associated with stronger AI knowledge outcomes. These findings provide a process-oriented account of collaborative AI chatbot development and extend AIED research on collaborative learning processes to AI education contexts. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Tang Z.; Ding A.; Wang W.; Zhou X.; Wang X.; Chen Q.; Zhang Y.; Chen H.
Title: TDRC: A Trend-Detail Reservoir Computing Framework for Model-Space Fault Diagnosis
Abstract: Time-series fault diagnosis (FD) requires extracting discriminative information from signals with complex temporal dynamics and limited labeled samples. Model-space learning offers an alternative perspective by representing signals through fitted dynamical models instead of raw observations. However, existing model-space approaches often rely on a single type of multi-scale expansion and may produce high-dimensional representations when multiple fitted models are directly used. To address these issues, this paper proposes a Trend-Detail Reservoir Computing framework (TDRC) for time-series FD. The method expands the original signal from two complementary perspectives: multi-scale pooling captures trend-scale dynamics, while recursive wavelet decomposition extracts detail-level information. Each expanded sequence is fitted by an Echo State Network, and the resulting readout weights are used as compact model-space representations. The concatenated readout weights are further reduced by principal component analysis for classification. Experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared with several baselines, particularly under limited-data conditions. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Real Estate Price Forcasting Using Random Forest Regression
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: Accurate real estate price prediction is a critical challenge in data-driven decision-making. This study explores the application of Random Forest Regression for real estate valuation, demonstrating its advantages over traditional predictive models. By effectively capturing complex, non-linear relationships among housing features, the model enhances prediction accuracy and robustness. Two experiments were conducted to analyze model optimization strategies. Experiment 1 investigated the impact of increasing the number of features in a predictor, revealing that more features do not necessarily improve accuracy. Experiment 2 examined the influence of hyperparameters on prediction performance, showing that increasing the number of trees had a greater impact on accuracy than adjusting tree depth or feature count. The results confirm that Random Forest Regression offers reliable performance on commercial real estate datasets. These findings highlight the model’s potential for real-world applications and suggest that future research should focus on hyperparameter tuning, feature selection techniques, and ensemble learning strategies to further refine predictive accuracy. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: MobileTestPro: A Real-World Evaluation
Abstract: This paper presents the validation of the MobileTestPro framework, a systematic, dimension-based approach to assessing the quality of mobile applications. The validation was conducted through an empirical case study involving three application contexts: video streaming, communication, and social media, using YouTube, WhatsApp, and Instagram as units of analysis. The framework assesses key quality attributes, including performance, usability, reliability, and resource consumption, under controlled testing conditions. Specific test cases were designed to simulate real-world scenarios, including variations in video resolution, message exchange processes, and user interaction patterns. Quantitative data were collected and analyzed to compare application behavior across the evaluated dimensions. The results demonstrate that MobileTestPro provides a consistent and replicable mechanism for evaluating mobile application quality. Furthermore, the framework facilitates the identification of performance issues and usability limitations. These findings confirm its effectiveness as a structured mobile testing tool. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: LADDM: A Flexible Tool for Log Anomaly Detection
Abstract: Log files keep track of everything that happens when services are used, and looking through them is important for finding any threats or problems that might come up because of mistakes. This paper looks at different cutting-edge ways to find log anomalies and presents a new one called LADDM (Log Anomaly Detection as a Docker Microservice). LADDM was made with a focus on the importance of logs at the enterprise level. To see how well it works, a synthetic dataset simulating enterprise logs was made. The solution is set up in a Dockerized environment, which makes sure it runs on its own and doesn’t depend on any other services. This approach not only highlights the importance of efficient log analysis in safeguarding enterprise operations but also demonstrates the practicality and scalability of containerized solutions in addressing security challenges. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: AI-Driven Personalized Symbol Generation for AAC Users: A Framework for Inclusive Communication
Abstract: Many traditional pictographic Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) symbol sets have been carefully designed with a focus on supporting language development. However, alongside these valuable resources, there is a growing need for symbol options that reflect wider cultural experiences and offer flexible ways to express identity, personal stories, and situations, particularly for people who have language but may have lost their voice. This paper aims to illustrate how generative artificial intelligence has the potential to produce personalized, pictographic symbols in designs that encompass both photorealistic and minimalist styles whilst being situationally specific. This type of symbol creation combines the use of text to image prompts with a series of trained symbol styles and hidden templates plus a chance to describe a specific culture. The goal was to enable users to be offered a set of improved AAC symbol choices for communication charts and other activities requiring symbolization. Initial feedback from an application usability survey indicated that Symbol Creator AI could be used without prior training. Further prompt data analysis showed that acceptable pictographic representation of users improved prompts was achieved, although additional development was required to collect more comprehensive outcome data and clarify where challenges emerged. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Enhancing Judicial Research Using a Pre-indexed Retrieval-Augmented Generation System
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: The paper outlines Smart Legal Document Search Engine for Judiciary, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system to locate structured, justified answers to a corpus of preindexed rubs (over 26,000) of Indian court judgements (1950–2025). It populates an offline Google drive dataset into the system, and that is processed by PDF parsing and OCR, legal aware chunking and dense embeddings and then bundled as a persisted FAISS based-vector index where there is external metadata to it. A Streamlit GUI facilitates retrieval with under 3 s latency using approximate nearest neighbors and is then elicited in a legal form to generate results based on priorities of future case summaries, issues, statutes, reason and results with respect to cited sources. The offline/online divide eliminates the processing overhead of its run time that makes it scalable and efficient. The structuring design options employed to obtain the chunk size specifications, retrieval hyperparameters and structuring of the swamp are determined in ways that are easy to understand and follow in law. Evaluation is quantified by retrieval measures (Recall@k). Results indicate that preindexing and structuring prompting are significantly more efficient so as to minimize hallucinations and latency and are trustworthy in the aspect of judicial search and review. Title: Making Money Understandable: Exploring Financial Literacy Needs of Persons with Intellectual Disabilities
Abstract: Objective: The primary aim of this study is to determine whether PWID require specific, accessible financial tools and to identify their specific issues related to the accessibility of financial services, money management, and financial literacy. This study focuses on the lived experiences of PWID, parents, and their caregivers in three European countries—Malta, Ireland, and Italy—to better understand everyday challenges and support needs. Hypothesis: PWID require accessible financial tools to improve their ability to interact with financial systems, increase independence, and deepen their financial understanding. Research Questions: What are the issues faced by PWID related to money management, financial services, and financial services? Do PWID need specific and accessible financial tools? Methodology: In this research, we collected structured feedback from PWID, parents, and their caregivers in Malta, Ireland, and Italy. The questionnaires were accessible and easy to read. The data collected were analysed using thematic analysis. Results: The results indicated that PWID face challenges with money management, difficulties understanding financial concepts, and difficulties accessing financial services. Most participants rely on caregivers, and financial education tools are not accessible or effective for PWID. The results suggested a need for simplified, visually supported, and user-friendly tools for PWID, along with approaches that incorporate real-life scenarios and caregiver involvement. Conclusion: This study shows the importance of developing inclusive and accessible financial literacy solutions. If we address existing barriers and design appropriate tools and support systems for PWID, we can enhance financial independence, reduce reliance on caregivers, and promote social and economic inclusion for PWID. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Supporting K-12 Teachers in the Presidential AI Challenge: A Case Study of a Faculty-Mentored Workshop for AI Tool Creation
Abstract: K-12 teachers are increasingly recognized as critical stakeholders in the design of AI technologies in education, necessitating a shift in their roles from passive consumers to active co-designers. The recent Presidential AI Challenge, established by U.S. national policy, provides educators with a unique situated learning opportunity to navigate this shift by engaging them in creating tangible AI artifacts. This paper presents a case study of a faculty-mentored workshop designed to support a team of three K-12 teachers who participated in this national competition. During an eight-week online workshop mentored by four university faculty, the teacher team developed “Math Mysteries,” a generative AI-powered, storytelling-based gamified platform for middle school mathematics learning. Analysis of pre- and post-workshop interviews reveals that the mentored design experience positively influenced the teachers’ AI literacy, self-efficacy, and perceptions of AI utility. These findings suggest that pairing high-stakes competitive challenges with structured university mentorship serves as an effective professional development model for empowering teachers to become AI creators. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Ben Sghaier O.; Weyssow M.; Sahraoui H.
Author full names: Ben Sghaier, Oussama (59663534000); Weyssow, Martin (57218143928); Sahraoui, Houari (57196894039)
Title: Balancing usefulness and naturalness: an LLM-based curation pipeline for code review comments
Abstract: Code review is a cornerstone of software development, where reviewers provide feedback through written comments to ensure code quality, maintainability, and correctness. The effectiveness of this process hinges on the quality of review comments: they must be clear, concise, actionable, and realistic enough to guide accurate code changes. As large language models (LLMs) gain traction in automating code review tasks, the utility of these systems is directly limited by the quality of the datasets on which they are trained. Unfortunately, existing code review datasets are often noisy, inconsistent, or poorly structured, which hinders the ability of LLMs to learn to generate accurate, helpful, and human-like review comments. To overcome these limitations, we propose two different curation pipelines designed to improve both the quality and the utility of large-scale code review datasets. In the first pipeline, all review comments are systematically reformulated by an LLM to improve their clarity, conciseness, and civility while preserving their semantic intent. The curated dataset resulting from this approach, called CuREV, offers cleaner, higher-quality, and easier-to-learn-from comments that lead to measurable improvements in downstream automation tasks, namely review comment generation and code refinement. Building on this, we propose an improved pipeline, guided by high-quality exemplars, that enhances the realism and diversity of curated review comments. This method first separates the dataset into high-quality (“good”) and low-quality (“poor”) reviews, based on a systematic quality assessment using an evaluation framework. High-quality comments are preserved in their original form and further used as in-context exemplars to inspire the reformulation of low-quality comments. By varying the exemplars provided, the reformulated comments are not only clearer and more actionable but also exhibit a broader range of writing styles, making them more realistic and human-like. The resulting dataset, called CuREV+, thus combines improved quality and utility with enhanced diversity of review comments. We evaluate both curated datasets using a comprehensive evaluation framework that assesses review comments along multiple quality dimensions (e.g., clarity, conciseness, civility, nature) as well as their impact on downstream code review tasks compared to the original dataset. In addition, we analyze the diversity of the curated datasets, CuREV and CuREV+. Our results show that while both approaches significantly enhance review comment quality and improve the performance of automated code review tasks, CuREV+ provides a more diverse dataset, enriched with broader vocabulary, varied lexical choices, and distinct writing styles. These findings demonstrate that curating datasets for code review requires not only refining quality but also balancing standardization with diversity. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Author full names: Cole, Carolyn (58536924300); Deschryvere, Matthias (55539475800); Ehsan, Toqeer (57214602093); Hajikhani, Arash (57105694200)
Title: From Policy Documents to Structured Survey Responses: Evaluating Large Language Models for Policy Monitoring
Abstract: Science, technology, and innovation policies are crucial for competitiveness, yet their diversity and scale make them difficult to map and monitor consistently. Existing approaches rely heavily on manual survey efforts, which are costly and challenging to scale across countries. Large language models (LLMs) enable new possibilities for extracting and structuring information from long and unstructured policy documents. This paper presents an application of LLMs as “AI respondents” for generating structured survey responses from policy texts. We develop a data extraction pipeline based on long-context in-context learning to map information from public web sources into predefined survey categories, including policy instruments, target groups, and thematic areas. The pipeline integrates a validation step using a secondary LLM to assess relevance and evidence, alongside comparisons with human-provided responses. Using a multi-country dataset, we evaluate the alignment between LLM-generated and human-generated outputs through overlap measures and cross-validation. Title: The Generalized Champollion Semantic System with the Logical Order Operator for the Interpretation of Conjoined Sentence
Abstract: In the field of artificial intelligence, accurately analyzing sentence semantics is crucial for many tasks, particularly in natural language processing. While Davidson event semantics offers an effective method for analyzing sentence semantics, it faces challenges when dealing with ambiguities in sentences combined with the logical word “and”, such as “John caught and ate a fish”. The ambiguity arises because it is unclear whether John ate the same fish he caught or a different one, due to the commutativity of “and”. Traditional event semantics are inadequate for addressing these ambiguities because they lack a consideration of event order. In this paper, we generalize the Champollion semantic system by the logical order operator, which resolves conflicts stemming from the commutativity of conjunctions by incorporating the logical order of events. We apply the generalized Champollion semantic system to existing research to demonstrate its potential for improving the accuracy of event semantics. Additionally, the generalized Champollion semantic system can help refine the interpretation of atomic events in sentences with “for-adverbial” clauses by preventing concurrent occurrences. © The Author(s) 2027.

Title: Kwame 2.0: Human-in-the-Loop Generative AI Teaching Assistant for Large Scale Online Coding Education in Africa
Abstract: Providing timely and accurate learning support in large-scale online coding courses is challenging, particularly in resource-constrained contexts. We present Kwame 2.0, a bilingual (English–French) generative AI teaching assistant built using retrieval-augmented generation and deployed in a human-in-the-loop forum within SuaCode, an introductory mobile-based coding course for learners across Africa. Kwame 2.0 retrieves relevant course materials and generates context-aware responses while encouraging human oversight and community participation. We deployed the system in a 15-month longitudinal study spanning 15 cohorts with 3,717 enrollments across 35 African countries. Evaluation using community feedback and expert ratings shows that Kwame 2.0 provided high-quality and timely support, achieving high accuracy on curriculum-related questions, while human facilitators and peers effectively mitigated errors, particularly for administrative queries. Our findings demonstrate that human-in-the-loop generative AI systems can combine the scalability and speed of AI with the reliability of human support, offering an effective approach to learning assistance for underrepresented populations in resource-constrained settings at scale. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Can language models persuade? Exploring the persuasive efficacy of Large Language and Vision Language models
Abstract: Persuasion has long been considered a unique human skill, rooted in emotion, context and intent. However, with rapid advances in communication technologies, particularly in Artificial Intelligence (AI), machines are beginning to replicate persuasive behaviour in more advanced ways. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into our daily lives, through virtual assistants and chatbots in areas ranging from customer service to healthcare consultations, a crucial question emerges: can language models not only inform but also persuade? Despite their widespread adoption, little is known about how effectively these models can influence human thinking, or how different prompting methods shape their responses. This paper presents an evaluation of state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in the domain of conversational AI. We assess seven LLMs and five VLMs by generating conversations based on gold-standard, human-written responses drawn from three persuasion datasets. Each model is evaluated using four distinct prompting techniques: zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting. Our goal is to analyse how these methods influence the models’ capabilities in generating persuasive responses. Both automatic and human evaluations are conducted to compare performance across models and prompting strategies. Our findings reveal that model architecture and prompt design significantly impact persuasive effectiveness. Among prompting strategies, few-shot prompting consistently produces strong results across models and tasks. While current models exhibit potential for generating persuasive dialogue, their effectiveness varies across domains. Structured prompting thus emerges as a vital factor for enhancing persuasive success in practical applications. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Who Benefits from LLM-Generated Learning Support Messages? Causal Evidence on Treatment Effect Heterogeneity
Abstract: This study examines the impact of LLM-generated learning support messages on learning outcomes in a large-scale open and distance learning course (N=28,833). Effects are estimated for the full randomized sample, among compliers, and across heterogeneous learner profiles. Assignment to the experimental group led to small but statistically significant improvements in course scores (0.60 points, p<.001) and final exam participation (1.9 percentage points). Effects were larger among learners who engaged with the messages (CACE=2.09 points on course scores). However, only 29% of treated learners interacted with the messages, indicating low compliance. Causal machine-learning methods reveal substantial heterogeneity in responsiveness. Model-based estimates suggest positive effects for approximately two-thirds of learners, particularly among those with moderate prior academic performance and among older age cohorts, with effects peaking around ages 34–40. No statistically significant effects are observed for final exam scores or for the measured engagement outcomes. The results indicate that the intervention affects learners differently and that targeted deployment based on learner profiles may be more effective than uniform exposure. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: IndoTaPas: ATaPas-based model for Indonesian table question answering
Abstract: Table Question Answering (TQA) has emerged as a vital paradigm for extracting insights from structured data. However, current advancements are predominantly centered on English, creating a significant disparity for low-resource languages like Indonesian. To bridge this gap, we introduce IndoTaPas, the first TaPas-based model specifically adapted for the Indonesian language. We pre-trained the model from scratch on 1.6M Indonesian text-table pairs and fine-tuned it on IndoHiTab, a newly constructed dataset comprising 2.8K question-table pairs featuring hierarchical structures and complex reasoning types. Experimental results demonstrate that IndoTaPas, employing a two-stage fine-tuning strategy, achieves an Exact Match (EM) score of 45.22%. This performance significantly outperforms most baselines, including neural semantic parsers, modern generative frameworks, and other zero-shot Large Language Models (LLMs), while remaining statistically comparable to the state-of-the-art Meta-Llama-3. Title: Snippet- and proposal-level discriminability modeling network for point-supervised temporal action localization
Abstract: Point-supervised temporal action localization (P-TAL) aims to identify and categorize action instances in untrimmed videos with only sparse temporal point annotations, which drastically cuts down the cost of manual annotation. Existing P-TAL approaches suffer from inadequate modeling of action, background and contextual information, leading to poor discriminability between action and background regions. This deficiency further causes frequent issues of instance merging and missing in localization results. To tackle these challenges, we propose a two-stage Snippet- and Proposal-Level Discriminability Modeling Network (SPDM-Net), which explicitly models and fuses discriminative features at both the snippet and proposal levels in a complementary manner. In the first stage, we model action and background semantics by integrating semantic prototypes with a lightweight gating mechanism, and capture multi-granularity temporal context through a dynamically weighted temporal pyramid to generate initial action proposals. In the second stage, we leverage proposal-level and contextual features to refine the temporal boundaries of proposals and optimize their confidence scores, while imposing explicit confidence penalties on background proposals to generate high-quality refined proposals. The synergistic interaction between snippet-level and proposal-level learning in SPDM-Net effectively alleviates the problems of instance merging and missing by enhancing the action-background discriminability throughout the entire localization process. Extensive experimental results on three widely used benchmark datasets (THUMOS14, GTEA and BEOID) demonstrate that our proposed SPDM-Net outperforms the state-of-the-art P-TAL methods by a significant margin, verifying its superiority in both localization accuracy and generalization ability. Title: Likelihood-Based Diagnosis with Generative Models: Confidence-Aware Measurement from Student Writing
Abstract: Generative modeling is rapidly reshaping student educational experiences, yet assessment still heavily relies on selected-response items like multiple-choice questions. A strong benefit of selected-response-based inference is its grounding in probabilities: beliefs about student skills are derived via likelihood functions relating student abilities to observed behavior. Inspired by this approach, we propose a method that leverages the likelihood computations of Large Language Models (LLMs) to produce analogous probabilistic judgments for student-written text. Specifically, we use an open-weight LLM to evaluate the likelihood of student-written text conditioned on contextual skill and misconception descriptions. Rather than generate new text or produce a rubric-based score, the LLM assigns conditional probabilities to observed student outputs. Inferences are made using posterior probabilities over conditioning statements, similar to latent class modeling. We illustrate the approach using student explanations to mathematics problems by comparing classifications to human labels. Early results show that accuracy on high-confidence predictions is competitive with zero-shot label generation from state-of-the-art models with orders of magnitude more parameters. In addition to providing classifications, our method produces a confidence signal computed from model likelihoods that is strongly correlated with classification accuracy, providing a principled route to educational measurement using free-response text. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: MoTE-Detox: Multi-dimensional Detoxification of Large Language Models via Mixture-of-Experts-Injected Dataset
Abstract: Mitigating toxicity in Large Language Models (LLMs) typically necessitates a trade-off between inference efficiency and control granularity. Existing decoding-time interventions offer precision but incur prohibitive computational costs, while dataset distillation methods provide universality but lack categorical granularity, relying on monolithic toxicity representations that lack nuance. In this paper, we propose MoTE-Detox (Mixture of Toxic-Experts Detoxification), a novel framework that fuses the precision of multi-expert ensembles with the efficiency of dataset distillation. Our approach introduces a two-stage paradigm: (1) We construct a Mixture of Toxic-Experts (MoTE), an ensemble of specialized models targeting distinct toxicity dimensions (e.g., identity hate, threats). (2) We propose Mixture-of-Experts-injected Contrastive Decoding, a distillation algorithm that aggregates fine-grained expert signals in the logit space to synthesize a compact, multi-dimensional detoxification dataset. This distilled dataset acts as a universal “detoxification patch,” transferable to any target LLM via standard fine-tuning. Experiments demonstrate that MoTE-Detox significantly outperforms single-signal baselines, reducing toxicity probability significantly while preserving downstream task performance (MMLU). MoTE-Detox effectively shifts the computational burden of MoE from inference time to an offline, one-time distillation phase. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: All Is Heard: Mitigating conformity bias via dual-branch collaboration in group recommendation
Abstract: Group recommendation aims to integrate members’ preferences for consensus-aligned recommendations. However, conformity bias often leads to a “pseudo-consensus” where active members dominate the aggregation process, suppressing the latent preferences of inactive members. To address this, we propose VAPrompt, a dual-branch collaborative framework that unifies member-level variational debiasing and group-level prompting consensus. Specifically, the member-level variational debiasing branch utilizes a variational hypergraph encoder and an efficient variational attention mechanism to capture member preference diversity and prevent active members from dominating the group representation. Furthermore, the group-level prompting consensus branch introduces a heterogeneity-aware prompt to guide a multi-view gating fusion mechanism, dynamically balancing contributions from different views to focus on the intersection of members’ real intentions. We evaluate the proposed method on four real-world datasets: Mafengwo, Mafengwo-S, Weeplaces-S, and CAMRa2011. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VAPrompt outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across all evaluation metrics. In particular, compared with the best baseline, VAPrompt achieves average improvements on the Weeplaces-S dataset, with gains of 18.26% in HR@10 and 16.84% in NDCG@10. Title: Immersive 3D Interface for Explainable Movie Recommendations
Abstract: Traditional recommender systems usually present recommendations by using static two-dimensional interfaces, that limits user exploration and often providing little insight into why items are suggested, that implies a lack of transparency in the system and reduces the users’ trustworthiness. In this work, we aim at improving both user exploration and transparency by means of an immersive virtual reality interface (VRI) and explainable movie recommender system that combines collaborative filtering, semantic recommendation, and local rule-based explanations within a unified three-dimensional environment. The proposed system combines a matrix factorization recommendation algorithm with BERT embeddings to generate both collaborative and semantic recommendations. To improve interpretability, LORE is incorporated as a post-hoc explanation module, integrated into the VRI, capable of generating local decision rules associated with recommended items. A further analysis of the recommendation outputs, in terms of coverage, diversity, and explainable model fidelity, is also performed. Title: Identifying High-Confidence Social Biases in LLMs for Trustworthy Conversational Tutoring Agents
Abstract: Conversational tutoring agents have been shown to improve learning engagement and student outcomes, and large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in these systems to provide scalable, personalized feedback. However, LLMs may perpetuate or amplify stereotypical social biases, posing particular risks in educational settings. In this study, we evaluate LLMs in conversational tutoring scenarios to identify high-confidence social biases, instances in which models fail to detect biased judgments while expressing strong confidence in their assessments, potentially affecting their reasoning and the feedback they provide to learners. Results indicate that bias detection is substantially more challenging in conversational tutoring contexts than in benchmark-based evaluations, and that state-of-the-art LLMs are overconfident in their incorrect assessments of stereotypical bias statements. Title: Automating Supportive Psychological Processes: How Source Attribution Shapes Perceived Empathy, Working Alliance, and Acceptability of a Supportive Conversational Agent
Abstract: As generative AI systems increasingly appear in supportive and self-regulatory contexts, understanding how users perceive affective qualities of human–AI interaction is critical for designing trustworthy AI-enabled learning environments. This study examined how source attribution (AI vs. human expert) shapes perceived empathy, working alliance, and acceptance of a supportive message attributed to a conversational agent. A randomized between-subjects design (N = 1,002) exposed participants to an identical standardized message labelled as AI- or human-authored. AI-labelled messages were rated as less empathic and relationally engaging than human-labelled messages. Acceptance-related outcomes were also lower, though AI support remained moderately acceptable for low-risk functions (e.g., reflection, psychoeducation). Positive attitudes toward AI increased acceptance, while privacy and responsibility concerns reduced it, especially for substitutive roles. Importantly, acceptance persisted for complementary, human-supervised uses. Findings indicate that attribution shapes relational and acceptance evaluations under minimal, non-interactive exposure. Although based on a single-message design, the results are relevant to AI-enabled learning environments where brief, text-based support is common. Title: APODigital: A Flexible Platform for Smart Surveys
Abstract: Digital data collection is shifting from web-based questionnaires to smart surveys that integrate respondent feedback with multimodal device data; existing platforms often lack the flexibility required for complex, context-aware research. Existing platforms focus on specific use cases but do not support a broad range of scenarios. This work presents APODigital, a configurable smart-survey platform that extends traditional digital questionnaires by collecting additional data, such as camera and GPS location data, and by providing user-interacting questions generated by generative AI. The system design goal was to create a platform with a high degree of flexibility for creating questionnaires, while remaining simple enough for non-technical users to design and deploy customized survey applications. In addition to conventional question types, APODigital supports advanced features such as camera-based inputs, grouped evaluations, ranking-based feedback, image classification, and generative AI-assisted workflows. The system supports the design and deployment of smart surveys for flexible use across diverse scenarios. To showcase this flexibility, we present three applications built on the same platform: two housing-related evaluations and one health survey application. We demonstrate the platform’s versatility through three distinct deployments: Meu Apê, a streamlined pilot involving 75 apartments; Como Você Mora?, a deep post-occupancy evaluation study with 246 participants; and a generic health questionnaire that showcases cross-domain reuse and the types of questions it supports. Title: MemoryPlayback: Leveraging Trajectory-Derived Priors for Robust Mobile GUI Execution

Abstract: Recent advances in large language models and vision language models have enabled the development of mobile GUI agents capable of performing multi-step tasks. However, existing approaches still struggle with long-horizon execution, where errors accumulate and lead to unstable task completion. A key limitation is the lack of effective mechanisms for reusing prior interaction experience. In this work, we investigate the use of historical user trajectories as executable memory for guiding GUI agent execution. Instead of treating trajectories as offline supervision or in-context examples, we operationalize them as reusable priors within the decision-making loop. To this end, we propose MemoryPlayback, a hybrid execution framework that integrates template-based action replay with VLM-based reasoning through a confidence-driven switching mechanism. This design enables efficient execution in stable scenarios while maintaining robustness under interface variations. To systematically evaluate the role of trajectory-derived knowledge, we construct a benchmark of 200 real-world mobile tasks and conduct both online and offline experiments on real devices. Beyond task success rates, we analyze step-level execution behavior, fallback patterns, and error distributions. Experimental results show that incorporating trajectory-level priors significantly improves execution stability, particularly in long-horizon tasks under UI perturbations. Title: Delineating Port Nautical Infrastructure Areas and Characterising Their Usage Based on AIS Data

Title: ArguMath: AI-Simulated Environment for Pre-service Teacher Training in Orchestrating Classroom Mathematics Argumentation
Abstract: Facilitating productive mathematical argumentation, especially asking rational questions, is essential yet remains challenging for pre-service mathematics teachers (PMTs), who often have limited opportunities to apply abstract theoretical knowledge in authentic practice. At the same time, recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have expanded the potential for simulating students in educational settings, enabling low-risk environments for instructional practice. To inform the design of a system that supports PMTs in orchestrating classroom argumentation, we conducted a formative study with eight experienced mathematics teachers to identify key design requirements, including personalization, realistic simulations, structured reflection, and ease of use. Building on these requirements, we developed ArguMath, an AI-simulated classroom environment that supports PMTs in practicing the orchestration of mathematical argumentation. ArguMath comprises three core components: (1) customization of classroom settings; (2) simulation of classroom discussions with AI-based students grounded in authentic transcripts and augmented with real-time instructional suggestions; and (3) structured reflection through discourse annotation and overall feedback. Title: Emerging Trends and Challenges Toward LLM Agents in Static Analysis
Abstract: Static analysis remains crucial for ensuring software reliability and security, yet it frequently struggles with false positives, rigid rule sets, and an inability to reason about semantic context. LLM-based agents show promise as a complement to traditional approaches by bringing autonomous reasoning and verification capabilities to the analysis pipeline. This paper introduces a taxonomy that organizes these agents along four key dimensions: architecture, integration patterns, grounding mechanisms, and application domains. Our framework captures how agents are structured, where they intervene in existing workflows, how they validate their outputs, and which tasks they address–from defect detection and code maintenance to security auditing. Title: A Laboratory Testbed for Benchmarking Orchestration Logic in Collaborative Environments
Abstract: The need for agile and decentralized supply chains, demanded by Industry 4.0, requires seamless integration among several Enterprise Information Systems. On this paper we present an architecture and laboratory exploration tool designed to test and benchmark orchestration algorithms within a collaborative environment. By conceptualizing the Enterprise Information Systems as digital representations of the ecosystem enterprises and using a modern context broker for synchronization, our laboratory tool acts as a decoupled orchestration architecture. We validate this tool through a First-Come, First-Served baseline algorithm and quantify the architecture performance via a set of laboratory experiments measuring the orchestration latency, throughput, fidelity and architecture resilience. The results demonstrate that our architecture provide a low-latency, scalable and resilient foundation for coordinating supply chains experiments, confirming the viability of the proposed transactional shared data model and offering a pathway for further tests with advanced planning algorithms in diverse industrial contexts. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: AI failures in the eyes of the downstream developer: a first look at concerns, practices, and challenges
Abstract: With the advancement of AI models, more software systems are adopting AI as a component to facilitate automation. Pre-trained models (PTMs) have become a cornerstone of AI-based software, allowing for rapid integration and development with lower training cost. However, their adoption also introduces failure modes such as data leakage and biased outputs, that may require careful handling by downstream developers. While previous research has proposed taxonomies of these technical concerns and various mitigation strategies, how downstream developers address these issues during the development of general AI-based software when reusing PTMs remains unexplored. Understanding downstream developers’ perspectives is essential because they directly influence how these potential failure concerns translate into practice, such as determining whether immediate risks like data leakage or model bias are recognised, mitigated, or inadvertently overlooked in real-world deployments. This study investigates downstream developers’ concerns, practices and perceived challenges regarding practical AI failures during the development of AI-based software. To achieve this, we conducted a mixed-method study, including interviews with 16 participants, a survey of 86 practitioners, and an analysis of 874 AI incidents from the AI Incident Database. Our results reveal that while developers generally demonstrate strong awareness of potential AI failures, their practices, especially during the preparation and model selection phases, are often inadequate. The lack of concrete guidelines and policies leads to significant variability in the comprehensiveness of their approaches throughout the development lifecycle, with additional challenges such as poor documentation and knowledge gaps, further impeding effective implementation. Based on our findings, we offer suggestions for AI model contributors, developers of AI-based software, researchers, and policy makers to enhance the integration of failure mitigation measures aimed at mitigating direct harms from AI failures. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Kim H.; Lee S.W.
Title: How users interpret AI-assisted reviews: Disclosure design and authenticity perceptions
Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly involved in digital content creation, disclosure messages play an important role in shaping how users interpret human–AI collaboration. Drawing on cue utilization theory, this study examines how two dimensions of AI disclosure—authorship dominance (human-centered vs. AI-centered) and AI role framing (logical, emotional, or integrity enhancement)—influence the perceived authenticity of online reviews across search and experience goods. A 2 × 3 × 2 mixed-factorial experiment was conducted with 272 Korean online shoppers. Linear mixed-effects analyses showed that human-centered disclosure produced higher perceived authenticity than AI-centered disclosure overall. However, AI role framing did not have a uniform main effect; instead, its influence depended on authorship dominance and product type. For search goods, human-centered disclosure enhanced perceived authenticity when AI was framed as supporting integrity, whereas for experience goods, this advantage emerged when AI was framed as supporting logical organization. No significant authorship-dominance difference was found under emotional-expression enhancement. Product-specific Bayesian mediation analyses further showed that disclosure configurations influenced purchase intention through perceived authenticity and platform trust, although the relative serial indirect effects differed across product types. For search goods, all comparison conditions produced lower serial indirect effects than the human-centered integrity-enhancement condition, whereas for experience goods, a significant difference emerged only for the AI-centered logical-enhancement condition. These findings demonstrate that AI disclosure functions as a set of interdependent interpretive cues through which users infer human agency, the nature of AI involvement, and the authenticity of AI-assisted reviews. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Early-warnings of critical transitions emerging from network hierarchies
Abstract: Societal systems are inherently vulnerable to abrupt, large-scale transformations, including financial crises and trade disruptions, driven by critical transitions that are difficult to predict. Although model-based early-warning indicators have been developed, their effectiveness is often constrained by system-specific assumptions, limiting their applicability to empirical social systems. This study proposes a model-free, data-driven Network Hierarchical Marker (NHM) framework that extracts early-warning signals (EWS) from temporal network hierarchies without requiring explicit system-specific governing equations, parameter identification, supervised training, or predefined crisis labels for the underlying socio-economic dynamics. Applied to international trade networks, NHM identifies warning signals associated with major disruptions in global trade, while revealing vulnerable commodity categories and geographic regions that contribute to systemic fragility. These results suggest that hierarchical network organization can serve as an interpretable structural marker for identifying increasing systemic fragility before or around critical transitions in complex socio-economic systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Exploring Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Approaches with Large Language Models in Cybersecurity Contexts
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: The objective of this work is to explore the relation between typical Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) algorithms and the potentiality of Large Language Models (LLMs) to classify and predict in the context cybersecurity environments, in particular, in network-based anomaly detectors in user profiles, benign and malicious traffic flows, including Denial of Service (DoS), large-scale attacks in Internet-of-Things (IoT) environment, malware memory analysis attack, network intrusion detection systems and in Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) security solutions. First, using open-source tools for AI/ML we explore exhaustively four benchmarking datasets and create several classification models for each one using Decision Trees (DT), Random Forest (RF), Gradient boosting and others. We evaluate the models using standard metrics, ensuring high accuracy relative to the specificity of each dataset. These models are typically used to classify and predict new cases. However, recognizing the efficiency of these algorithms in handling tabular data and for predicting as well as the potentialities of LLMs, we propose to convert a DT and RF tree in rules and knowledge from the AI/ML models into prompts and feed them into the LLMs, aiming to enhance their performance to classify and predict new cases. We compare and achieve high performance in terms of accuracy using the AI/ML approaches with the ChatGPT, Gemini and Ollama. With this hybrid view and the promising results of both approaches we create an instrumental tool to elucidate the predictions to prevent new cases in the context of cybersecurity environments. To foster further research in this context the datasets, code, benchmark, and pretrained models are available on the GitHub open-source repository. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: From Traditional AWE to AI-Aided Learning: Enhancing EFL Nursing Students’ Writing Through a Multi-feedback Model
Abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of a Multi-Feedback Model applied to EFL nursing students’ writing development, bridging the transition from traditional Automated Writing Evaluation (AWE) systems to AI-aided learning environments. Conducted in a Taiwanese junior nursing college, the study addresses the persistent gap in writing proficiency among EFL learners in junior colleges, who often demonstrate comparatively lower writing proficiency in writing compared to other language skills. While traditional AWE systems provide surface-level corrections in grammar and mechanics, their limited adaptability, lack of contextual awareness, and one-size-fits-all feedback have limited their pedagogical effectiveness in supporting deeper writing development. In response, this study proposes a progressive shift toward AI-aided AWE, integrating artificial intelligence as an adaptive feedback facilitator capable of offering real-time, personalized, and discourse-level writing support. The research integrates an AI-enhanced version of the ATPR feedback cycle—comprising (A) AI-generated preliminary feedback, (T) teacher’s summary commentary supported by AI analytics, (P) peer collaborative feedback augmented by AI scaffolding, and (R) refined AI feedback after student revisions. The model not only reduces teacher workload but also promotes learner autonomy, metacognitive awareness, and deeper engagement with writing as a communicative process. Students participated in writing tasks designed around real-world internship scenarios and workplace communication needs, with genre-specific support integrated into the AI system. The AI-aided model contextualizes writing support, fosters process-oriented learning, and cultivates reflective revision practices. Findings suggest that this transition enables more nuanced, responsive, and effective writing instruction in EFL contexts, paving the way for smart, AI-integrated educational ecosystems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Multi-domain Embodied Intelligence Training and Testing Scenarios: A Unified Framework, Design Language, and Multidimensional Conformation
Abstract: Embodied intelligence, a cutting-edge field, relies heavily on high-quality training and testing scenarios, which are crucial for agent applicability and robustness. Designing such scenarios efficiently is a key challenge. Current languages often fail to meet multifaceted needs like systematic design, diversity, and cross-domain compatibility. To address this, we propose a unified mathematical framework based on fiber bundle theory and a supporting design language. The framework uniformly models environments, tasks, systems, and events, offering four core strengths: 1) Unification & Universality​ for a concise description of infinite scenarios; 2) Intrinsic Consistency, using structural groups to ensure physical and logical validity; 3) Operability, enabling scenario transformation and composition; and 4) Analyzability, providing geometric invariants for difficulty assessment. The instantiated design language further enables: 1) Recursive Modular Design​ for complex task building; 2) Goal-Driven Automated Generation​ from high-level constraints; 3) Computable Scenario Metrics​ to quantify challenge; and 4) Ecosystem Compatibility​ via a cross-platform intermediate representation. This work establishes a formal, extensible foundation for constructing, analyzing, and evaluating embodied intelligence scenarios, supporting efficient testing and a standardized scenario ecosystem. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Scaffolding Epistemic Agency: Evaluating AI-Partnered Affective Feedback for Emotional Regulation in Knowledge Building
Abstract: Epistemic emotions such as enjoyment, confusion, and boredom are critical in knowledge building, shaping learners’ engagement and persistence during conceptual uncertainty. However, capturing these emotions in authentic learning contexts remains challenging, limiting empirical understanding of how emotions mediate collaborative knowledge construction. This paper reports the use of EmoSense, a novel emotion-aware AI system, to investigate students’ epistemic emotions during student Knowledge Building Design Studio (sKBDS) activities in K–12 environments. EmoSense integrates multimodal facial features with self-reports to provide affective feedback during collaborative inquiry. Rather than positioning AI as an autonomous classifier, EmoSense is designed as a human-centered tool supporting reflection, co-regulation, and sensemaking. A theory-informed rule-based inference system operationalizes epistemic emotion constructs, enabling interpretable alignment between theory and observed activity. Analysis of 575 pilot data sets indicates a substantial level of agreement between student self-reports and AI detections (kappa = 0.70), suggesting context-specific, rule-based approaches are viable for “cold-start” deployment in local K-12 settings. Beyond detection accuracy, lag sequential analysis suggests the system functioned as a protective scaffold, with the AI feedback significantly inhibiting confusion transitions to boredom (Z = −1.99, p <.05). With EmoSense, students can actively validate or contest AI feedback, fostering human-AI co-regulation. These interactions are essential for building datasets reflecting local affective expressions, facilitating the transition toward large-scale models natively trained on collaborative K-12 discourse. By centering the human experience, this paper demonstrates how AI functions as both a research instrument and pedagogical partner to empower students as active partners in knowledge building and emotional growth. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Multi-RAG: A Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Adaptive Video Understanding
Abstract: To effectively engage in human society, the ability to adapt, filter information, and make informed decisions in ever-changing situations is critical. As intelligent agents become more integrated into human life, there is a growing opportunity–and need–to offload the cognitive burden on humans to these systems, particularly in information-rich scenarios. To fill this need, we present Multi-RAG, a multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system designed to provide adaptive assistance to humans in information-intensive circumstances. Our system aims to improve situational understanding and reduce cognitive load by integrating and reasoning over multi-source information streams, including video, audio, and text. As an enabling step toward long-term human-computer partnerships, Multi-RAG explores how multimodal information understanding can serve as a foundation for adaptive assistance in dynamic, human-centered situations. To evaluate its capability in a realistic human-assistance proxy task, we benchmarked Multi-RAG on the MMBench-Video dataset, a challenging multimodal video understanding benchmark. Our system achieves superior performance compared to existing open-source video large language models (Video-LLMs) and large vision-language models (LVLMs), while utilizing fewer resources and less input data. The results demonstrate Multi-RAG’s potential as a practical and efficient foundation for future human-in-the-loop systems in dynamic, real-world contexts. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Agentic SABRE: An uncertainty-aware neuro-symbolic multi-agent framework for adaptive ransomware detection
Abstract: Ransomware has evolved into a complex, adaptive, and fast-moving adversary category in which static signatures and monolithic classifiers fail to generalise under concept drift, evasion, and behavioural polymorphism. In this paper we present Agentic SABRE (Semantic-Behavioural Arbitration for Ransomware Evaluation): an uncertainty-aware, neuro-symbolic, multi-agent framework for adaptive ransomware detection. SABRE fuses semantic (representation-based) and behavioural (time-window forensic telemetry) evidence, and employs Monte Carlo Dropout inference to quantify epistemic uncertainty for each agent.We introduce a decision-layer orchestrator that performs risk- and uncertainty-aware triage via two interpretable thresholds: a risk score τ and an uncertainty budget κ. High-confidence, high-risk samples are automatically contained, while uncertain or borderline cases are escalated to human analysts, establishing a flexible computational contract between autonomous response and analyst oversight. To support auditability and trust, SABRE integrates post-hoc explainability mechanisms including gradient saliency, permutation importance, and counterfactual analysis, enabling both local and global interpretation of agent decisions.Extensive evaluation on RDset and RanSMAP demonstrates that Agentic SABRE preserves perfect discrimination on saturated semantic datasets (AUC (Formula presented) ) while improving robustness under weak behavioural signals, achieving up to a 4.9% relative reduction in false escalations at equal recall and maintaining calibrated predictive uncertainty. Counterfactual analysis further shows that semantic and behavioural decisions can be flipped with bounded perturbation cost, indicating stable and interpretable decision boundaries. Overall, Agentic SABRE is not merely a higher-accuracy detector but an agentic cyber-defence system that combines uncertainty-aware automation, explainable reasoning, and adaptive triage under evolving ransomware threats. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Exploring the Effect of GAI in VR-Based Learning
Abstract: While Virtual Reality (VR) provides highly immersive environments for self-regulated learning, the lack of real-time human guidance often leaves learners susceptible to excessive cognitive load and social isolation. Traditional VR feedback mechanisms, which are predominantly static and unidirectional, struggle to provide adequate psychological and cognitive support. This study investigates the effectiveness of integrating a Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) voice assistant to enhance learners’ basic psychological needs, intrinsic motivation, and academic performance in a VR embedded systems course. A randomized controlled trial was conducted with 62 university students, who were randomly assigned to either an experimental or a control group. The experimental group interacted with a real-time, dynamic GAI voice tutor, while the control group received traditional, preset feedback. The results revealed that the experimental group demonstrated significantly higher levels of autonomy (p <.05), competence (p <.01), and relatedness (p <.001) compared to the control group. Furthermore, the GAI voice assistant significantly boosted learners’ intrinsic learning motivation (p <.01) and, after controlling for prior knowledge, significantly improved their post-test scores (p <.05). These findings indicate that by synergizing dynamic cognitive scaffolding with anthropomorphic emotional support, GAI voice tutors effectively fulfill learners’ basic psychological needs. This fulfillment acts as a crucial psychological buffer, transforming learners’ cognitive appraisals of technical challenges, and ultimately driving sustained growth in learning motivation and academic achievement within immersive learning environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Designing Scenario-Based Tasks for Assessing AI Literacy
Abstract: As AI systems become increasingly embedded in educational activity, there is a growing need for assessment tasks that capture how AI literacy is enacted during AI-supported work, rather than through decontextualized self-reports or isolated judgments. This paper presents a scenario-based assessment task designed to elicit evidence of learners’ AI literacy through extended, goal-directed interaction with an AI chatbot. The task unfolds across multiple phases that vary in use of scaffolding, the role of AI, and the associated risks, creating opportunities for learners to evaluate AI output, verify information, and reason about responsible use. To examine how these design choices function in practice, we conducted cognitive lab interviews with 15 high school students, analyzing think-aloud data to understand how learners reasoned, strategized, and adapted to challenges during the task. Drawing on these findings, we articulate four design patterns that address challenges in AI literacy assessment, including how to calibrate AI use, surface limitations with AI, support open-ended workflows, and elicit ethical reasoning. Title: The Effects of AI-Generated Bilingual Picture Books on Enhancing Reading Interest and Learning Outcomes
Abstract: With the rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, the field of education has increasingly integrated AI into teaching to enhance learners’ interest and learning outcomes. Traditional bilingual teaching materials are predominantly text-based and often lack visual support and interactivity, which may affect students’ learning motivation and language comprehension. This study aims to investigate the effects of AI-generated images in bilingual picture books on second-grade elementary school students’ reading interest and learning outcomes. This study adopted an experimental design, in which participants were divided into an experimental group and a control group. The experimental group learned using bilingual picture books incorporating AI-generated images, while the control group used traditional bilingual picture books. Pre-test and post-test analyses were conducted using a reading interest scale and learning achievement tests to evaluate learning effectiveness. The results indicated that the use of bilingual picture books with AI-generated images significantly enhanced students’ reading interest and learning motivation and had a positive impact on their learning outcomes. The findings provide empirical evidence supporting the application of AI technologies in education and offer valuable implications for the design of bilingual teaching and digital learning materials. However, the participants in this study were limited to second-grade elementary school students. Future research may expand to learners of different age groups or language backgrounds to examine the applicability of AI-generated bilingual picture books across diverse populations. In addition, future studies are recommended to incorporate qualitative research methods to gain deeper insights into learners’ experiences and learning processes when using AI-generated picture books, thereby further optimizing instructional design and teaching strategies. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.
